articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake
articles.summary: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.

Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.

blocks.caption: Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal border

blocks.text: More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.caption: Sludge inundates homes after flash floods in Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.
after newsletter promotion
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.
In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”
The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: A creative journey for a cause
articles.summary: Art can offer more than something to look at. For the artists participating in “Journeys,” it is also a way to help give underprivileged children an alternative outlet through free art workshops.…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Arts and Culture
'Journeys' showcases works by established and emerging Filipino artists, with proceeds supporting free art workshops for underprivileged children
Art can offer more than something to look at. For the artists participating in “Journeys,” it is also a way to help give underprivileged children an alternative outlet through free art workshops.

Organized by Erehwon Art Foundation Inc. in cooperation with Art Lounge Manila (ALM), the fundraising exhibition brings together established and emerging Filipino visual artists, with proceeds from the sale of their works going toward free art workshops for children from disadvantaged communities. The initiative aims to provide them with a creative outlet while steering them away from violence.
The exhibition features works by National Artist nominee Luis “Junyee” Yee, modern sculptor Julie Lluch, and Filipino printmaker Pandy Aviado, alongside works by a younger generation of artists.

articles.title: Jumping beans: UK shoppers turn to legumes to save cash and improve diet
articles.summary:
Sales of beans, lentils and soya bean derivatives on rise while Britons buy less real and fake meat

British shoppers are munching more beans, lentils, tofu and tempeh – while cutting back on…

blocks.text: British shoppers are munching more beans, lentils, tofu and tempeh – while cutting back on real and plant-based fake meat – to save money and improve their diet.

The amount of beans, pulses and soya bean derivatives sold in the UK increased by 7.3% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, led by a rise in cheap dried lentils, an analysis has found.
That was led by a 23% surge for cheap dried lentils, according to data from the market research firm NielsenIQ evaluated by the climate advocacy group Madre Brava.
Shoppers turned to more upmarket legumes, including organic and jarred varieties, with sales of canned and jarred butter beans up by 30.3%.
That growth was partly driven by new products and brands – such as the Bold Bean Co, Navarrico and Marks & Spencer’s own-label – as well as recipes going viral on social media.

Baked beans, once the titans of the supermarket tinned section, initially appeared to have become has-beens in the frenzy, with 1.2% fewer cans sold – but the decline is actually down to a drop in cans also containing sausages.

Fake meats, once seen as the future of vegetarian and vegan diets, also continue to fall out of favour, with 4.3% fewer packages sold. The decline was down to sales of textured soya, pea and wheat protein products, which offset a renewed growth in mycoprotein – sold under the brand name Quorn.

“Shoppers are not abandoning plant proteins – they’re shifting toward simpler, higher-fibre foods, whose prices are rising more slowly than food inflation, widening the price gap with meat,” the Madre Brava report said.
“This indicates that, while food inflation and affordability remain key factors, nutrition and health benefits are also driving purchasing decisions.”

Amid high inflation of meat prices, especially for beef and lamb, in recent years the amount sold by retailers fell by 1.8% year on year according to Madre Brava’s analysis of Euromonitor International data.

The evidence of changing diets comes after the launch of the Bang in Some Beans campaign kicked off last year – led by celebrity chefs including Jamie Oliver and Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall and supermarkets – aiming to double UK bean consumption by 2028.
after newsletter promotion
That steps up a longer-term push by campaigners for people to include more legumes – which are healthier and more environmentally friendly than meat – in their diets.

Chloe MacKean, the food business transformation manager at the Food Foundation, said: “We aren’t surprised to see the rise in bean sales. Beans are a triple win for health, sustainability and our wallets.
“They are a healthy and affordable protein source, high in fibre and emit far fewer greenhouse gas emissions than animal protein.”

She said large food companies were also aware of the commercial opportunities of beans, and 29 companies, including Sainsbury’s, Lidl GB, M&S, Subway and Harvester, had all made commitments through the Bang in Some Beans campaign to sell more.

Lidl set a target in 2025 to increase the share of plants as a proportion of its overall protein sales as part of its sustainability objectives. The cut-price chain’s introduction of new products including flavoured tofu has driven a 694% rise in sales of all plant-based foods compared with 2020.

articles.title: Ombudsman orders Legarda, son to answer plunder complaint
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered Senator Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas First District Rep. Leandro Leviste, to answer the plunder and graft complaints against them over the alleged…

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 6:04pm
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered Senator Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas First District Rep. Leandro Leviste, to answer the plunder and graft complaints against them over the alleged failure of Leviste’s firm to provide solar power as provided under its congressional franchise, Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said.
At the same time, Clavano questioned Legarda's extended medical leave due to a serious illness as announced by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
“There was already an order to file a counter-affidavit,” Clavano said.

“Kung talagang meron siyang serious illness, sana isa lang po yung hiningi niya na medical leave, hindi yung pa-extend-extend. And that is the only reason why the Office of the Ombudsman had to flag that type of pattern. If you are out of the country, it adds to the speculation or adds to the suspicion of the Office of the Ombudsman,” Clavano added.
Other Stories
Clavano said that it behooves any individual to stay put in the country if they are already facing investigation.

“Electricity prices went up due to unfulfilled promises of that franchise, and a lot of the allocations for solar power were given to this company, and yet they were not able to deliver. The public is feeling the brunt of their decision,” Clavano said.
“Sana po ay manatili muna kayo dito sa bansa para po medyo maliwanagan po tayo doon sa nangyari at maliwanagan din ang taong-bayan sa katotohanan,” Clavano added.

Ahead of the Ombudsman investigation, the Department of Energy (DOE) already filed a complaint against Leviste and five officials of the Solar Para sa Bayan Corporation (SPBC) for alleged violations of the Public Service Act before the Justice Department.

In an earlier statement on the Ombudsman investigation, Legarda said, "All my public life since 1998, I have always upheld my integrity, which I value dearly. This baseless allegation is a smear on my person that is totally undeserved."

“We have not received any communication from the Office of the Ombudsman regarding the reported preliminary investigation, but I can categorically state that the reported accusations are utterly false and baseless. No public funds were involved. We are prepared to bring out the truth,” she added.
Legarda urged the public to be discerning, “especially in light of the timing and nature of these allegations.”
She has been on medical leave since August 3. She extended her leave up to the first week of September.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘This whole thing’s a farce’: New Orleans Catholic church sex abuse settlement brings anger and shock
articles.summary:
Survivors begin receiving letters with payment amounts months after $305m settlement agreement was struck

Survivors of child rape and other
articles.byline: Ramon Antonio Vargas and David Hammer of WWL Louisiana in New Orleans

blocks.text: Survivors of child rape and other sexual abuse within New Orleans’s Roman Catholic archdiocese learned that $641,000 or so is the most they can individually get under a settlement approved in December to resolve a years-long bankruptcy protection case.

Those amounts were communicated in letters that hundreds of clergy abuse survivors participating in the New Orleans archdiocese’s bankruptcy began quietly receiving on Tuesday. The figures are well below a $2.4m jury verdict awarded to an unrelated Louisiana religious sexual abuse claimant in June 2025 after the state’s legislature temporarily eliminated filing deadlines for such cases.

The amounts cited in the recent letters were also substantially below out-of-court settlements that a handful of clergy abuse survivors in the New Orleans area have reached in the verdict’s aftermath with Catholic institutions not affected by the bankruptcy, which evidently have been more or less comparable to the jury award.

Survivors say the amounts in the letters aren’t just insulting – but also the latest evidence of the disproportionate advantage enjoyed by the more than 40 Catholic institutions that have gone to federal court to declare amid the financial fallout of the church’s worldwide clergy molestation scandal, including nearly 30 such groups that have settled.

“This whole thing’s a farce,” Aaron Hebert, who was abused by Lawrence Hecker, a late, convicted child rapist and longtime archdiocesan priest, said on Thursday. Richard Coon, who has testified to being molested by three men with links to the archdiocese, added: “There’s a lot of survivors that are hurting right now.”

Driving the despair which Coon and Hebert described are two elements: the $305m settlement that the archdiocese as well as its insurers on 8 December agreed to pay to clergy abuse survivors to resolve a bankruptcy protection case opened in 2020; and a zero- to 100-point system determining each individual victim’s payment.

Settlement disclosure documents that disgusted victims virtually from the outset detail how points would be assigned based on the nature of the abuse, among other elements. Rape, for instance, equated to 75 points within the system; oral or digital abuse was 56 units; and grooming behavior was five.

Additionally, the archdiocese and others made comments in open court promising payments by the end of spring 2026. The process instead dragged, with settlement trustee Don Massey filing motions in court to get the church to turn over records needed to make payment determinations.

“Any promises made by the debtor (the archdiocese and its affiliates) were not made by the settlement trust,” Massey said when asked about payments not yet having been doled out. “The settlement trust was not consulted by the debtor prior to making this uninformed promise.”

By Thursday, days after the abuse claims valuations concluded, the Guardian and reporting partner WWL Louisiana had confirmed the maximum 100-point payout equated to an “estimated distribution” from the settlement of $641,425.64. That meant each allocated point was worth $6,414.26.
Hebert shared his letter with the outlets. He had been awarded 56 points – or an estimated settlement distribution of $359,198.

Meanwhile, having endured rape and oral sexual abuse by multiple clergy predators, Coon was allocated 98 points. He said it was “shocking” that he did not get maximum points given the circumstances surrounding his claim.

Coon, Hebert and bankruptcy claimant Brian Manix all expressed disbelief that allocation letters given to survivors failed to break down precisely how the claims evaluator, personal injury attorney Richard Arsenault, arrived at their points total. The missives just contained the final sum, the estimated settlement distribution, and an acknowledgment that the bankruptcy may have required them “to revisit deeply personal and difficult experience”.
Survivors have 30 days to ask for reconsideration, but without the basis for the points total, they’re left to guess why they didn’t receive what they expected.

“We asked … for that,” Manix said on Thursday. While he declined to publicly disclose his allocation, he confirmed he was not awarded maximum points, saying, “I was raped. I was made to give oral sex, and I was groomed … I need somebody to tell me … what’s missing.”
Arsenault did not respond on Thursday to a request for comment.

Sources familiar with the process say more than 800 abuse claims were given points allocations. Among them were more than 100 which got scores of zero – such as for claiming abuse by a predator or entity not affiliated with the archdiocese.

Furthermore, the sources said that about $56m from the settlement was being held back for a time to account for successful appeals. And any remaining money held back would then be redistributed to survivors based off their points allocations.

Still, that provided little comfort to Coon, Hebert, Manix and other survivors with whom they said they spoke in recent days. Perhaps most frustratingly for them, survivors who challenge their allocations must pay $1,000 out of pocket, according to a protocol established in December and which the vast majority of claimants approved.

Attorney Richard Trahant, who is part of a legal team representing Coon, Hebert, Manix and roughly 80 other abuse claimants in the New Orleans archdiocese’s bankruptcy, said a number of his clients would appeal their points and dollar amounts.
“The $1,000 fee for reconsideration of the point total is obnoxious,” Trahant also said. “And we will figure out how to address that in the coming days.”

Coon, Hebert and Manix said such factors combined to convince them that bankruptcy court was the wrong venue to be fairly compensated for their abuse – despite assertions by the archdiocese that it was the venue providing the most equitable solution.
As Coon put it: “The bankruptcy was all about protecting the church.”

articles.title: Trump official faces inquiry over claims he diverted wildfire resources to his own property
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Michael Boren, a senior official overseeing the US Forest Service, is accused by Democratic senators of ‘inappropriate interference’

Donald Trump’s administration…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s administration is facing calls to launch an investigation into allegations that Michael Boren, a senior official who oversees the US Forest Service, pressed agency staff to deploy additional resources to fight a fire burning near his Idaho ranch.

Three Democratic senators accused Boren of “inappropriate interference” in a letter seen by the Guardian, demanding answers from Brooke Rollins, US agricultural secretary. Boren serves as undersecretary of agriculture for natural resources and environment.

Senators Ron Wyden, Amy Klobuchar and Martin Heinrich expressed “serious concern” over reports that Boren used his federal government position in July to remove firefighting personnel and resources from active fires elsewhere to tackle a fire near his private ranch in Idaho.

“We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response,” they wrote.

Their letter follows a report from the Washington Post earlier this month, in which several forest service officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that Boren – who reportedly owns a 480-acre ranch in the Sawtooth national recreation area – contacted forest service officials multiple times in mid-July to question why more aircraft were not being used to fight the Cabin Creek fire in Idaho, which spread across several acres in Idaho’s Sawtooth national forest.
The fire began on 12 July, as a result of an unattended campfire and was 100% contained by 15 July. It reportedly ultimately burned seven acres.

Six current and former forest service officials described the response to the fire to the Post as greater than would typically be expected for a fire of that size, which posed no significant threat to life or property. Communications reviewed by the Post also reportedly confirmed that Boren personally contacted forest service staff about the fire.
The USDA did not respond to a request for comment on the senators’ letter.

In a statement last month to the Guardian responding to the initial report, a USDA spokesperson said Boren “is expected to have regular contact with the agencies he oversees” and the “fact that a senior government official would be monitoring and communicating with other government officials about an event he oversees is a non-story”.

“Undersecretary Boren did report a fire that was near property he owns, just as one would hope any citizen in an area under threats from wildfires would do,” they said. “However, at no point did he pressure leadership or order more resources to fight this or any other fire.”

In the letter from the Democratic senators, sent on Thursday, they wrote that “during this record setting fire season, fires of much larger size have not received even a fraction of the same commitment of resources”.
“The personal interests of political employees should not be a factor that influences the allocation of wildfire resources to communities threatened with devastation,” they added.

They argued that Boren’s reported “actions constitute potentially a misuse of taxpayer funds and put American families at further risk by diverting scarce resources from high-priority wildfires threatening communities elsewhere in the region and country”.

“Political interference in wildfire response jeopardizes lives, property and federal resources,” they wrote. “We request that you respond by September 10th detailing how the Department will prevent this type of inappropriate interference, or even the appearance of it, in wildfire response going forward.”

articles.title: Healey’s budget to duck setting a date for 3% defence spending target
articles.summary:
Roadmap for increasing department’s share of GDP will be deferred until next year’s review

The chancellor will delay setting out when the UK will meet the target of allocating 3% of GDP on…

blocks.text: The chancellor will delay setting out when the UK will meet the target of allocating 3% of GDP on defence until next year’s spending review, the Treasury has confirmed.

John Healey resigned as defence secretary in June under Keir Starmer’s leadership, accusing the prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”.
However, since succeeding Rachel Reeves following Andy Burnham’s arrival at No 10, Healey has declined to set a date for meeting the 3% target, which he had previously insisted should be hit by 2030.
Treasury sources confirmed that instead, the focus in Healey’s first budget on 28 October, would be fully funding the defence investment plan.

blocks.caption: John Healey will deliver his budget on 28 October. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/PA

blocks.text: The three-year DIP was one of Starmer’s final announcements – but about £1.2bn a year was left unaccounted for, with Healey’s predecessor Reeves suggesting the money would have to be found through cuts in other Whitehall departments.
The Treasury confirmed on Friday that there would be no further detail about the timeline in the budget. A spending review is expected to be held next year but no date has yet been set.

A government spokesperson said: “The first duty of government is to keep its citizens safe. The prime minister and chancellor are committed to fully funding the defence investment plan. At the spending review we will set out a pathway to meet our Nato commitment of 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and will set a target date to hit 3% on that path.”
Defence spending is on track to reach 2.7% of GDP by 2030, funded partly by Starmer’s decision to cut the UK’s aid spending.

Healey had previously said that this figure should rise to 3% urgently, given the growing global conflicts and security risks. He wrote in his resignation letter to Starmer in June: “As we have regularly discussed, I am certain that a headmark date for 3% of GDP on defence in 2030 is what Britain must set.”
So far, the prime minister, Burnham, has refused to commit to the 3% target.
In an interview with Sky News on Friday, Healey said fiscal discipline was the “first priority” for any chancellor.
after newsletter promotion
“It’s the bedrock for economic stability,” he said. “We simply can’t deal with the problems we face as a country by maxing out the country’s credit card.”
The chancellor will fly to North Carolina this weekend for a meeting of G20 finance ministers, chaired by the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent.
Healey and his colleagues will discuss the prospects for global growth, against the backdrop of continued high energy prices, volatile government bond markets and the US-Canada trade war.

articles.title: ‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return
articles.summary: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disaster
articles.byline: Henry Belot, Nino Bucci and Kat Wong

blocks.text: The families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.

Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal police on Friday said more than 1,500 people remained missing and 469 have been confirmed dead after massive flash floods and landslides tore through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins.
One Australian woman contacted her family on Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.
Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.
“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.
“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”
Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.
Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
The family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.
“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.
“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”

Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.
The family had been training together for the long walk, she said.
“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.
“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.
“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”
Vaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.
“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”
Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.
Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.

“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”

blocks.caption: Sumi Adhikari was travelling as part of an Isha Foundation pilgrimage. Illustration: supplied

blocks.text: Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.
He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.
Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.
“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.
Suhasini Kandimalla, a mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, has also been reported missing.
Her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla, said that she was doing the hike with another Springfield local.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Suhasini Kandimalla from Queensland who has been reported missing in Nepal. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.
“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini told the Guardian.
“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

A Brisbane man, Narayan Panthi, is also missing in the region. According to Nepal police, he was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday but he has also been conducting charity work in the capital with an education fund, the NeNas Foundation.

blocks.caption: Narayan Panthi from Brisbane is missing in Nepal. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, said his family was devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.
“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”
Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.
New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife, Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were also among the 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash.
So too were Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20.
The brothers played cricket for West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

“WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement.
“We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.”
The University of Newcastle’s vice-chancellor, Alex Zelinsky, said Rishab and Rudhra were both medical students the at the university.

“We are thinking of them, their families, their fellow students and teaching staff, as well as the many people who have been impacted by this devastating event and we hope that both students can be located soon,” Zelinsky said in a statement.
Separate groups of Australians – 11 travelling with Trekkers Society and six with Kailash Journeys – are also unaccounted for. Both tour companies have been contacted for comment.
Several other Australians were travelling with other tour groups. It is understood the majority of missing Australians are from New South Wales, but there are also some from Victoria and Queensland.
The founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Sagar Pandey, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people, which included the 15 Australians.
Pandey told the Guardian on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area, where the tour was staying, since the flood and had little hope they survived.
“To be honest … you would think there was no human civilisation there at all.
“The flash flood swept away everything, everything. You couldn’t see any human creations.
“Still, I have a hope.”
The Isha Foundation confirmed that 11 Australians were among a group of 80 missing pilgrims who had been in an immigration building when the flood hit.
The foreign minister, Penny Wong, spoke to her Nepali counterpart, Shisir Khanal, on Friday evening to convey Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods.
She outlined Australia’s humanitarian assistance package in which Australia was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response” to the flooding.
Wong said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.
“The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.”

Led by the Provincial Cooperative and Enterprise Development Office (PCEDO) with the Anti‑Red Tape Authority (ARTA), the program focused on Republic Act 11032 or the Ease of Doing Business Act.
Topics included citizen’s charters, client satisfaction measurement, and complaints handling.
Governor Daniel R. Fernando, in his message, reminded public servants that leadership is measured by action.

“Efficiency at work creates trust and confidence among our people. That trust attracts businesses and investments. And when there are more businesses and investments, there are more opportunities -- that’s what grows our local economy,” he said.
The training is part of Bulacan’s Ease of Doing Business Champion Program, which rewards LGUs that excel in citizen‑centered governance and smooth investment processing.

articles.title: Roblox agrees to integrate PhilSys for age, identity checks in PH
articles.summary: Roblox may soon require national ID from Filipino users for identity and age verification.

blocks.text: A child poses as he plays a video game on a tablet on the online game platform and game creation system Roblox developed by Roblox Corporation in Terville, northeastern France on March 11, 2026.
AFP / Jean-Christophe Verhaegen

MANILA, Philippines — Roblox has agreed to integrate the Philippine Identification System into its age and identity verification system for users in the country, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center said Friday, August 28.

The commitment came after Philippine government officials met with Roblox executives in Singapore on Thursday, to discuss stronger safeguards against online grooming and extremist recruitment, according to the CICC.

"We are pleased with the direction of our discussions with Roblox and the willingness they have shown to work with the Philippine government. This is an important beginning, and we want to build on it to create a safer gaming environment for our children," CICC Executive Director Renato "Aboy" Paraiso said in a statement.
The details of how PhilSys will be integrated into Roblox's existing age-check system have yet to be finalized.
Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda said a Roblox team is expected to arrive in the Philippines in the first week of September to study the technical implementation.

"Nag-agree sila [Roblox] this year na mag-iintegrate na sila sa PhilSys. Sabi nila [Roblox] pagdating sa identity at age verification, ready na sila mag-integrate sa PhilSys," Aguda said in a dzRH interview Friday.
("Roblox agreed that this year, they will integrate with PhilSys. They said that when it comes to identity and age verification, they are ready to integrate with PhilSys.")
Aguda said the integration could be in place by October.
Age-based restrictions
Roblox already requires users to complete an age check to access chat. Its existing system allows age verification through a government-issued ID or facial age estimation.
The company says its facial age estimation technology has a mean absolute error of about 1.4 years for users younger than 18.
According to the CICC, accounts that do not undergo an age check will have chat disabled and will have more limited access to games on the platform.
Roblox also committed to tighter age-based restrictions on communication, aimed at limiting interactions between children and users outside their age groups, the agency said.
Aguda said requiring stronger identity checks would not only help verify young users but could also make it harder for adults seeking to harm children to hide behind false identities.
"Hindi lang kasi 'yung minor ang kailangang mag-authenticate para magkaroon ng value. 'Yung adult ba na potentially predators, potentially groomers malalaman na natin," Aguda said.
("It is not only minors who need to authenticate for this to have value. We will also be able to identify adults who could potentially be predators or groomers.")
Roblox also plans to establish an office in the Philippines by October to allow faster coordination with government authorities, according to the CICC.
Talks with Meta
Philippine officials also met with executives of Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, in Singapore over child safety and harmful online content.
"Sabi ni Facebook, 'we hear you, we acknowledge the gaps and we will do better,'" Aguda said.
("Facebook said, 'We hear you, we acknowledge the gaps and we will do better.'")
Aguda said the government and Meta are working on a memorandum of understanding that is expected to be signed in the Philippines once the document is finalized.

The meetings involved officials from the CICC and Department of Information and Communications Technology, along with representatives from the National Bureau of Investigation, National Telecommunications Commission, Congress and Office of the Executive Secretary.

The discussions come amid heightened government scrutiny of social media and gaming platforms following recent incidents of school violence and concerns over online grooming, violent content and extremist influence.

blocks.text: The BBC has seen widespread devastation on the way from Nepal's capital of Kathmandu to Trishuli, one of the areas worst-hit by flooding on the Tibetan border.
As well as ambulances, hearses were also seen along the route, where rescuers said entire villages had been washed away by floodwaters.
South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri reports.

articles.title: Satellite images show bedrock and glacier collapsed on Nepal-China border, then rivers flooded
articles.summary: As rescue teams searched for missing people following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, Earth scientists reviewed satellite imagery for clues to the cause and assessed the…

blocks.text: As rescue teams searched for missing people following catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border, Earth scientists reviewed satellite imagery for clues to the cause and assessed the devastation.

blocks.caption: This satellite image provided by Vantor shows Syapru Besi, Nepal on Oct. 18, 2023. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP)

blocks.text: This satellite image provided by Vantor shows Syapru Besi, Nepal on Oct. 18, 2023. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP)
The flooding Wednesday killed hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet, and hundreds more are missing, including foreigners and pilgrims.

Geomorphologists Kristen Cook and Dan Shugar said initial images from Nepal were obscured by clouds and dust from the debris, so they could only see that part of a glacier had broken off from Langtang Lirung peak, near the border with Tibet. In clearer images from Thursday, they said they could see that the bedrock underneath the glacier had collapsed, taking the massive chunk of ice down with it and sending boulders and ice into the valley.

"It shows the whole area without anything hidden, and we could see that, yes, it looked like there was not only this glacier that had failed, but a much larger chunk of the bedrock of the mountainside itself that had given way," said Shugar, associate professor at the University of Calgary. "You have this big bedrock failure that took part of the glacier with it."
Shugar said it's heart-wrenching to look downstream from there on the images, to where people were living, and see how the debris has buried villages.

After slamming to the valley floor, the debris maintained its momentum through the steep, narrow valley as ice melted, said Cook, at the Université Grenoble Alpes in France. Water and mud several stories high swept through communities.

The Trishuli River surged during the flooding. Before and after satellite images of the Kolpurtar, Betrawati and Syapru Besi areas of Nepal show that the river is now much wider, and brown and black, because it overtopped its banks in some areas and filled with debris in others. The change in the color of the water shows how much sediment the flow was carrying, turning from greenish to very brown because it's full of mud, Cook said.
Towns and villages that were devastated along the river banks are submerged in debris and mud. They appear as areas of brown. Some houses are still poking through in an image of the Betrawati area.

The flooding toppled and swept away buildings in Syapru Besi, a popular tourist spot where a famous trek to Langtang begins. In before and after images, a side river is now wider too, because the flow was so powerful it pushed upstream.

The flooding "left a wasteland in its wake" that will take many years to recover from, said Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado at Boulder. Byers lived in Nepal and now returns there yearly to study glacial hazards and work with communities to prepare. This is the largest glacier flood he has seen, by far.

Byers, faculty research scientist at the university's Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, said he thinks Wednesday's flooding is related to climate change. The Earth's warming is melting glaciers and permafrost, causing instability and the breakage of massive amounts of snow and ice at high altitudes. That can be a catalyst for a series of cascading events, he said.

"All the indicators, to me, point to the impacts of warming trends," he said. "In this case, the permafrost that for millennia has helped to hold together high-altitude rock and ice and soil and glaciers is now weakening and becoming unstable."

Cook and Shugar said that at this point, they can't say for sure there's a direct link to climate change. Slopes fail and landslides happen, Cook said, though permafrost is melting and that is destabilizing mountainsides.

"While we cannot at this point directly link this collapse to climate change, it is not unexpected to see more events of this type with a warming climate," Cook said. "Not this big, hopefully not this big."

articles.title: 'Not far enough' - US parents and teens on Meta's new limits for young users
articles.summary: As part of an $18bn settlement in a child-safety lawsuit, Meta announced new restrictions on its apps. We asked families what they thought.

blocks.text: For Elizabeth Cardner, a mother of two girls in Houston, Texas, Meta's new limits on how teenagers can use its platforms are a welcome sign that more people are aware of social media's potential dangers.
But, she tells the BBC, they probably won't help much in the long-term.
"It will save a few arguments at home, but it doesn't go far enough," she says.

This week, Meta announced new restrictions on its platforms - which include Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - as part of an $18bn (£13.25bn) settlement with US states in a lawsuit on social media's effects on children.

The company said it would set a daily two-hour time limit, hide the number of likes that a post receives, remove autoplay on videos, mute push notifications during school hours, and ban extreme make-up filters.
It also announced changes to its age-verification process and parental controls as well as agreeing to appoint an independent auditor to check the measures are implemented and maintained.

Many parents across the US see the restrictions as helpful, but are still sceptical. Those who spoke to the BBC described feeling stuck - where they feel they can't cut their children off from social media but also can't protect them from the harms they believe it causes - and they are waiting to see how much of a difference these new rules will make.

Cardner's 14-year-old, Paige, believes the restrictions will lead to "more real-life scenarios" and less "fake content", which she says dominates social media. She and her sister both approve of hiding the numbers of likes and restricting filters.
But Paige sees those gains as short-lived, "since AI is evolving".

"People will find new ways to have fake filters, and correct certain parts of their videos or pictures," she says. "So I think it'll help until people use other resources to try and find new ways to do that."
Cardner says banning her daughters entirely from social media would only result in them being left out by their peers.
"Damned if you do, damned if you don't," she says. "I don't think there's any winning on it."

Another mother of two teens, Andria Rose, told the BBC that she feels defenceless and "no matter how much I protect my kids, Facebook, Instagram - they're coming in and literally, like, taking them out of their rooms".
Even though she calls Meta's changes "fantastic", Rose, who lives near Boston, Massachusetts, doesn't believe they are fully addressing the problem.
"They're trying to limit the drug, but they're not controlling the drug," she says. "They're still dealing."
Rose notes her personal use of social media costs her sleep at night.
"I'm hooked," she says. "So what do you think is going to happen to a kid?"
The settlement was announced on Wednesday in the middle of a highly-anticipated trial, where Meta owner Mark Zuckerberg was expected to testify. The settlement did not include any admission of fault.

The lawsuit was originally filed in 2023 by 29 US states, alleging Meta deliberately designed its platforms to be addictive and lied about risks. They also accused it of violating a federal law on collecting children's personal information.
The settlement - announced this week - included 48 states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.

Several studies have found social media to be harmful to mental health, especially for children. Last year, a BBC investigation found children were being exposed to content about bullying, suicide and weapons on social media platforms.

For Rose, Meta's settlement payment "is like throwing a couple of dollar bills at a problem", given how much money the company makes and how much she believes the industry profited from children during the pandemic.
Joanie Story, a mother of four boys in Long Island, takes issue with another part of Meta's announcement - its conditions involving other platforms.
The company will withhold $5bn of the settlement, and only release it if YouTube, TikTok and others also enter into similar agreements.
It also said it would further tighten its time limit to one hour if other platforms implement similar restrictions. Story sees that as "petty".
"That's like saying: 'You know, we have the ability to fix what is broken, but we're only gonna fix it halfway,'" she says.

Still, Story is greeting the new rules as "good controls". She says she saw what a lack of controls could do when two of her sons were accidentally exposed to explicit content on a non-Meta platform. One boy has been in therapy for four years, she says.

articles.title: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped
articles.summary: Her family is among hundreds anxiously waiting for news after the deadly flash floods.

blocks.text: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped

blocks.caption: Image caption, Subhrasree Chakraborty in Kathmandu a day before she set out for the pilgrimage

blocks.text: Image source, Sudipto Bhattacharya
Subhrasree Chakraborty in Kathmandu a day before she set out for the pilgrimage
Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.
She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.
Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.

Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.

The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years.

Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.
But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message.
"After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Chakraborty sent her husband a photograph showing her Nepal immigration clearance before she crossed towards Chinese immigration (blurred from source)

blocks.text: Image source, Sudipto Bhattacharya
Chakraborty sent her husband a photograph showing her Nepal immigration clearance before she crossed towards Chinese immigration (blurred from source)
Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.
The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement.

In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square.
She told her husband the countryside was beautiful.
"She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."
The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.
She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night.
She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.

Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one.
A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.
There was little to suggest what was coming.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Chakraborty told her husband she the pilgrimage was her 'dream trip'

blocks.text: Image source, Sudipto Bhattacharya
Chakraborty told her husband she the pilgrimage was her 'dream trip'
"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."
The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.

Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.
After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.
Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck.
"I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."
At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.
He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.
The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since.
"Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."

He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards.
"Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."
Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The death toll has risen to 475, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border region

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The death toll has risen to 475, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border region
For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.
They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.
Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.
Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu.
"She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."
Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family.
"She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."
She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said.
The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre.
Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Rina Banerjee, a private tutor, had travelled widely in the hills and was an experienced trekker

blocks.text: Image source, Dwaipayan Mukherjee
Rina Banerjee, a private tutor, had travelled widely in the hills and was an experienced trekker
"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."
For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.
Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains.
Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.

Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list , externalof 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.
For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

articles.title: PRC responds to San Lazaro Hospital's call amid leptospirosis surge
articles.summary: Amid the increasing number of leptospirosis patients, the Philippine Red Cross (PRC) has responded to San Lazaro Hospital’s call for additional manpower, deploying its Medical Corps Volunteers to…

blocks.text: Amid the increasing number of leptospirosis patients, the Philippine Red Cross (PRC) has responded to San Lazaro Hospital’s call for additional manpower, deploying its Medical Corps Volunteers to help augment the hospital’s healthcare workforce as it manages the surge.

In a letter addressed to PRC Chairman and CEO Richard Gordon, San Lazaro Hospital formally requested additional medical and support personnel in preparation for an anticipated increase in leptospirosis patients.
The hospital sought personnel who could help augment its workforce, including those with nursing and hemodialysis-related experience.

PRC Medical Corps Volunteers began providing support on Aug. 25. On their first day of service, the team catered to 67 patients in the hospital wards, assisting with patient monitoring and other essential nursing support.

The response continued on Aug. 26, with the PRC mobilizing 22 personnel composed of seven registered nurses, 13 senior nursing students or underboards, and two support volunteers. The deployment will continue as needed in coordination with San Lazaro Hospital.

Gordon said the PRC remains ready to respond to health institutions that require additional support, “When there is a call for help, the Philippine Red Cross responds. We work closely with our health institutions to determine their needs and provide the support that we can.”

PRC Secretary General Dr. Gwendolyn Pang said the Medical Corps Volunteers are providing additional manpower while the hospital manages the surge, “Our Medical Corps Volunteers are providing additional support to San Lazaro Hospital’s healthcare workers and patients during this surge. We will continue coordinating closely with the hospital and adjust our support according to the needs on the ground.”
Beyond San Lazaro Hospital, Gordon has also directed PRC chapters nationwide to check hospitals within and near their respective areas amid the rising number of leptospirosis cases.
The initiative will allow the organization to identify healthcare facilities experiencing increased patient loads or manpower requirements and determine where PRC assistance may be needed.
The PRC will continue monitoring the leptospirosis situation nationwide and coordinating with health institutions to provide support where it is needed.

articles.title: ADHD and autism costs in England ‘running out of control’, NHS leaders warn
articles.summary:
Soaring demand for services has led to tenfold increase in spending in a year in some areas, says NHS Alliance

NHS leaders have warned that the costs of meeting soaring demand for attention…

blocks.text: NHS leaders have warned that the costs of meeting soaring demand for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism services in England are “running out of control” and have become unsustainable, with spending in some areas rising by as much as tenfold over the course of a year.
The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, said the rise in demand since the coronavirus pandemic was forcing some to close waiting lists and look at reining in other services they provide.
One integrated care board (ICB) cited in a report said its monthly spend had risen from £146,000 in 2024-25 to £1.5m last year.
Another said spending on adult ADHD services had risen from £11m in 2023-24 to a projected £51m this financial year.

Increased demand and a lack of NHS capacity has led to a big influx of new providers, the report said, fuelled by patients’ right to choose which allows people seeking diagnosis for themselves or a child to opt for any qualified provider.
One ICB told the NHS Alliance it now had 80 providers on its patch. Another said that two years ago it had received invoices from 12 to 14 providers, a figure which had risen to 48.

The rapid expansion of new providers has also prompted concerns from ICBs about quality assurance and regulation, especially when large numbers of small, non-regulated providers enter the market that are able to deliver assessments but not ongoing care, the report said.

This increased capacity has helped to ease some delays for assessments, but – due to the lack of a national tariff – has resulted in huge variations in the prices paid for services, adding to already severe cost pressures, the report said. One ICB told the NHS Alliance it was paying £300 to £3,000 for similar services.
Rebecca Gray, the director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said: “Local health leaders are caught between a rock and a hard place.

“They understand the anguish and frustration caused by long delays in the system as people wait for assessments, treatment and support. But in working to meet rising demand they face soaring costs that are running out of control.
after newsletter promotion
“As commissioners they must balance their budgets. Unplanned overspends on ADHD and autism assessments and treatment can impact on other activities and disrupt long-term planning.
“The current situation is unsustainable and delivers a bad deal for patients and taxpayers.”
The NHS Alliance is calling for a national mandatory price (or tariff) for ADHD and autism services and a national service specification applied consistently across all NHS-funded providers.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V dies at 89 and his son becomes King Haakon VIII
articles.summary: STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of potential brides from the…

blocks.text: STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of potential brides from the European nobility so he could marry his school sweetheart, died Friday. He was 89.

blocks.caption: FILE - Norway's King Harald arrives at a central London hotel for a pre-royal wedding dinner hosted by Lady Elizabeth Anson and attended by members of the British royal family and foreign royal families, in London, on April, 28, 2011. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant, File)

blocks.text: FILE - Norway's King Harald arrives at a central London hotel for a pre-royal wedding dinner hosted by Lady Elizabeth Anson and attended by members of the British royal family and foreign royal families, in London, on April, 28, 2011. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant, File)
The palace said he died at the National Hospital in Oslo at 6:35 a.m.

Harald was Europe's oldest monarch. The popular king modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. His son automatically became King Haakon VIII.

Like other royal houses in Europe, the Norwegian monarchs serve a largely symbolic role, enjoying celebrity status while real power in the democracy of 5.5 million rests with an elected parliament. Harald was crowned after his British-born father, King Olav V, died in January 1991, and reigned during an oil-and-gas-driven economic boom in his country.

"A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement. "For more than three decades as monarch, Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves — and in one another."
Royal family fled Norway during World War II

Harald was born in 1937 in Asker, near Oslo, becoming the first Norwegian prince to be born in the country since King Olav IV in 1370. In the following centuries, Norway didn't have a king of its own until Harald's grandfather, Haakon VII, was elected king following the 1905 dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway.

Harald was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II. To avoid capture, his mother fled with him and his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, first to Sweden and then by boat to the U.S., while Harald's father and grandfather went into exile in Britain with Norway's government.
Haakon's refusal to go along with German demands garnered respect among his people.

During their time in the U.S., the Norwegian royals were often guests at the White House. Harald was 6 when he carried out his first official duty, christening new warplanes at a Norwegian air base in Canada.
The family was reunited in Norway in June 1945, shortly after the end of the war in Europe. Harald attended public schools, the Norwegian military college and Oxford University.

Like his father — an Olympic champion sailor in 1928 — Harald loved the sea and sailboats. He represented Norway at several Olympics, and in 1987 he skippered his yacht to gold in the World Championships.
Harald married his high school sweetheart

As a young man, Harald was urged to find a bride among Europe's noblewomen and princesses. For nine years he shunned a series of prospects, holding out until he finally won his father's permission to marry his school sweetheart, Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a successful businessman.

King Olav had feared the marriage would weaken Norway's still-young monarchy. Instead, Norwegians greeted the Aug. 29, 1968, wedding with jubilation, and later embraced Sonja as their queen. The couple had two children, Haakon and his older sister, Märtha Louise.

The Norwegian Constitution was altered in 1990 to allow the first born, regardless of gender, to take precedence in the line of succession. However, it was not applied retroactively, meaning that Haakon continued to take precedence over his sister.
When Harald assumed the throne on Jan. 21, 1991, he adopted the same motto his father and grandfather had used: "All for Norway." He spent the next years trying to modernize the monarchy.

"It has been my experience that the monarchy stands strong," he once said. "This is not least because my father and grandfather did most things right. That puts me under pressure, but I take it as a challenge."
Harald won the praise of the country with an emotional speech at a memorial service after a right-wing extremist, Anders Behring Breivik, killed 77 people in bomb and gun attacks in Norway in 2011.

"I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear. I remain convinced in the belief of an open Norwegian democracy and society. I remain convinced in the belief in our ability to live freely and safely in our own country," the king said.

In 2016, Harald gave an unexpected and impassioned speech in support of LGBTQ+ equality, refugees and religious tolerance, saying "Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other." He added that many Norwegians have emigrated from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Poland and other countries and that they "believe in God, Allah, the universe and nothing."
The public speech extolled the diversity of the Scandinavian nation and was viewed on social media by millions.
Recent scandals have put royal family under scrutiny

Scandal and serious allegations have hung over the Norwegian royal family this year. Harald's daughter-in-law, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, faced renewed scrutiny over her connections with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. That raised questions over her judgment, though she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Mette-Marit apologized for the situation she put the royal family in, part of a broader apology for all those she had "disappointed."

At around the same time, her eldest son, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in a high-profile trial and sentenced to four years in prison. Høiby, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship before she met Haakon, has no royal titles or official duties.

In 2022, Harald's daughter Märtha Louise gave up royal duties after raising eyebrows by saying she could communicate with angels and becoming engaged to an American man who identifies as a shaman. They married two years later.
In January 2024, after the abdication of Denmark's Queen Margrethe — his second cousin — Harald said that he stood by the oath he made when ascending the throne: "It lasts for life."

However, he was hospitalized twice on foreign trips after that, including during a 2024 vacation in Malaysia when he was fitted with a pacemaker and during a February 2026 holiday on the Spanish island of Tenerife when he had a skin infection.

articles.title: Meta pledges to share data over imminent threats, says Hontiveros
articles.summary: In a meeting in Singapore, Meta commits to sharing subscriber and traffic data when Philippine authorities identify imminent threats of violence

blocks.text: RISA. Senator Risa Hontiveros speaks at a plenary session on August 25, 2026
In a meeting in Singapore, Meta commits to sharing subscriber and traffic data when Philippine authorities identify imminent threats of violence

items: Senator Risa Hontiveros announced that the Philippine government secured a commitment from Meta to provide user data to law enforcement when there is an imminent threat of violence.
The agreement was reached during a meeting with Meta's Asia-Pacific policy officers, focusing on the company's responsibility to combat violent extremism on its platforms.

Hontiveros linked this commitment to the upcoming Child Online Safety and Protection Act, which aims to strengthen protections for children on digital platforms and hold technology companies accountable for harmful content.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Risa Hontiveros on Friday, August 28, said the government has secured a commitment from Meta to respond to requests from Philippine law enforcement authorities for user data when there are indications of an imminent threat of violence.

Hontiveros sent representatives on Thursday, August 27, to join a Philippine delegation of key government officials in a roundtable meeting with Meta’s top Asia-Pacific policy officers at the tech giant’s regional headquarters in Singapore.

The meeting focused on the responsibilities of Meta’s platforms, particularly Facebook, in addressing the spread of nihilistic violent extremism and preventing online activity from translating into real-world attacks.

As the meeting neared its conclusion, Hontiveros’ representatives pressed Meta to commit to providing subscriber information and traffic data to Philippine authorities once an imminent threat to public safety has been identified.
Meta agreed to the request, according to Hontiveros.

“Napapayag natin, napa-commit natin ang Meta na ibibigay nila sa ating mga awtoridad ang subscriber information at pati traffic data once na may ma-identify silang banta sa kaligtasan ng ating mga bata bago pa may mangyaring aktwal na pag-atake,” Hontiveros said.
(We were able to get a commitment from Meta that they will provide subscriber information and traffic data once they identify a threat to the safety of our youth before an attack even happens.)

Hontiveros also linked the agreement to the looming passage of the Child Online Safety and Protection Act or Senate Bill No. 2424, a priority measure that seeks to strengthen safeguards for children on digital platforms.
The bill consolidates social media regulation bills pertaining to children’s use of such platforms.

Under the bill, children below 16 years of age shall not be allowed to create, access or maintain accounts on these platforms, with corresponding penalties to platform owners, as well as parents if proven willfully negligent.

The proposed legislation builds on protections established under Republic Act No. 11930, or the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse and Exploitation of Children and Anti-Child Sexual Abuse or Exploitation Materials Act.
The senator stressed that technology companies operating in the Philippines should be held accountable for harmful content distributed through their platforms.

Her remarks come amid growing scrutiny of social media companies over the role their platforms play in the spread of extremist content, violent threats and other harmful material. At a Senate hearing on August 20, police revealed that it had handled 74 cases linked to nihilistic violent extremism so far.

At the same hearing, Hontiveros had castigated Meta for allowing a livestreamed video of the Ateneo de Zamboanga shooting incident to remain published online for 14 minutes. She said: “Linisin niyo ang kalat niyo, ang basura niyo sa inyong powerful platform, linisin niyo. Huwag niyo iwan lahat sa CICC (Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center).”

blocks.caption: Zamboanga school shooting kills at least 2 | The wRap

blocks.text: (It shouldn’t be the CICC that cleans up after Meta. Clean your mess up, your trash on your powerful platform. Don’t leave it up to the CICC.)
