articles.title: Peso plunges past ₱62:$1 to new record low of ₱62.265
articles.summary: Demand for the safe-haven United States (US) dollar surged amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty, sending the Philippine peso tumbling to a fresh historic low of ₱62.265 on Friday, Aug. 28, from…

blocks.text: Demand for the safe-haven United States (US) dollar surged amid heightened geopolitical uncertainty, sending the Philippine peso tumbling to a fresh historic low of ₱62.265 on Friday, Aug. 28, from the previous record of ₱61.888 just a day ago.

The local currency slid to an intraday low of ₱62.27 and hit a high of ₱62 after opening at ₱62.05. Total trading volume climbed to $1.962 billion from Thursday’s $1.79 billion, according to the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP).

Singapore-based DBS Bank Ltd. noted that the Philippine peso was the only Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-6 currency to weaken against the greenback so far in the third quarter of 2026, declining by 0.8 percent, while its regional peers appreciated by 0.9 to 1.7 percent over the same period.

Reyes Tacandong & Co. senior adviser Jonathan Ravelas said the US dollar-peso pair rose again “after the greenback strengthened anew on Middle East worries and ahead of the Jackson Hole speech by US Federal Reserve (Fed) Chair Kevin Warsh.”

Similarly, Ruben Carlo O. Asuncion, chief economist at Union Bank of the Philippines (UnionBank), cited the dominance of offshore developments rather than domestic developments. “Markets remain focused on broad US dollar strength, elevated oil prices, and lingering uncertainty in global financial markets,” he said.

Asuncion noted that the local currency still slipped even as the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) decided to further raise key borrowing costs by a quarter point to five percent—a move that typically supports the currency.

“Demand for dollars from importers and investors has also likely contributed to the peso’s weakness,” Asuncion said, noting that the net oil-importing country remains vulnerable during periods of a sustained rally in the greenback.

“More broadly, the peso’s recent weakness is consistent with the challenges often faced by emerging market (EM) and regional currencies during periods of dollar strength and heightened global uncertainty,” he added.

Ravelas expects the currency pair to trade within the range of ₱61.9 to ₱62.3 despite the support from the BSP’s tightening. He said geopolitical risks are expected to continue driving this dimmer outlook for the peso.

articles.title: Role of infrastrusture, farmers' empowerment underscored in agri sector development
articles.summary: DAVAO CITY – Cotabato Governor Emmylou Taliño-Mendoza has underscored the vital role of reliable infrastructure as well as empowerment of farmers in the development of the agriculture sector. In her…

blocks.text: DAVAO CITY – Cotabato Governor Emmylou Taliño-Mendoza has underscored the vital role of reliable infrastructure as well as empowerment of farmers in the development of the agriculture sector.

In her speech before the delegates of the 14th National Palm Oil Congress here, Mendoza also emphasized the role of local governments, saying that it should never be just limited to distributing planting materials and farm inputs.

The local government, she said, must become an ecosystem builder while the Department of Agriculture (DA) provides national policy and resources; banks provide financing; and private companies provide technology as well as market access.
Mendoza said that local governments should turn farmers into productive assets to avoid creating dependency.

“The government provides the right starting input, the knowledge, and the technical support. But the farmer takes responsibility for the investment,” she said while referring to the provincial government’s program called Plant Now, Take Care (PNTC).
Under the program, the provincial government distributes high-quality oil palm seedlings to qualified local farmers.

She explained that under the scheme, beneficiaries who could successfully achieve an 85% survival rate for the seedlings during the first year, they do not have to pay back or return the cost of the planting materials.

From 2012 to 2026, according to the governor, the PNTC investments have reached approximately P272 million, benefiting 3,640 farmers and establishing 7,497.94 hectares of oil palm across the province.
In 2026 alone, Mendoza added, the program allocated P35 million, benefiting 521 farmers and establishing approximately 942.5 hectares of oil palm farms.
“These are not just numbers in a government accomplishment report. They represent farms. They represent families,” she said before the delegates.
When government assistance is linked to responsibility, accountability, and actual farm productivity, the governor further said, public resources transform into long-term economic assets.
Mendoza also called for stronger cooperatives and farmer organizations to be able to aggregate production, negotiate better terms, access financing as well as a better transport system.
Moreover, Mendoza also underscored the role of reliable infrastructures in the development of the oil palm industry since its produce is particularly dependent on efficient logistics.

“That means farm-to-market roads matter. Bridges, collection points, hauling facilities, drainage and transport matters,” she said before the delegates of the two-day event that culminated today, August 28.

Mendoza also noted that agricultural policy and infrastructure policy cannot be treated separately. “Infrastructure must follow the value chain. And the provincial government will continue to advocate for infrastructure investments.”

Under the Department of Agriculture's Philippine Rural Development Project (PRDP) Scale-Up, Mendoza said, the province has a portfolio of approximately P996 million in priority infrastructure and water-system investments aimed at improving connectivity, water access, and rural productivity.

“These are not merely construction projects. If properly planned, they become economic infrastructure. They reduce logistics costs. They improve market access. They make farms more viable. And they make investment more attractive,” she added.
Furthermore, the governor also acknowledged the role of technology in producing reliable data in the agriculture sector.
Mendoza said that farmers should maximize all available modern technology such as drones, remote sensing, farm monitoring systems and data-driven fertilizer application,
She also emphasized the value of having accurate data to be able to appropriately respond to the needs of farmers.

Organized by the Philippine Palm Oil Development Council, Inc, the event gathered industry leaders, experts, stakeholders, and partners for a two-day discussion on networking opportunities, and the latest developments in the Philippine palm oil industry.

articles.title: ‘We praise God’: Australian woman feared missing in Nepal flooding makes contact with family
articles.summary: Cara Severino has spoken with her parents – but still faces a trek of more than 110km to reach Kathmandu on foot

blocks.text: An Australian woman has made contact with her family, more than two days after she was reported missing in flash flooding in Nepal.

At least 469 people have been killed and more than 1,500 are missing after a catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday. Cara Severino, 25, is the first of 39 Australians reported missing in the tragedy to have been confirmed safe.
But she is still hiking away from the disaster zone, attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.

Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, confirmed in a statement that she had no phone reception, and her own phone had a flat battery, but that she had contacted them on Friday morning to say she was safe.
“She was hiking the Langtang trek and was stranded,” they said in a statement. “With communications down we had no contact.”
“This morning she was able to call us from Gosainkunda where she has been able to reach along with some other [Nepali] hikers. We understand that they are attempting to reach Kathmandu on foot.
“We eagerly await more information about her safe return. We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news.”
after newsletter promotion
As of Friday evening, 38 Australians were missing. Of the 35 missing Australians whose details were released by Nepali police, Severino was the only one not listed as travelling with a tour agency.
The others were from four other groups, many of them organised to take part in the Mount Kailash Hindu pilgrimage in the region.

articles.title: Palace: Philippines won’t enter deals that put Filipinos at a disadvantage
articles.summary: Malacañang assured the public that President Marcos will not enter into any deal with another country that would put the Philippines and its people at a disadvantage. "Nagsalita din po ang Pangulo,…

blocks.text: Malacañang assured the public that President Marcos will not enter into any deal with another country that would put the Philippines and its people at a disadvantage.

"Nagsalita din po ang Pangulo, hindi maaaring gumawa ng anumang transaksyon na ang Pilipinas o mga Pilipino ang siyang madidehado (The President also said that no transaction should be made if it would put the Philippines or Filipinos at a disadvantage)," Palace Press Officer and Communications Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a recent Palace briefing.
She made the statement after the United States imposed hefty tariffs on Canada for refusing to agree to a trade deal that would grant the former exclusive access to its critical minerals.

Given that the US-led Pax Silica is making its way to the Philippines, the Palace official was asked what safeguards Manila has put in place to ensure that Washington will equally respect the Philippines' demands.
Castro did not cite a specific measure, but assured the public that the Marcos administration will only carry out projects and deals according to laws.
She also stressed that just because the government is pursuing investments does not mean that it will allow Filipinos to suffer.

"Kailangan po natin na magkaroon ng mga investments pero hindi nangangahulugan na ang ating mga kapuwa Pilipino ang magdurusa (We need to attract investments, but that does not mean our fellow Filipinos should suffer as a result)," Castro said.

"So maliwanag po iyan, hindi po natin pababayaan kung ano ang itinatalaga ng ating batas, hindi po natin iba-violate ang karapatan ng ating mga kapwa nating Pilipino (So, that is clear: we will not disregard what is mandated by our laws, and we will not violate the rights of our fellow Filipinos)," Castro added.

articles.title: PNP weighs home inspections for gov’t firearms, backs campus security law amid school shootings
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police said Friday, Aug. 28, it will conduct further study and consultations with stakeholders on the proposal to inspect residences where government-issued firearms are kept…

blocks.text: The Philippine National Police said Friday, Aug. 28, it will conduct further study and consultations with stakeholders on the proposal to inspect residences where government-issued firearms are kept as authorities seek to prevent weapons from being accessed by minors and used in school attacks.

Police General Jose Melencio C. Nartatez, Jr. said the measure aims to compel firearm holders to be more responsible and compliant with conditions of gun ownership but he stressed that consultations must be held to ensure privacy rights are not compromised.

“We are in the process of strengthening our measures to ensure that government-issued weapons are properly stored and kept. This will be carefully studied and we assure that the concerns and sentiments of all the sectors involved will be respected and factored in,” Nartatez said, noting that the police organization will coordinate with the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) for the guidelines of the proposal.

DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla earlier proposed during the House committee hearing on the budget of the agency that police should be allowed to conduct an inspection in the homes of individuals who had government-issued firearms to ensure they are properly stored and kept away from unauthorized persons.
He later clarified that inspections would not be conducted through search warrants but through waivers signed by gun owners, with one day’s notice.

The push for tighter firearm controls followed two school shooting incidents in Tacloban City on June 22 and Zamboanga City on Aug. 18 involving minor students who gained access to firearms that turned out to be government-issued.
Nartatez said any inspection scheme should have clear procedures and safeguards as these should protect the rights of gun owners and police officers from any form of harassment.
He also assured the public that the PNP would keep any action within existing laws and respect individual rights.
PNP backs Comprehensive School Safety Act
Meanwhile, the PNP also expressed support for a proposed law that seeks to strengthen security measures in schools following recent school shootings.

Nartatez said Senate Bill No. 2426, or the Comprehensive School Safety Act, filed by Sen. Bam Aquino, seeks to establish a nationwide system for school safety and provide sustained funding for campus protection programs.

“We support measures that strengthen the protection of our learners. The PNP is ready to work closely with DepEd [Department of Education] and other stakeholders to ensure that schools remain safe and secure environments,” Nartatez said.

The measure covers prevention, response and recovery programs including risk assessments, safety training, emergency procedures, and active safety drills. It also provides for psychosocial and mental health support for affected students, families, and school personnel.

“School safety must be preventive, responsive, and supportive. We will continue strengthening police visibility, threat assessment, emergency preparedness, and coordination with school authorities,” Nartatez said.
The proposed legislation would also complement existing DepEd and PNP efforts such as the School Safety Campaign, stricter campus inspections, visitor management, and increased police patrols.

“Our first priority will be to ensure seamless coordination with DepEd and local stakeholders and to strengthen our police units’ capability to prevent and respond to threats against schools,” he said.

MANILA, Philippines – Surigao del Norte 1st District Representative Francisco “Lalo” Matugas and his son, former representative Francisco “Bingo” Matugas II, are facing malversation and graft complaints before the Office of the Ombudsman over their alleged involvement with a contractor, the investigative body announced on Friday, August 28.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said the Ombudsman has recommended complaints for alleged violation of sections 3(e) and (h) of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act and malversation of public funds against the two Matugases.

Section 3(e), one of the most commonly cited offenses against government officials, covers causing undue injury to the government or giving any party unwarranted benefits. Section 3(h), meanwhile, prohibits public officials from having a direct or indirect financial or business interest in matters where they intervene in their official capacity.
Malversation, depending on the amount involved, could be a non-bailable offense.

The criminal complaints have been endorsed for preliminary investigation, meaning Ombudsman prosecutors will now determine whether there is sufficient evidence to pursue the cases. If the evidence is sufficient, the prosecutors will indict file the cases with the Sandiganbayan.

Meanwhile, the Ombudsman also announced that administrative complaints are also pending against the two Matugases. Unlike criminal cases that may carry jail time, administrative actions may result in the penalty of suspension or disqualification from holding public office.

According to the Ombudsman, the complaints, which also include several unnamed Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials as respondents, stemmed from their alleged link to Boometrix Development Corporation.

“DPWH records represented that P80.61 million Mahayahay-Tuburan road project in Del Carmen as fully complete and Boometrix was fully paid. An Ombudsman site inspection in April 2026 found the project [was] only 65 to 70% accomplished. At least P31 million was released despite its actual condition,” said Clavano.
“Investigators also documented P457 million pesos in loans between the former legislators and Boometrix, supporting the conclusion that both held direct pecuniary interest in the contract,” he added.

Mayor Matugas was one of the incorporators and shareholders of Boometrix when they set up the company in 2013. Although she was no longer an owner, the company shares are still held by her son, Ronald Abejo, as of 2025. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Celeste Legaspi’s candid BINI take divides fans online
articles.summary: Celeste Legaspi isn't that crazy about BINI. And that was more enough to get some fans talking. The veteran singer and actress has found herself at the center of an online discussion after clips of…

blocks.text: Celeste Legaspi (Facebook)
Celeste Legaspi isn't that crazy about BINI.
And that was more enough to get some fans talking.

The veteran singer and actress has found herself at the center of an online discussion after clips of an old interview in which she praised P-pop boy group SB19 but admitted she was less enthusiastic about BINI, resurfaced.
During her guest appearance on the YouTube show “Senior Moments with Louie Montalbo,” Celeste was asked what she thought of the two popular P-pop groups.

“I like the SB19 a lot. They are really, really good. I’m not so crazy about the BINI kasi parang… Hindi sila masyadong… Anyway… SB19—they’re really, really good. I’m so proud of them when I see them next to the Koreans,” she said.
Celeste went on to single out SB19 member Stell Ajero, recalling how impressed she was by his performance during OPM icon and National Artist Ryan Cayabyab’s 70th birthday concert in 2024.
While some respected her preference, others were disappointed.

"With all due respect to Ms. Celeste Legaspi, everyone is entitled to their own opinion. But comparing BINI to SB19 was so unnecessary. You didn’t have to drag them into this interview. This is so disappointing, coming from a well-respected icon in Philippine music industry," One fan tweeted.
Meanwhile, some fans understand why Celeste made the statement.

"I still have respect for her as one of the pillars of OPM. So I don’t take it against her, and I disagree with the current negative sentiment against her. Iba-iba naman talaga ang preferences ng mga tao eh,” one netizen said.
Ah, the internet. Even musical taste can apparently become a team sport.

items: Rising school violence in the Philippines in 2026 necessitates urgent action and collaboration among various stakeholders, including schools, families, and local governments.
MovePH is launching 'Civic Circles,' a panel discussion and workshop aimed at developing actionable strategies to enhance school safety and address issues like online violence.

MANILA, Philippines – What can we do, together, to make children and schools safe?

Rising school violence across the Philippines in 2026 demands urgent and coordinated action. Beyond the classroom, children also face growing dangers in the digital landscape, including online grooming and violence.

Education advocates have earlier called for better school safety, emphasizing that keeping children and schools safe is a shared responsibility among schools, families, local governments, law enforcement, civil society organizations, and communities.

To foster this collaboration, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH is launching “Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?” — a panel discussion and workshop aimed at building actionable strategies to stop school violence. This particular session is done in collaboration with CyberGuardiansPH and Mental Health Youth Hub.

blocks.caption: LISTENING CIRCLE. FEU participants share insights and perspectives during a listening circle, exploring community needs and ways to turn their training into initiatives for the university and its communities during the RappLearn Accelerator Program, July 30, 2026 at the Rappler newsroom.

blocks.text: Civic Circles is a pilot initiative led by MovePH that aims to turn discussion into community-led action. It builds on MovePH’s previous community campaigns such as responsible digital citizenship, scam prevention, fighting disinformation, and disaster preparedness, among others.

The session will take place on Thursday, September 10, from 12:30 pm to 5 pm. Interested participants can join on-site at the Rappler civic hub in Pasig City or online via the Education chat room on the Rappler app.

The program will kick off with a panel discussion with experts and practitioners working on education, law enforcement, child protection, and community safety. This will be followed by a brief Q&A for the participants.

The panel features Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte, Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group spokesperson Police Captain Wallen Arancillo, and Philippine Pediatric Society child protection specialist Dr. Princess Gairanod.
Rappler’s head of community, Pia Ranada, will moderate the discussion, which will be followed by an interactive Q&A session with participants and Rappler app users.

After the panel discussion and Q&A, participants joining on-site can take part in a hands-on workshop to collectively develop concrete and actionable responses to threats facing children and schools across four Civic Circles:

items: Campus security and physical safety
Psychosocial care and mental health
Policy, governance, and accountability
Digital safety and off-campus hotspots

blocks.text: The solutions generated during the session may be featured on Rappler to encourage a broader discussion and possible adaptation by local governments, schools, families, and communities.

articles.title: Weather tracker: More extreme rain in Japan and a tornado in France
articles.summary:
Flash flooding and mudslides in Ishikawa and Toyama prefectures, while convective storms hit western Europe

After an “unprecedented” deluge
articles.byline: Brendan Wood and Faye Hulton for MetDesk

blocks.text: After an “unprecedented” deluge in Chiba in mid-August, Japan has experienced further extreme rainfall in recent days. Moisture from the Sea of Japan brought relentless heavy rain to the prefectures of Ishikawa and Toyama on Thursday.

In Himi, Toyama, 361.5mm of rain fell in 24 hours, equivalent to half the average annual rainfall in London and Paris. Several rivers burst their banks, triggering flash floods and mudslides, felling and damaging buildings.

Japan’s Meteorological Agency issued its highest-level rain warning for the two prefectures this week, as well as landslide warnings, leading to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people. Models on Thursday indicated that a further 200mm of rain could fall just south of this region as moisture continued to move in from the west.

Two days earlier, Typhoon Saudel had passed through the prefectures of Kagoshima and Okinawa Island, south-west of the mainland, bringing winds of 100mph (160km/h) and extreme rainfall. In the Amami region, 230mm rain fell in a day. The storm was forecast to move into south-east China by the end of the week, with much weaker winds.

While the warm ocean waters surrounding Japan often contribute to increased typhoon activity at this time of year, this year’s developing El Niño could explain why so many storms have approached the island nation and why there have been so many extreme rain events.

Unlike during La Niña years, when the semi-permanent North Pacific High often extends west towards Japan, in El Niño years, the ridge tends to extend northwards, allowing weather fronts to push through more easily and tropical storms developing farther south to “recurve” towards Japan.

blocks.caption: Destroyed houses after a tornado in Pomas, France, on Wednesday. Photograph: Idriss Bigou-Gilles/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Over the past few days, severe convective storms have struck western Europe, particularly the Alpine regions. The storms have brought intense rain, strong winds, large hail and even tornadoes. Spain, France, and Italy have been particularly affected, with hailstones up to 10cm in diameter reported in Catalonia and a significant tornado developing in the village of Pomas, south-west France.

The severe weather developed due to a combination of factors, including a low-pressure system tracking along the western coast of Europe, high levels of convective instability and strong vertical wind shear.

blocks.text: World

Jurrors are deliberating in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman charged with murdering her three children. Clancy's lawyers say she's not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. At rallies outside the courthouse and in the discourse happening online, a similar message emerged: new moms need help, and they aren't getting it.
Jurors began deliberations Thursday in case where defence blames postpartum psychosis

blocks.caption: Lindsay Clancy sits at the defence table Thursday during her murder trial in Plymouth, Mass. Clancy's lawyers don't dispute that she killed her three children but argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Greg Derr/Pool The Pa…

blocks.text: WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and suicide.

Outside the Massachusetts courtroom where Lindsay Clancy is on trial in connection with the deaths of her three children — she doesn't deny that she killed them, but jurors must decide if she's criminally responsible — Clancy's supporters have gathered again.

On Thursday, ahead of the closing arguments, they were again dressed in pink. Once again, they were mostly women. And just like during their previous gatherings and in the discourse happening online, a similar message emerged: new moms need help, and they aren't getting it.

"As a physician myself, I’ve been on both sides of this coin when women are dismissed for our concerns, and it’s not fair," supporter Marta Quijano told The Associated Press outside the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Thursday.

items: What to know about the trial of Lindsay Clancy, woman accused of killing her 3 children

blocks.text: "I don’t think people really understand unless they’ve been through it," said Danielle Buckley, who drove five hours from Maine to watch the closing arguments.
"They just want to see her be punished for what happened to her children."

blocks.caption: Aimee Breault of Acushnet, Mass., livestreams a demonstration Thursday in support of Clancy outside the Plymouth Superior Court where she's on trial. (Josh Reynolds/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children in 2023 while her then-husband was running an errand. Jurors have heard that Clancy strangled Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then attempted to take her own life by jumping out of a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed.

Clancy's defence doesn't dispute the killings. But they argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.
Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.
On Thursday, after lawyers finished their closing arguments in the month-long trial, jurors started their deliberations.

If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If she's found not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility, or by reason of insanity, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital.
The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health
'I am Lindsay Clancy'

Court heard that Clancy suffered from hallucinations and delusions that started after her third child was born. On the day of the killings, Clancy said she heard a voice telling her, "This is your last chance. Kill the children so you can kill yourself," according to her lawyer during opening arguments.

In addition to the courthouse rallies, there's been a massive wave of online empathy. On social media, people have been sharing their own experiences with trying to get mental health support after childbirth. Some have posted statements like, "I am Lindsay Clancy." Others have posted photos of themselves during times of struggle along with the words, "same, Lindsay."

"No matter what we say, nothing useful happens. Many of us lie, fearful of having our kids taken. Those of us who tell the truth are usually met with some combination of stigma, dismissal, and blame — rarely any meaningful support," Zawn Villines wrote on Substack Thursday.

items: What is postpartum psychosis, the illness at the centre of Lindsay Clancy's murder trial?
Testimony concludes in trial of U.S. mother accused of killing her 3 children

blocks.text: "This Lindsay Clancy trial has hit me so viscerally, and it’s so close to home," Liz Cadeaux said in a tearful TikTok video where she urged other moms having a hard time to seek help.

Conversely, there's also been backlash against the social media campaigns, and opinion pieces and columns that question how so many mothers can possibly sympathize with a woman who killed her children.
Dr. Crystal Clark, the head of psychiatry at Women’s College Hospital in Toronto, says she thinks people are resonating with the trial, but not because they identify with Clancy's final actions.

"They resonate with the suffering, the help-seeking, the distress and despair she was experiencing prior to that, that they recognize in themselves," Clark, also the Canada Research Chair in reproductive mental health, told CBC News.

Because of the overall increased awareness of mental conditions like postpartum depression, Clark says more people are able to identify and name what they have experienced. And that can include not feeling heard.
"Not being heard is very scary."
Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial hears closing arguments
More support needed: psychiatrist

Jurors have heard that Clancy was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications across different providers, and her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help, including going to the emergency room, calling a suicide hotline and checking herself into a psychiatric hospital.

The trial is triggering for many women, who have a long history of having their health and mental health concerns dismissed or misinterpreted, psychotherapist Kaytee Gillis recently wrote in Psychology Today.
"It touches something many women already know intimately: the feeling of asking for help and being unable to find it," Gillis wrote.

blocks.caption: A poster sits on the floor in a corner near Lindsay Clancy during her murder trial Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (John Tlumacki/Pool The Boston Globe/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: In Canada, postpartum depression and anxiety affect almost one-quarter of mothers who recently gave birth, according to 2019 Statistics Canada data. Postpartum psychosis — the sudden onset of psychotic symptoms after childbirth — is much more serious. Researchers estimate that the condition afflicts one to two women per 1,000 after delivery.

Clark, with Women’s College Hospital, says she doesn't believe new moms are getting enough support during what can be a very vulnerable and scary time. More needs to be done to identify when moms are suffering and need help, and to provide early intervention, she says.

While the trial has raised awareness of postpartum psychosis, Clark says she's worried about increasing stigma. For instance, Clark says she's seen an uptick in the number of patients worrying about whether they could be at risk of killing their children, even though it's an extremely rare outcome of a rare postpartum mental illness.
According to a 2024 research paper published in the Archives of Women's Mental Health, untreated postpartum psychosis is associated with an infanticide rate of about four per cent.
"Postpartum depression, postpartum anxiety and postpartum OCD are not associated with postpartum psychosis. It is very unlikely that those illnesses will lead to infanticide," Clark said.
Deliberations in Clancy's trial will resume Friday at 9 a.m. ET.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

items: Canada's Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorialmental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling onthe website.

articles.title: How teen accounts on Instagram and Facebook are changing after Meta's $18B US settlement
articles.summary: Changes are coming for teen Instagram and Facebook users after parent company Meta agreed to platform changes in a landmark U.S. settlement to resolve claims of online harms to youth. Experts tell…

blocks.text: World

Changes are coming for teen Instagram and Facebook users after parent company Meta agreed to platform changes in a landmark U.S. settlement to resolve claims of online harms to youth. Experts tell CBC News what's changing, how widely and what impact this might have going forward.
'Writing is on the wall for the social media industry,' says analyst

blocks.caption: Meta, parent company of social media platforms Instagram and Facebook, has agreed to a multi-state settlement worth up to $18 billion US, with American officials billing it the largest state consumer protection settlement in history outside of the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s. (Richard Dr…

blocks.text: Changes are coming for teen users of social media platforms Instagram and Facebook.

Parent company Meta agreed this week to make platform design changes for young users and pay up to $18 billion US over the next decade to resolve claims of online harms to youth stemming from nearly every U.S. state and territory.
A coalition of U.S. attorneys general have described it as the largest state consumer protection settlement in history outside of the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.
"The writing is on the wall for the social media industry. This is their tobacco moment," said Canadian tech analyst Carmi Levy.
"Things change for Meta and other companies like it from this point forward."
What's changing for teens?
New measures are coming for the Instagram and Facebook accounts of users under 18, including:

items: Time limits and pauses: a default time limit of two hours daily across both platforms in total, plus prompts and pauses after 15, 60 and 90 minutes of continuous use to disrupt "endless scrolling."
Blackout periods: blocks on most usage between midnight and 6 a.m. and notifications muted between the general school hours of 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. (excluding security or safety alerts).
More control over feeds: the ability to choose a non-algorithmic feed by default (along with periodic reminders about this feature) and being able to switch off autoplaying content.
Limits to social comparison features: hiding "like" counts/reactions and blocking "extreme makeup" filters.
Stronger age verification and age-related content restrictions.

blocks.text: Meta says it will continue existing work blocking strangers from contacting teen accounts and improve reporting tools and parental controls.

It also vowed to toughen some of its new measures — for instance, further reducing the daily time limit to one hour — if rival social platforms Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube also adopted comparable ones.
Could Meta’s $18B settlement change social media forever?
Does this affect Canadian teens too?

Technically the settlement applies to the U.S. market — and American teens should expect to see these changes in the next few months, Levy says — but teens everywhere should get ready. Levy says these tweaks will likely spread wider given the concern in so many countries about negative social media impacts on youth.
"Historically, whenever technology companies like Meta introduce significant changes to their infrastructure in a certain region, eventually they do go global," he said from London, Ont.

"I would expect over time Canada will see these changes as well. It's a lot easier for these companies to maintain a common set of tools and features around the world than to have unique features for each country where they do business."
What could the Meta settlement in California mean for Canada?
Does this make social media safer?

The settlement is a step in the right direction, says Jenny Perez, mom of a middle-schooler and founder of the parental advocacy group Unplugged Canada. Yet she sees a much longer list of safety concerns for social media companies to tackle.

items: Meta trial begins with states accusing social media giant of exploiting, intentionally addicting children

blocks.text: Adding a few measures to address what kids experience "is somewhat helpful, but doesn't fix the fact that these products are addictive," she said from Vancouver.

Digital media expert Richard Lachman lauds the interruption to infinite scrolling — a time-suck that's not unlike what researchers of gambling addiction explore, he noted. Yet the computer scientist and digital media professor at Toronto Metropolitan University says he'd rather not solely rely on what a company says it's doing to make itself safer.
"Right now we have Meta's designers saying 'These are the steps we're going to take. Trust us,'" Lachman said. "I would be much happier with an independent, third-party [review]."
Meta agrees to platforms changes, pay up to $18B US to settle lawsuit

Luke Stark, an associate professor of information and media studies at Western University, says the announced measures will help stem some compulsive social media use by teens. Yet he pointed out the measures are limited, noting for instance that older users are also drawn in by addictive platform design.
"These systems affect everybody," he said from London, Ont.
Though Stark calls the settlement "a big example — of which there are not very many — of Meta changing its design under threat of legal action," he thinks it could have gone further.
"The general business model of Facebook hasn't really been touched by this."
What does this mean for proposed regulations in Canada?

Thousands of U.S. state and federal lawsuits still face Meta, Snap (parent of the platform Snapchat), Alphabet (YouTube) and ByteDance (TikTok), but American cases must be considered very differently from those in Canada or internationally, said Toronto tech analyst Ritesh Kotak.
Still, he thinks this week could be a hint of what's to come. "Meta may consider settling and just ending some of these lawsuits once and for all."

items: B.C. lawsuit accuses Meta of harming the mental health of kids
Ontario school boards clear hurdle in lawsuits against Meta, Snapchat, TikTok

blocks.text: The decision to settle "indicates to me that Meta understands that it's got a problem and that it has to kind of get ahead of any kind of regulatory effort," said David Fewer, a law professor at the University of Ottawa.

Fewer suggests Meta's moves could pave the way to fulfilling requirements for Canada's proposed online safety legislation, though there's still "a lot more regulatory clay" to work with, he said, like Canadian calls to tackle addictive algorithm design. "We shouldn't mistake what Meta can live with, with what Canadians deserve."
Back in Toronto, Lachman thinks Meta is eager to resolve its social media woes so as to shift its attention to artificial intelligence.
"They want this to go away so they can focus on AI," he said.

blocks.text: "They don't want to be mired in this. And even though $10, 15, 20 billion US sounds like a lot of money to us, in the size of the potential market for its AI ambitions, with the reach they have into regular daily use by billions of people around the world, this is where [CEO Mark Zuckerberg] wants to play."

articles.title: Despite Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario, Great Lakes endure as symbol of U.S.-Canada collaboration
articles.summary: It's unclear whether Trump can unilaterally rename the lake, whose name predates European colonization of the Americas and has been widely recognized internationally for centuries. But the renaming…

image.caption: A view of Lake Ontario from Tommy Thompson Park in Toronto. The Great Lakes support about 40 million people in the region. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Science

It's unclear whether Trump can unilaterally rename the lake, whose name predates European colonization of the Americas and has been widely recognized internationally for centuries. But the renaming belies a concerted push by the Trump administration to hold back important U.S.-Canada collaboration on scientific research and restoration work in the Great Lakes.
Renaming Lake Ontario may sound like a joke, but environmental threats to the Great Lakes are very real
Listen to this article
Estimated 5 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

blocks.caption: A view of Lake Ontario from Tommy Thompson Park in Toronto. The Great Lakes support about 40 million people in the region. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: The Great Lakes, one of the largest stores of freshwater and a source of water for some 40 million people, have long symbolized how closely intertwined Canada and the U.S. are.

U.S. President Donald Trump took a public sledgehammer to that relationship Thursday as part of his trade war with Canada, signing an executive order directing that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America.

It's unclear whether Trump can unilaterally rename the lake, whose name predates European colonization of the Americas and has been widely recognized internationally for centuries. But the move comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration that has hindered U.S.-Canada collaboration on scientific research and restoration work in the Great Lakes.

items: Scientists at U.S. weather forecasting agency ordered to get clearance before talking to Canadian counterparts
The U.S. is cutting billions from science. Canadian researchers say it's time to step up

blocks.text: "The way that this current administration in the United States views the environment and views science is demoralizing," said Aaron Fisk, professor at the Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research at the University of Windsor.

"With the U.S. moving away from evidence-based decisions about the environment … that's a real concern to me because we need them to be a world leader. This really goes against their long term investment in good science," he said.

As part of its massive cuts to the federal public service, the Trump administration has made major cuts to iconic U.S. scientific agencies such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Environmental Protection Agency. Those cuts have, in turn, affected monitoring and research in the Great Lakes.

"The water does not respect political boundaries, and you have to manage it as a water body, as a watershed, not just as a national or state or provincial boundary," said Joel Brammeier, president and CEO of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, a U.S. non-profit that advocates for Great Lakes conservation and restoration.

blocks.caption: The Lake Michigan coast in Chicago. U.S.-Canada collaboration is essential to manage and restore the shared waters of the Great Lakes. (Charles Rex Arbogast/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: "Which is why it's always a bit painful when we see somebody out of the U.S. side challenging that collaboration. Because, honestly, the Great Lakes don't get cleaned up and they don't get protected unless the U.S. and Canada collaborate and co-operate."
Bipartisan support saves key Great Lakes program

Even amid the cuts, support for the Great Lakes has crossed political lines. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, a two-decade-old program to restore ecosystems and clean up industrial pollution, was targeted for near-total elimination by Trump during his first administration.

blocks.caption: In this 2014, file photo the water intake crib for the city of Toledo, Ohio, is surrounded by an algae bloom on Lake Erie. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative program has funded work in Ohio to slow down Lake Erie's toxic algae. (Haraz N. Ghanbari/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: The U.S. House of Representatives voted to reauthorize the program through 2031, with nearly $500 million US in federal funding per year going to local communities in the region. The measure received both Democratic and Republican support and is now working its way through the U.S. Senate.
"There are few issues that unite political parties like the Great Lakes. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has been so successful in doing that," Brammeier said.

The Great Lakes region has been central to industrial growth in both the U.S. and Canada, Brammeier said, hosting major industries such as steel, chemical and aluminum manufacturing. That growth has also left widespread industrial contamination that communities across the region want cleaned up.

"Even though a lot of damage was done across a large part of the Great Lakes, in an odd way that's actually led to this near universal support for the restoration program because so many decision-makers, so many members of Congress have seen the harm in their own communities," he said.
Climate change brings new threats

Historical pollution is not the end of the Great Lakes' problems. Climate change is bringing extreme heat and shifting precipitation to the region, which researchers say requires close study on both sides of the border.
Mike Shriberg, director of the University of Michigan's Water Center, said water availability and access are emerging challenges.
"This summer's a great example. We've had increasing drought and then increasing intensity of precipitation. So water flows have changed because of climate change," he said.

That, combined with future water demand from data centres, power generation and especially agriculture — which is expanding farther north as the climate warms — could create problems in the coming years. Shriberg also said he expects more people to move to the region from parts in the U.S. facing water shortages, particularly in the West, potentially putting further strain on the Great Lakes.
Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’

Andrew Gronewold, professor at the University of Michigan, is also thinking about future demand. "I think we're going to face some very difficult choices and questions about how Great Lakes water is used," he said from Hamilton, Ont., where he was meeting with Canadian and First Nations research partners.

Gronewold pointed to efforts by a group of Great Lakes state governors and premiers to "future-proof" the Great Lakes compact and agreement, a set of pacts among U.S. Great Lakes states, Ontario and Quebec governing how the water is used.

"I think over the next several decades, there's going to be increased pressure from outside of the basin for that water, whether it's for agriculture or industry or other uses. That's something that we need to be paying attention to," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: In honour of Coyote vs. Acme, we salute some excellent anti-capitalist movies
articles.summary: Coyote vs. Acme, which opens in theatres Aug. 28, is not only the latest chapter in a timeless battle of wills, but the newest entry in the pantheon of anti-capitalist films. Here are seven of our…

image.caption: A still from the film Coyote vs. Acme. (VVS Films)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Coyote vs. Acme, which opens in theatres Aug. 28, is not only the latest chapter in a timeless battle of wills, but the newest entry in the pantheon of anti-capitalist films. Here are seven of our favourites.
Looney Tunes feature is latest entry in long line of films that stick it to the corporate man
Listen to this article
Estimated 5 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

blocks.caption: A still from the film Coyote vs. Acme. (VVS Films)

blocks.text: Wile E. Coyote has employed every conceivable gadget in his fruitless, decades-long pursuit of the Road Runner.

But what if this futility isn't his fault? What if it's the fault of the Acme Corporation? What if the company behind such items as the "Instant Tunnel" and the "Do-It-Yourself Tornado Kit" just makes bad products?

That's the premise of Coyote vs. Acme, in which our hapless hero engages an equally hapless lawyer to take on the Acme Corporation in court for the physical suffering he's endured using their products.

The film finally hits theatres Friday after taking a circuitous route to the big screen. (Completed in 2023, it was shelved by Warner Bros. Discovery as a tax write-off, and only revived when independent distributor Ketchup Entertainment bought the rights last year.)
To celebrate the spirit of the film, we've catalogued our favourite anti-capitalist movies from the last 40 years.
RoboCop (1987)

A once-outlandish film that feels more like a documentary with every passing year, Paul Verhoeven's RoboCop imagines a near future where a company called Omni Consumer Products essentially runs the Detroit police department. Omni's killer app is the titular man-machine (played with deadpan sass by Peter Weller), who soon learns of the brutal lengths Omni executive Dick Jones is willing to go to scale the corporate ladder. The only complication: Robocop has been expressly programmed not to harm Omni executives.
Money quote: "What did you think? That you were an ordinary police officer? You're our product, and we can't very well have our products turning against us, can we?"
They Live (1988)

In John Carpenter's iconic sci-fi pic, a blue-collar schlub (Roddy Piper) finds a special pair of sunglasses that allow him to see what's really going on: that a race of aliens is passing as humans and transmitting subliminal messages telling people to consume and conform. And why are these dastardly extra-terrestrials doing this? To distract us while they pillage the planet's resources.
Money quote: "They're free-enterprisers. The Earth is just another developing planet. Their third world."
Fight Club (1999)

Something of a spiritual sequel to They Live, Fight Club also posits that society conditions us to buy, buy, buy. This realization doesn't sit well with the unnamed protagonist (Edward Norton), who meets Tyler Durden (Brad Pitt), an enigmatic stranger (or is he?) who suggests the only way to feel alive in this consumer hellscape is to punch the crap out of other people (in the spirit of camaraderie, of course). Their fight club soon branches out into anti-capitalist violence, culminating in the epic demolition of several bank towers to the strains of the Pixies' Where Is My Mind?
Money quote: "The things you own end up owning you."
Michael Clayton (2007)

This film is a bracing indictment of how far corporations will go to hide their guilt. George Clooney stars as a fixer conscripted to help a law firm representing U-North, the defendant in a multibillion-dollar class-action lawsuit over a pesticide that killed several people. The scene in which two assassins wordlessly dispatch a lawyer who possesses incriminating evidence against U-North is one of the most cold-blooded moments in cinematic history.
Money quote: "Not only is this a great product, it is a superb cancer delivery system."
WALL-E (2008)

Another anti-commercialist screed, this time dressed up as a winsome Pixar romance between two robots. It's the 29th century, and rapacious consumerism has made Earth uninhabitable for everyone but our trash-compacting hero, WALL-E. Meanwhile, humans have moved to massive spaceships like the Axiom, operated by the conglomerate Buy N Large, which ensures they spend their days devouring obscene amounts of fast food and trash TV.
Money quote: "A is for Axiom, your home sweet home. B is for Buy N Large, your very best friend."
Sorry to Bother You (2018)

In this mind-bending satire from director Boots Riley (an avowed communist), a Black everyman named Cassius Green (Lakeith Stanfield) lands a job as a telemarketer and finds his impeccable "white" accent is a ticket to huge sales. A promotion puts him at odds with his unionizing colleagues but brings him in league with the CEO, who reveals that the multi-pronged conglomerate has been breeding a slave labour force of half-humans, half-horses called "Equisapiens."
Money quote: "Let me give you a tip. You wanna make some money here? Use your white voice."
How to Blow Up a Pipeline (2022)

A group of idealistic youngsters determines the best way to challenge the hegemony of the fossil fuel industry is to take out some of its infrastructure. Alas, that requires stealth, discretion and an ability to handle explosive materials. This indie thriller's politics are dead obvious, but the film extracts maximum tension by exploring all the ways such a brazen act of environmentalism could go wrong.

Money quote: "If we want to survive, we must damage and dismantle CO2-emitting devices, demolish them, burn them, blow them up. Let those who profit from mass death know their properties will be trashed."

articles.title: ACEN, Yanara secure RCBC loan for Pangasinan solar plant
articles.summary: Ayala-led ACEN Corp. and partner Yanara Philippines Corp. have secured a ₱2.3 billion project financing facility from Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC) to fund the construction of a 75-megawatt…

blocks.text: Ayala-led ACEN Corp. and partner Yanara Philippines Corp. have secured a ₱2.3 billion project financing facility from Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC) to fund the construction of a 75-megawatt solar farm in Pangasinan.

In a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange, ACEN said the loan was extended to project company Renovable Earth Corp., a joint subsidiary of the two developers, to support the ongoing development of the Sual solar project.
The agreement is Yanara’s first renewable energy deployment in the Philippines alongside ACEN, expanding its footprint in the Southeast Asian market.
The project was earlier awarded under the government’s fourth Green Energy Auction Program, an initiative designed to scale up clean energy capacity through competitive bidding.

When operational, the Sual solar plant is expected to generate approximately 112 gigawatt-hours of clean electricity per year. That is enough output to power about 69,000 households and eliminate 86,000 tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually. Construction activity is anticipated to create roughly 1,500 local jobs.

“As demand for reliable and sustainable power continues to grow, investments such as Sual Solar help strengthen the country's energy security, support local economic development, and advance the transition to a cleaner energy future,” said Patrice Clausse, Group Chief Investment Officer of ACEN.
Jerome Ortiz, Chief Executive Officer of Yanara, said the financing agreement underpins the shared commitment of both companies to help accelerate the country's clean energy transition.

The Pangasinan facility forms part of ACEN’s broader push to expand its generation assets. The company has earmarked an annual capital expenditures budget of more than ₱80 billion for 2026 as it works toward bringing its operating renewable capacity to over eight gigawatts by the end of the year.

ACEN currently holds a total capacity of approximately seven gigawatts across its primary operations in the Philippines, Australia, Vietnam, India, Indonesia, Laos, and the United States. Yanara specializes in multi-technology renewable power plants that integrate solar, wind, and battery storage solutions, maintaining operations in India, Australia, and the Philippines. (Gabriell Christel Galang)

articles.title: Great Deals targets ₱20-billion H2 sales on AI-commerce push
articles.summary: The Philippines’ largest e-commerce enabler Great Deals E-Commerce Corp. (GDEC) is ramping up its artificial intelligence (AI)-powered commerce operations in the second half of the year as it targets…

blocks.text: The Philippines’ largest e-commerce enabler Great Deals E-Commerce Corp. (GDEC) is ramping up its artificial intelligence (AI)-powered commerce operations in the second half of the year as it targets ₱20 billion in sales during the period.

During the company’s ninth anniversary celebration on Friday, Aug. 28, GDEC chief executive officer (CEO) Steve Sy said the company plans to add 40 new AI livestream sellers this year on top of about 20 currently operating across its 28 studios.

The expansion forms part of GDEC’s push into AI-commerce as the company seeks to harness the technology to scale its live-selling operations while maintaining a workforce that combines human talent with AI.
Sy told reporters that a single AI live-selling account on Shopee generated ₱730,217 in sales over 241 straight hours of livestreaming.

At the same time, Sy dismissed concerns that greater AI adoption would necessarily come at the expense of human workers, saying the technology could instead create different types of jobs and business opportunities.

“When you see the company, there will be more business opportunities you can create. But the kind of work will be different… Right now, we have a blended culture: it’s human talent plus AI-powered system[s],” Sy said.
Sy said GDEC’s employees now work alongside AI “teammates” to improve productivity, while the company’s AI livestream sellers are modeled after its human staff and agents.

GDEC began integrating AI into its operations three years ago, particularly in customer support. Sy said the integration has reduced the company’s customer chat support requirements by 60 percent, with AI now handling 40 percent of customer inquiries.
Beyond its AI-commerce expansion, GDEC is investing in leadership and workforce development in the second half of the year.

Its initiatives include a six-course leadership program for managers, employee engagement activities, AI-based onboarding training for new hires, Claude Pro subscriptions for its leadership team and select roles, and Pusong GDEC, the company’s volunteer program.
The company’s increasing adoption of AI is also expected to support its longer-term growth ambitions.
GDEC’s revenues rose by 28 percent year-on-year to ₱10.6 billion in the first half of 2026.
Last year, Sy said GDEC had grown its revenue more than tenfold over five years, from ₱1.1 billion in 2019 to ₱12.71 billion.
GDEC continues to target ₱100 billion in revenue by 2030, with AI-commerce emerging as another growth driver toward that goal.

The expansion comes amid continued growth in the country’s digital economy. According to last year’s e-Conomy SEA report by Google, Temasek, and Bain & Company, the Philippine e-commerce market is projected to reach approximately $60 billion by 2030. - Danielle T. Bayani

articles.title: Filipino artist Sigwada Knicolai uses art to talk about mental health
articles.summary: In the art world, sadness and other difficult emotions can become sources of inspiration. But when an artist’s work directly confronts mental health conditions, the conversation can become more…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Arts and Culture
Through playful characters, paintings, sculptures, and a children's book, she opens a gentler conversation about bipolar disorder and mental health

In the art world, sadness and other difficult emotions can become sources of inspiration. But when an artist’s work directly confronts mental health conditions, the conversation can become more difficult. Heavy themes can make audiences and even art collectors hesitant to engage, something Filipino visual artist Sigwada Knicolai has experienced firsthand.

For her latest exhibition, “Nikolai’s Ever-Changing Sky,” Sigwada chose to approach the subject differently. Instead of presenting mental health through an entirely heavy lens, she uses playful characters, paintings, sculptures, and a children’s book to make conversations about bipolar disorder easier to understand.

The exhibition, which opened on Aug. 22 at Improv Art Gallery in Quezon City, shares its title with Sigwada’s newly released children’s book. The project was inspired partly by her search for children’s literature about mental health.
“Why not create something light so that it's easier to digest for everyone?” Sigwada tells Manila Bulletin Lifestyle.

The idea also drew inspiration from “Winnie the Pooh,” whose characters, she noted, have been analyzed in relation to different personality traits and mental health experiences. From there, Sigwada developed characters that could represent changing moods in a way that would feel accessible, particularly to children.

At the center of the exhibition and book is Nikolai, a wooden astronaut who travels through changing inner worlds. Her “moods” appear as Rosie, a rag doll associated with bright, seemingly unstoppable energy; Mr. Grey, a masked beluga weighed down by sadness; and Ambrosia, a jack-in-the-box consumed by anxious “what ifs.”

The exhibition features 15 paintings and three sculptures, while the book was created with art and story by Sigwada and text by Hazel Pascua. Its story introduces children and caregivers to changes in mood, energy, and behavior while showing how support can come through family care, professional guidance, treatment, healthy routines, and patience.

For Sigwada, making the book accessible is also personal. She used to teach children and says children’s books, comics, and picture books are close to her. “I like being playful,” she says. “And I believe we Filipinos can find lightness in something heavy.”

That lightness serves a larger purpose: encouraging empathy from a young age. She hopes the book can help children understand adults who experience changing moods, including those who may have parents living with bipolar disorder.

She also hopes the project can help challenge the stigma surrounding mental health in the Philippines, where she says people can still feel uncomfortable sharing their diagnoses and may even experience internal stigma.
“Somehow, I hope to eradicate the stigma around it,” she says, adding that she wants people with mental illness to understand that “it is manageable. We can do something about it.”

The advocacy extends beyond the gallery. Fifty copies of the book were donated to the Philippine Mental Health Association, which will be sold during Mental Health Week, with proceeds supporting its programs.
For Sigwada, art can be more than something aesthetically pleasing. “It’s a good tool to communicate important things," she says. “Like an advocacy.”
“Nikolai’s Ever-Changing Sky” runs at Improv Art Gallery until Oct. 3.

articles.title: Alex Eala to face Janice Tjen in PH Arena homecoming
articles.summary: Staging the tennis exhibition at the 55,000-seater Philippine Arena gives tens of thousands of Filipinos the chance to catch Alex Eala in action on home soil

blocks.text: TROPHY. The Philippines' Alex Eala wins the 2026 Washington Open in the United States.
Mubadala DC Open Facebook page
Staging the tennis exhibition at the 55,000-seater Philippine Arena gives tens of thousands of Filipinos the chance to catch Alex Eala in action on home soil
MANILA, Philippines – Once her historic 2026 season is over, Alex Eala is headed home.
The Filipina tennis star will headline the “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate” on December 8 as she battles Indonesia’s Janice Tjen at the Philippine Arena in Bulacan.
“Every time I play abroad, I carry the Philippines with me. To come home and play in front of our fans will be incredibly special,” Eala told event organizer Tatler Philippines.

blocks.caption: Alex Eala to face Janice Tjen in PH Arena homecoming

blocks.text: Staging the event at the 55,000-seater arena gives tens of thousands of Filipinos the chance to catch Eala in action on home soil for the first time since she bannered the inaugural staging of the Philippine Women’s Open in January.

The event also has a chance to go for the world record for largest crowd at a tennis match, a distinction held by the Match for Africa exhibition in 2020 where 51,954 spectators witnessed Roger Federer beat rival Rafael Nadal, 6-4, 3-6, 6-3.
“I want this to be a day where we celebrate our love for tennis, our culture, and the young players who will take the sport forward,” said Eala.
A celebrity exhibition match, live musical performances, and interactive fan experiences will also be part of the event.

Eala is currently in New York for the US Open, the last major of the year, hoping to go on a deep run after she made history last year by becoming the first Filipino to win a Grand Slam main draw match in the Open era.
Ranked 18th in the world, Eala will be seeded in a major for only the second time in her career. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Mali’s preserved remains unveiled at National Museum
articles.summary: The preserved remains of Mali, the longtime Manila Zoo elephant, went on display Thursday, Aug. 27, at the National Museum of Natural History in Ermita. Vishwa Ma’ali, widely known as Mali, was born…

blocks.text: The preserved remains of Mali, the longtime Manila Zoo elephant, went on display Thursday, Aug. 27, at the National Museum of Natural History in Ermita.
Vishwa Ma’ali, widely known as Mali, was born in Sri Lanka and orphaned after hunters killed her mother.
Brought to the Philippines as a gift, she became one of the country’s most recognized animals until her death at 43 on Nov. 28, 2023, from congestive heart failure.
Manila Mayor Francisco “Isko Moreno” Domagoso joined museum officials in unveiling Ma’ali’s new home.

In a Facebook post, he assured residents: “Sa mga Batang Maynila, pumanatag po kayo. Nasa maayos at ligtas na pangangalaga si Ma’ali (To the children of Manila, rest assured. Ma’ali is in good and safe hands).”
“With the capabilities, skills, and experience of the National Museum, Ma’ali is in good hands,” he added.

He invited Manileños and Filipinos who grew up with Mali to visit her again: “Tinatawagan ko ang lahat ng mamamayan ng lungsod ng Maynila, ang mga dumadayo sa Maynila, at lahat ng Pilipinong may karanasan at alaala kay Ma’ali—muli ninyo siyang masisilayan sa kanyang bagong tahanan sa National Museum (I invite all residents of Manila, visitors, and all Filipinos who have experiences and memories with Ma’ali to see her once again at her new home at the National Museum).”

Domagoso also expressed gratitude to the museum: “Again, to the National Museum, thank you, thank you sa inyong lahat. Malaking bagay ito para sa mga Batang Maynila (This means a lot for the children of Manila).”
The exhibit is open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. with free admission. (Shane Quiachon)

articles.title: Leptospirosis cases reach 5,486; DOH warns numbers may rise
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) has recorded 5,486 leptospirosis cases nationwide this year and warned that infections may continue to rise in the next two weeks following recent rains and flooding.…

blocks.text: (MB FILE PHOTO)
The Department of Health (DOH) has recorded 5,486 leptospirosis cases nationwide this year and warned that infections may continue to rise in the next two weeks following recent rains and flooding.
During a press briefing on Friday, Aug. 28, DOH Undersecretary Gloria Balboa said the cases were recorded from Jan. 4 to Aug. 26, 2026.
She noted that the figure was 23 percent lower than the 7,163 cases logged during the same period last year.

“Base sa aming datos mula Jan. 4 hanggang Aug. 26, 2026, nakapagtala na po ang DOH ng 5,486 na kaso ng leptospirosis sa bansa, na mas mababa ng 23 percent kumpara sa 7,163 na kaso noong nakaraang taon sa parehong period po (Based on our data from Jan. 4 to Aug. 26, 2026, the DOH recorded 5,486 leptospirosis cases nationwide, 23 percent lower than the 7,163 cases logged during the same period last year),” she said.
The health department identified the National Capital Region (NCR), Region II, and Region III as the regions with the highest number of cases.
According to Balboa, the DOH is closely monitoring areas in Metro Manila with elevated case numbers.

“Nakita natin nitong August 27, as of yesterday po, 521 na ang pasyente na naitala rito sa Metro Manila, at 158 po rito ay nasa San Lazaro Hospital (As of yesterday, Aug. 27, we recorded 521 patients here in Metro Manila, 158 of whom were at San Lazaro Hospital),” she said.
DOH Secretary Edwin Mercado said the agency expects more cases to emerge because leptospirosis symptoms may develop days after exposure to contaminated floodwater.

blocks.caption: (MB FILE PHOTO)

blocks.text: (MB FILE PHOTO)

“Inaasahan po ang pagdami ng kaso sa susunod na dalawang linggo matapos ang pag-ulan at pagbaha. Kaya ngayon, patuloy na pinaiigting ng DOH ang aming surveillance (We expect cases to increase in the next two weeks following the rains and flooding. The DOH is therefore continuously strengthening its surveillance),” he said.
The DOH chief assured the public that the agency’s facilities would remain operational and adequately supplied amid the increase in cases.
Likewise, he noted that the health department opened leptospirosis fast lanes in 33 DOH hospitals across affected regions to facilitate the immediate assessment and treatment of patients.

“Binuksan na rin natin ‘yung mga leptospirosis fast lane. Ito po ay nandoon sa ating 33 DOH hospitals, doon po sa affected regions (We have also opened leptospirosis fast lanes in our 33 DOH hospitals in the affected regions),” said Mercado.

“Dito po ay agarang tutugunan ang pasyente dahil kapag may sintomas nang nilalagnat, nagkakaroon po ng pagmamanas, at nahihirapan nang umiihi (Patients will be immediately attended to because symptoms may include fever, swelling, and difficulty urinating),” he added.

blocks.caption: (MB FILE PHOTO)

blocks.text: (MB FILE PHOTO)
Mercado said the DOH convened a command conference on Aug. 25 to strengthen coordination among its hospitals in handling leptospirosis patients.

“Kaya nga po doon, tuloy-tuloy na ang koordinasyon ng DOH hospitals para sa referral ng mga pasyente. Nakikipag-ugnayan na rin po tayo sa mga LGU at city health offices (The coordination among DOH hospitals for patient referrals is continuing. We are also coordinating with local government units and city health offices),” he said.
Balboa urged people who had waded through floodwater to immediately visit the nearest health center, regardless of whether they had wounds or were experiencing symptoms.

“Kung sila po ay lumusong sa baha, may sugat man o wala, at may sintomas man o wala, ay dapat pumunta na sa pinakamalapit na health center para maagapan at mabigyan ng tamang advice ng ating health workers (Those who waded through floodwater, whether or not they have wounds or symptoms, should visit the nearest health center for prompt intervention and proper advice from our health workers),” she said.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), leptospirosis is a bacterial disease affecting humans and animals that can be contracted through direct contact with the urine of infected animals or contaminated surroundings.
The bacteria may enter the body through broken skin or the mucous membranes of the mouth, nose, and eyes, while person-to-person transmission rarely occurs.

articles.title: Dolphin dies from H5 bird flu in SA as researchers withdrawn from sub-Antarctic island over ‘psychosocial risk’
articles.summary:
Expeditioners at research station on Macquarie Island will be evacuated over possible ‘psychological stress’, while 100 dead little penguins found on Tasmanian island

  • Get our
articles.byline: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: A dolphin has died from H5 bird flu in South Australia, marking the second native mammal species known to have contracted the virus.

On Friday afternoon, the Tasmanian government said it was assessing the discovery of about 100 dead little penguins on King Island but it was unable to test them for H5 bird flu due to their “decayed condition”.

It comes as the federal government announced it would withdraw researchers from the sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island research station due to the “psychosocial risk” of witnessing potential mass seal deaths from H5N1 during the upcoming seal breeding season.

The common dolphin was found recently deceased near Goolwa on South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula. State tests confirmed the animal was positive for H5N1, with samples sent to the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness for further analysis.
It follows two earlier detections in long-nosed fur seals in SA at Beachport and the Pages Islands and a case in a red fox – a feral pest species – near Port Adelaide.
The federal government’s risk assessment rated common dolphins at high risk from bird flu, meaning they potentially face severe population declines where the virus takes hold.

“While the detection in the common dolphin is a new development in Australia, there is evidence of dolphins and porpoises catching H5 bird flu overseas,” a spokesperson for SA’s Department of Primary Industries and Regions said.
“Dolphins would not commonly eat birds but it is not unusual for them to sometimes interact.”

In Tasmania, the state government said about 100 dead little penguins were found at Stokes Point, the southern tip of King Island, during wildlife monitoring activities. The government has labelled the deaths a mass mortality event but said the cause had not been established.
The natural resources and environment department said the birds were not considered suitable for H5 bird flu testing due to their decayed condition.

Brendon Clark, north-west regional manager for the state’s parks and wildlife service, said authorities were working to “assess the circumstances surrounding the discovery and determine whether any further management actions are required”.
“Any loss of wildlife is concerning, and we recognise this discovery will be upsetting for residents, visitors and others who care deeply about Tasmania’s unique wildlife.
“While assessments of the site have identified injuries on many of the birds, it is not possible to definitively determine the cause of death from the information currently available.”
He said monitoring of the site would continue.
The federal government said on Friday it would withdraw 24 expeditioners based at the research station on Macquarie Island in the Southern Ocean about 1,500km south-east of Tasmania.

While bird flu had not yet been detected on the island, it was home to large elephant seal populations close to station buildings. Expert assessments had predicted “a high likelihood of a significant mortality event during the upcoming breeding season”.

“While the risk to humans remains low, a significant mortality event during the upcoming seal breeding season could expose expeditioners to prolonged psychological stress and other workplace impacts,” the department said.
The department’s deputy secretary, Sean Sullivan, said: “This is an unusual measure, but is the most appropriate course of action, based on our assessments of risk, and operational realities.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Thousands of little penguins being vaccinated against H5 bird flu in Victoria – video

blocks.text: “Our first priority is the health and safety of our expeditioners. While the risk to humans of H5 bird flu is considered low, we can’t ignore the psychosocial risks of living near potentially large numbers of affected animals.”
Sullivan said the researchers lived and worked in one of the world’s most remote and challenging environments.
“We’ve seen what this disease can do, based on our experience at Heard Island and McDonald Islands.”
Drone surveys detected more than 13,000 dead southern elephant seal pups on Australia’s Heard Island in 2025 and 2026.
Sullivan said the decision had been made to minimise the risks to researchers and “across the whole Antarctic program” in advance of any mass mortality event.
He said Macquarie Island was unique in that thousands of elephant seal pups were born close to the station every spring.
“No other Australian Antarctic station is in this position, and there are no elephant seal colonies on mainland Australia,” he said.
Sullivan said the government was exploring options for monitoring the situation on Macquarie Island, with a view to “returning expeditioners to the station in coming seasons”.

The SA government said on Friday it would move to confirming H5 bird flu cases in the state through local laboratories. Until now, state-based test results have required verification by the CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness in Geelong. The state government said improvements to its testing processes meant confirmation of H5N1 cases could now be done locally.
The New South Wales government also announced its plans to vaccinate wild populations of little penguins at Manly and Barunguba Montague Island.

The government also said “trial cohorts” of some captive bird populations, including little penguins, Carnaby’s black cockatoos and red-tailed black cockatoos, had received the first vaccinations at Taronga zoo this week.
