articles.title: Himalayan ‘tsunami’: Over 350 dead, 1,400 missing
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino was reported to be among the more than a thousand people missing in the flash floods and landslides that occurred on the Nepal-Tibet border, where the confirmed death…

blocks.caption: ENGULFED Surveillance video at a Nepal-China border crossing shows a massive wall of water, mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing the structure and the entire complex as dozens of people run for their lives below. — CCTV SCREENSHOT VIA AFP

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino was reported to be among the more than a thousand people missing in the flash floods and landslides that occurred on the Nepal-Tibet border, where the confirmed death toll had reached at least 359 people as of Thursday.
The lone Filipino was on the initial record cited by the Nepal Tourism Board, though it was yet to be confirmed by the Philippine government at press time.
The tsunami-like rumble of water and mud struck villages and towns on the path of two rivers—Bhote Koshi and Trishuli—on Wednesday night.

A terrifying clip of surveillance video from the Chinese side of the frontier shows a massive wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing it as dozens of people ran for their lives below.
The surge swept away buses and cars like they were toys.
The US Geological Survey believes the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a flow of debris engulfing homes along the way.

blocks.caption: SWAMPED Local residents watch as a helicopter flies above houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Aug. 27 —AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: According to the Nepal Tourism Board, its preliminary record as of 2:45 p.m. on Thursday (Philippine time) showed 644 travelers reported missing in the affected areas, including one Filipino.
The agency gave no further details about the missing Filipino, saying the information was still being verified and crosschecked with travel agencies and other local authorities.

In Manila, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (Owwa) have started coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos, Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
Based on information from the DFA and Owwa, there are 128 Filipinos in Nepal, mostly women married to Nepalis. Among them are 18 overseas workers.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the disaster.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flash flood yesterday,” Mr. Marcos said in a social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones, and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
Wall of mud, debris

blocks.caption: Aerial views show houses inundated by mud and water in Nuwakot district—AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: The Nepali police on Thursday said they had recovered 162 bodies, as rescue teams rushed to find more than 1,400 people still missing.
Another 823 people, including 579 Nepali and foreign tourists, remained out of contact in Nepal, according to the country’s disaster agency.
Across the border, Chinese state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet claimed three lives while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were still missing.
Raju Bhadel, 56, a businessman in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, recounted receiving a call from his brother-in-law in distress.
“They were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” he said.
Also at Nuwakot, teacher Manok Mishra witnessed “nine trucks being swept away by the floods, including people.”

blocks.caption: Aerial views show houses inundated by mud and water in Nuwakot district—AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: ‘Inland tsunami’
Rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multistory buildings.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians, and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea, and the United States, Nepal’s tourism board said.
Hiking company Himalayan Glacier told Agence France-Presse (AFP) 47 people from a group including two children were missing in Nepal.

The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami, traveling nearly 170 kilometers down the Bhote Koshi valley into Central Nepal,” said environmental historian Ruth Gamble of La Trobe University in Australia.
“It is a popular route for international tourists traveling from Kathmandu to Lhasa,” she added.

blocks.caption: GRIEF A girl cries as she waits for news of relatives missing after flash floods in Bidur, Nepal, on Aug. 27. —AP

blocks.text: Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected. But deaths have been reported from seven Nepali districts in total as the floodwaters raged through to Chitwan in the south, on the border with India.
The Nepali Army was carrying out flights and had rescued scores of people, while others living near the river in danger zones had been told to relocate.
Tibet government officials mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s state-run news agency Xinhua said.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers, and body bags.
Seismic event

blocks.caption: Himalayan ‘tsunami’: Over 350 dead, 1.4K missing

blocks.text: The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear in the hours after it occurred early Wednesday, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
“This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said.

“Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.”
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, warned of the potential for a second flood.

“With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP. —With a report from AFP

articles.title: UN body calls for release of Cumpio, activists from arbitrary detention
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Human rights group Karapatan on Wednesday welcomed the findings of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (UN WGAD), which declared as arbitrary the detention…

blocks.caption: JAIL VISIT Frenchie Mae Cumpio (right) is visited at Tacloban City Jail by UN Special Rapporteur Irene Khan, who was in the Philippines in January on an official trip. — PHOTO FROM IRENE KHAN’S OFFICIAL X ACCOUNT

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Human rights group Karapatan on Wednesday welcomed the findings of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (UN WGAD), which declared as arbitrary the detention of Tacloban community journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio, humanitarian worker Marielle Domequil and human rights worker Alexander Abinguña.
The UN WGAD stated its findings in its opinion report, which was released only recently and first adopted during its 105th session held from March 23 to April 1.

“The UN WGAD opinions reaffirm our position that the charges against Cumpio, Domequil and Abinguña are baseless and trumped-up, that their rights under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights were violated, and that their release from prison is long overdue,” Karapatan secretary general Cristina Palabay said in a statement.
The rights groups called for the release of the three, noting that they have been detained for more than six years following their arrest on Feb. 7, 2020.
Terrorism financing

Cumpio and Domequil were convicted in January by the Tacloban City Regional Trial Court for “terrorism financing” and sentenced to 12 to 18 years in prison. From the Tacloban City Jail, they were transferred in April to the Correctional Institute for Women in Mandaluyong City where they remain detained after their petition for bail was denied by the court. They have appealed their conviction before the Court of Appeals.

“The inordinate delay of the court proceedings that has prolonged their detention is an additional layer of injustice against the three. Their release should immediately be given due course,” Palabay said.
The UN WGAD found a lack of factual and legal basis for the criminal charges against the three, concluding that their deprivation of liberty was arbitrary.
It also determined that their detention stemmed from the exercise of their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association.
Based on the UN body’s report, the three have been targets of Red-tagging and accused of associating with the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People’s Army.
It said the appropriate remedy would be the immediate release of Cumpio, Domequil and Abinguña, along with an enforceable right to compensation and other forms of reparation under international law.
Probe pushed

The UN WGAD also called for a full and independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding their arbitrary detention as it urged authorities to hold accountable those responsible for violating their rights.

articles.summary: The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Friday expressed support for a proposal to restrict internet use among children aged 14 and below.

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 1:26pm

The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Friday expressed support for a proposal to restrict internet use among children aged 14 and below.
At a press conference, DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the proposal has already been taken up in Congress and received support during a recent budget hearing.
“We gave our opinion. Dapat 14 years and below ay restricted na ang use of the internet,” Remulla said.

“But it is not our call. Congress na lang ‘yan.So it was taken up yesterday during the budget hearing and they were in support of it. But we will see how the legal process goes, how the process of the lawmakers does that will result in this,” he added.
Other Stories
The proposal comes amid growing concerns over the exposure of minors to harmful content and individuals who allegedly seek to manipulate or recruit children online.
These concerns were also linked to the fatal shootings in Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City on August 18 and San Jose National High School in Tacloban City on June 22.

Pasig Representative Roman Romulo, House Committee on Basic Education and Culture chair, earlier said the lower chamber is drafting a measure that would impose a total social media and online gaming platform ban on children aged 13 and below, while regulating social media use among those 14 to 17 years old.
Meanwhile, Senator Robin Padilla also sponsored a bill seeking to set 16 as the minimum age for creating and maintaining a social media account. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Please don’t rearrange our shoes when we turn up, paramedics in Japan urge
articles.summary:
It is polite to reposition a guest’s shoes when they arrive, but the emergency services in one city advise just skipping that part

Etiquette, manners and consideration for others are…

blocks.text: Etiquette, manners and consideration for others are integral pillars of Japanese society but there are times when they might go a step too far, according to one city’s emergency services.

The fire department in the central city of Kanazawa has urged people not to tidy up the shoes that paramedic crews have taken off when entering a house, warning it could hinder their ability to get in or out quickly, particularly when carrying someone on a stretcher.

In an Instagram video that has amassed more than half a million views since it was posted on 5 August, the firefighters demonstrate how paramedics leave their shoes positioned at entrances in precise spots so that three stretcher bearers can step straight into them without shaking the patient around, or risking dislodging their oxygen mask.

It is customary for anyone entering a Japanese home to shed their footwear, and for homeowners to rearrange the shoes of guests or customers to face the doorway so that they can slip them on easily when they leave.
Allow Instagram content?

Interviewed by TBS News Dig this week, firefighter Daisuke Yamashita said, “Emergency crews decide the direction of their shoes according to their roles, so if someone changes their position out of kindness, it can interfere with putting them back on and delay the transport of the patient. From our experience, it can result in a loss of about 30 seconds.

“We do appreciate the kindness behind straightening the shoes,” added Yamashita in the video. “During an emergency, it is extremely helpful if people instead prepare the patient’s My Number card [a social security number] or another form of identification in advance.”
Most of the comments underneath the video expressed gratitude at the advice.
“I didn’t know this. I will remember this for the future!” wrote one.

Another user attracted more than 800 likes for suggesting that strict etiquette could perhaps be forsaken at such times: “It’s an emergency. I would just tell them: ‘Please step inside with your shoes on!’”

articles.title: Iran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade chokes Iran’s oil imports
articles.summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a…

blocks.caption: Before the Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz carried around 20% of global crude exports from the Persian Gulf. Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a domestic shortfall.

The visit by Qatar’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman’s top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen Hormuz.

It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called “economic asphyxiation.”
Iranian state television said Al Thani, who is also Qatar’s prime minister, had met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without providing details.
In a statement after the talks, Al Thani said they focused on efforts to de-escalate tensions and boost security in the region.
“Qatar believes that dialogue and diplomacy remain the best way to overcome crises,” he wrote on X.
Qatar’s foreign ministry said they discussed the proposed framework for Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
“Talks stressed the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law,” Al Thani added.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
Fuel shortage

Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough gasoline to cover a shortfall in domestic production.
“Gasoline production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it,” he was quoted by the official IRNA news agency as saying.
In recent days, many Iranians have been seen queuing outside gas stations. Presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei said gasoline quotas would be reviewed, without elaborating.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidized gasoline, making changes to pricing politically sensitive.
As the US seeks to strangle Iran’s economy, Iranian officials have dismissed the measures as “failed policies” that will not force Tehran to change course.
“The country is in an all-out economic war,” said Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in a statement carried by local media.
“We will see that the government … will defeat the enemy on this ground as well,” he added.
Even before the war, Iran’s economy was battered by decades of international sanctions and has long suffered from chronic inflation and a weakening currency.
Talks on Hormuz

Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman, which also overlooks the Strait of Hormuz, over a framework agreement that would establish a “temporary corridor” for shipping and provide for clearing mines Tehran says were laid during the war.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Wednesday said the two countries had agreed on each country’s share of the waters and any revenues collected from managing the waterway.

Tehran has nonetheless insisted that the strait will not be reopened unless Washington meets its demands, including lifting its naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and removing oil sanctions.
Since the war broke out, Iranian forces have required vessels to obtain permission to transit the waterway and struck ships that failed to comply.
Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait — a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.

articles.summary: Palace has suspended classes and government work by midday on Friday, Aug. 28.

blocks.text: Pedestrians struggle with their umbrellas against strong winds during a sudden heavy downpour in Quezon City on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang announced the suspension of government work and classes at all levels in public and private schools in Metro Manila and 16 provinces starting 1 p.m. Friday, Aug. 28, as heavy rains from the southwest monsoon persist.

In a news release, the Presidential Communications Office said Executive Secretary Ralph Recto issued Memorandum Circular No. 132 upon the recommendation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.
The suspension covers:

items: National Capital Region
Abra
Benguet
Ilocos Sur
La Union
Pangasinan
Bataan
Bulacan
Nueva Ecija
Pampanga
Tarlac
Zambales
Batangas
Cavite
Rizal
Oriental Mindoro
Occidental Mindoro

blocks.text: The suspension was ordered due to the expected further enhancement of the southwest monsoon, or habagat, by a low pressure area that has entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility, Malacañang said.
Government agencies providing basic and health services, disaster preparedness and response, and other vital services will continue to operate, it added.
It also directs local chief executives to suspend classes or government work in their respective areas depending on local conditions.
For the private sector, the suspension of work or adoption of alternative work arrangements will be left to management.
Heavy rains over Luzon. The suspension comes as the southwest monsoon, or habagat, continues to bring heavy rain over large parts of Luzon.
PAGASA earlier said Metro Manila, the Ilocos Region, parts of Central Luzon, Calabarzon and Occidental Mindoro may experience heavy rain Friday.
La Union, Benguet, Bataan, Zambales and Occidental Mindoro may receive 100 to 200 millimeters of rain, while Metro Manila and several other provinces could receive 50 to 100 mm.
PAGASA warned that rainfall could be heavier in mountainous and elevated areas, while flooding and landslide risks may be worsened in places already saturated by previous rains.

articles.title: Nepal flash flood 'unlikely' in PH --weather specialist
articles.summary: A weather specialist of weather bureau PAGASA on Friday said he believed that the landslide and flash flood that occurred along the Nepal-Tibet border is unlikely to occur in the Philippines.

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 1:00pm
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.
A weather specialist from PAGASA believes that the flash flood that occurred along the Nepal-Tibet border is unlikely to occur in the Philippines.

“Based on ‘yung ating construction ng mga kailugan po sa ngayon is somehow hindi naman ganoon ka-drastic talaga, hindi comparable doon sa nangyari sa may area ng Himalayas kasi sobrang lawak naman po atsaka ang tataas talaga ng mga bundok nila doon,” PAGASA weather specialist Benison Estareja said in an interview on Super Radyo dzBB on Friday.

(Based on the current construction of our rivers, it is somehow not that drastic and is not comparable to what happened in the Himalayan region, which is much more extensive and has much higher mountains.)

“‘Yung potential energy coming from ‘yung pinakamataas papunta sa ibaba, talagang sobra ‘yung impact. Unlike dito na, yes may tendency na talagang dumami ‘yung tubig, pero ‘yung ragasa po hindi naman siya nakikita halos maladelubyo,” he added.
Other Stories

(The potential energy from the highest point moving down to the lower areas has a tremendous impact. Unlike here, where there is a tendency for the volume of water to increase, but we are not really seeing a massive surge that would cause a catastrophe.)
The flash floods and landslides killed at least 165 people and swept away entire villages.
Rivers, dams
When asked about possible landslides from mountains falling into dams, Estareja said that the country has no glaciers.
He also assured that the the government has a warning system in place.

“Kung magkaroon man ng ganoong instance na sobrang lakas ng ulan sa taas and then nagkaroon ng pagkasira ng gates and then nag burst open ‘yung ating mga rivers. At least po meron tayong mga warnings,” he said.

(If such an instance were to occur where there is extremely heavy rainfall in the upper areas, followed by damage to the gates and the rivers suddenly bursting open, at least we have warnings in place.)

According to Maki Pulido’s report on Saksi, though experts are still looking into the cause of the incident, University of the Philippines (UP) Resillience Institute Executive Director Mahar Lagmay said what occured may be a “debris flow.”
“Parang baha pero may laman na mga bato, graba, buhangin na pagka umagos ay parang wet concrete. Debris flow ang tawag diyan. Boulders na tangay-tangay nung baha na more than 50% ang bato,” he said.

(It is like a flood, but it carries rocks, gravel, and sand, and when it flows, it behaves like wet concrete. That is called a debris flow. Boulders are carried along by the flood, with more than 50% of the flow consisting of rocks.)
Lagmay said a debris flow occurred at Compostela Valley in 2012, where more than 500 people died, while several barangays in Oriental Mindoro were burried in 2015 by rocks from a debris flow.
“Marami tayong bundok. Kapag nagkaroon ng landslide because of a storm, thousands of landslides doon sa mountains, meron tayong source material,” he said.
(We have many mountains. When a storm causes landslides, potentially resulting in thousands of landslides in the mountains, we have a source of material.)
He said that the UP Resillience Institute has identified more than 1,000 places that has communities along the river. —Joahna Casilao/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: DILG: Over 200 BFP personnel under probe over 'slot-for-sale' recruitment scheme
articles.summary: More than 200 personnel of the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) are being investigated over an alleged “slot-for-sale” recruitment scheme, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG)…
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published August 28, 2026 12:56pm
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

More than 200 personnel of the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) are being investigated over an alleged “slot-for-sale” recruitment scheme, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said Friday.
At a press conference, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the investigation covers personnel nationwide and is part of a broader effort to eliminate corruption within the BFP.
“Binabalaan ko na ang lahat ng opisyal ng BFP. Lumabas na kayo ngayon at umamin kayo o hahabulin namin kayo hanggang matapos ang career niyo,” Remulla said.
“Ang iniimbestigahan namin ngayon ay lumagpas ng 200 tao na tungkol sa slots for sale,” he added.
Other Stories

(We are warning all (involved) BFP officials. You better come out and admit your fault or we will go after you until your career ends. We are investigating over 200 people over the slots for sale [scheme].)
The investigation followed an entrapment operation conducted by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) Region 3 in San Fernando City, Pampanga on August 24.
The operation resulted in the arrest of a 32-year-old BFP personnel who was caught accepting P300,000 from the complainant in exchange for securing a position in the bureau.
Other applicants allegedly paid between P100,000 and P800,000 for BFP slots under the illegal scheme.
“It's a P15 billion a year industry,” Remulla said.
A senior BFP officer in Calabarzon allegedly linked to the recruitment scheme was also relieved from their post and placed under restrictive duty pending investigation.
Remulla vowed to clean the BFP and resolve the matter within six months. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst
articles.summary: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel in Kathmandu, Sam Jones and Amy Hawkins

blocks.text: The international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet on Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.
The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.

Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.
Nepali army helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by the devastating flood.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said Nepal army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”
The prime minister’s office said the army was working in tough conditions and had already rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel amid the risky conditions.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the border with India. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
Videos from Wednesday showed a massive wall of water crashing down on the border as people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.
Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.

Tom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.

Nepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.
Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.
“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”

Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”

Kamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”

Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”

People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.

Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.

blocks.caption: Flooding has caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Nuwakot, Nepal.   Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”

More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.
Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.

Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, causing the flood of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.

Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.

“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”

Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.

blocks.caption: People look at the devastation left by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.  Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

blocks.text: Scant information emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.

Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups and experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”
She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.

articles.title: How policy choices left Philippines behind Taiwan in global chip race
articles.summary: Foreign factories aren't enough. What UP researchers say Pax Silica needs:

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines risks repeating the failures of the 1970s Bataan export zone if the vaunted Pax Silica site in New Clark City draws foreign investors without a government-led push into chip design and fabrication, a University of the Philippines study said.

Beyond the manufacturing side, the study points out how the government's historic "paltry" budget for science and technology, an unfocused education system, and decades of brain drain hollowed out the country’s pool of experts, while Taiwan heavily bankrolled its own research and development and aligned its schools with industrial goals.

The study, published last month as a discussion paper by the UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies, compares how Taiwan and the Philippines developed their semiconductor industries after both entered the business in the late 1960s as low-cost sites for the assembly, testing and packaging of chips made elsewhere.

Taiwan spent the three decades that followed building an industry that now spans design, fabrication and advanced packaging — investment that led it to become today's source of about 90% of the world's most advanced chips.
The Philippines, however, is still constrained to back-end assembly and testing, and has yet to build a single wafer fabrication plant, the paper said.

The paper's authors, Lianne Angelico Depante of the National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies in Japan and Kirsten Lianne Mae Dedase of the UP National College of Public Administration and Governance, argue that the vast difference between Taipei and Manila's chip industries was more a product of policy decisions between the 1970s and the 1990s than market forces.
The researchers examined the policies Taipei and Manila governments adopted between the 1970s and the 1990s, when the foundations of both chip industries were laid.

Without domestic fabrication, or the ability to manufacture microchips locally, the Philippines will continue to be "a processor of upstream foreign value rather than a producer of its own," the paper read.
Pax Silica

The research noted that the Philippines is now betting much of its chip industry outlook around the planned 1,619-hectare economic security zone in New Clark City, which President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. touted in his most recent State of the Nation Address.

The zone sits within the larger Luzon Economic Corridor, a logistics network linking Subic, Clark, Manila and Batangas that is being developed with United States backing under the Pax Silica initiative.
The paper argues that this has essentially been done before, the paper contends, with the creation of the Bataan Export Processing Zone (BEPZ) in 1972.

The study notes that the BEPZ was designed "primarily to attract foreign investment and generate employment" through "a combination of fiscal and non-fiscal incentives, including the provision of physical infrastructure and government-guaranteed financing and policies permitting full foreign ownership and duty-free production."
This drew large manufacturers, including Intel and Texas Instruments. Buoyed by this success, the government eventually pursued more economic zones in Baguio, Cavite, and Cebu.
However, the BEPZ itself did not lead to more advanced manufacturing and failed to bring about local technology transfer due to several factors.

Among others, the Bataan zone was far from major academic and commercial centers, as well as remote from Metro Manila. Because of its remote location, its potential to generate knowledge spillovers and facilitate technology transfer among firms was limited, the study read.

"Site selection was not solely determined by economic or logistical factors but also by political considerations, which influenced the placement of several zones and, in some cases, reinforced their spatial disconnect from key hubs of industry and knowledge," the paper read.
The government eventually decided, with the 1995 PEZA law, to largely turn ecozone development over to the private sector.

While the hands-off approach allowed more foreign investors in, the researchers say it turned the nation's industrial parks into isolated "enclaves with minimal integration into the domestic economy."

Unlike Taiwan, which tightly linked its tech zones to national innovation systems, Philippine zones suffer from a "paucity of deliberate policies" to build local supply chains or spur local technology transfer.

Taiwan's own cluster, the Hsinchu Science Park, opened in 1980 next to two engineering schools, National Tsing Hua University and National Chiao Tung University, and within reach of the state research institutes that would later spin off its largest chipmakers.

The study is careful not to present the planned economic zone in New Clark City as doomed. The project under Pax Silica could still anchor a genuine cluster of assembly firms, startups, universities, public research bodies and prospective fabrication and design companies, the study read, but only alongside industrial and fiscal policies that go beyond building roads and ports.
Those would include shared fabrication, design and testing facilities, research consortia for joint work and technology transfer, and dedicated funding for spinoffs and university research.

Without them, the paper warned, the site "risks repeating history and becoming yet another primarily logistics-oriented initiative, while exposing the country to geopolitical risks without commensurate gains in development."
Paltry budget for science and technology
The study also noted that while Taiwan aggressively funded its chip ambitions, the Philippines starved its primary science agency of funding.

Over the years, the Department of Science and Technology has received a "paltry budget" of less than 1% of total national spending. The researchers argued this limited support and funding, especially for research and development, kept back the country's industry from moving beyond low-value assembly lines.

In contrast, Taiwan used public capital to back risky, unproven technologies. The Taiwanese government directly funded up to 49% of the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's initial capital — spinning the global chip giant off from its state research institute, ITRI — and empowered public labs to co-invest alongside private enterprise.
Tech-voc gap and brain drain

Among many differences in both economies' approach to education, the study noted that technical and vocational education and training (TVET) formed the backbone of Taiwan's strategy, while the Philippines left higher education largely to market forces.

Taiwan aligned its school system directly with its industrial goals. By 1980, TVET students in Taiwan "outnumbered their university counterparts by more than 50 percent," providing the necessary backbone of technicians and engineers for its "burgeoning electronics and semiconductor industry."

The Philippines meanwhile was largely hands off and left universities to offer programs based on what it argues was short-term market demand. As a result, students historically "gravitated toward law, business administration, education, and the humanities, leaving science and engineering underrepresented."
TVET in the Philippines is also mostly privately run and tailored toward the service sector rather than manufacturing, the study noted.
This is further compounded by "longstanding cultural norms" where technical and vocational fields were "commonly viewed as less prestigious" than white-collar professions.

The two economies also diverged sharply in how they supported their engineers and scientists. While Taiwan brought back overseas engineers and executives to build domestic tech giants, the Philippines to this day experiences a persistent "brain drain" where professionals would move overseas for better career opportunities.

Manila's efforts to bring its scientists back struggled to gain ground because the domestic economy lacked the commensurate high-tech jobs. The government's Balik (Return) Scientist Program — modeled directly after Taiwan's — has achieved limited success, the paper noted.

Of the 320 scientists who joined the program in the early 2010s, more than half eventually decided to again move overseas because talent retention was severely "constrained by the country's limited industrial base."
What the study recommends
The study lists seven recommendations for developing countries trying to build chip industries.

Among others, it said public research agencies should be given mandates that allow "calculated risk-taking," including the power to incubate spinoff firms and run applied research in design, advanced packaging and lab-scale wafer fabrication.
That "does not imply indiscriminate spending but a willingness to tolerate failure as an inherent part of learning," the paper said.
Governments must also fund capital-intensive segments that private firms avoid "in the absence of state commitment and risk-sharing mechanisms," it said.
For the Philippines, the study proposed a dedicated semiconductor development fund offering equity, matching grants, concessional financing or research subsidies to local firms and startups.
Support should be conditioned on "technology transfer, workforce upgrading, local supplier development, patent generation" and not on profit alone, it said.

articles.title: Danielle Smith takes questions at virtual town hall on data centres in Alberta, NDP calls for pause
articles.summary: Premier Danielle Smith and three of her ministers spent an hour Thursday fielding calls and online questions from Albertans who say they are concerned about artificial intelligence data centres being…

image.caption: Premier Danielle Smith said her government is considering feedback from Albertans who attended town halls to express concerns around data centres. Smith is seen in this photo speaking to media in Calgary on Feb. 1, 2024. (Emilio Avalos/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Premier Danielle Smith and three of her ministers spent an hour Thursday fielding calls and online questions from Albertans who say they are concerned about artificial intelligence data centres being built in the province.

The virtual town hall was tame compared to the two in-person events held earlier this month, where Technology Minister Nate Glubish was repeatedly hit with criticism, profanity and demands for additional safeguards.
For Thursday's call, Albertans could either submit questions online or, if they registered in advance, over the phone.
Moderator Justin Wright, the province's primary care minister, said over 12,500 people had tuned in.
Smith's government has been trying to position Alberta as an ideal destination for data centres, saying they could generate new jobs and billions in royalties and taxes for the province.
The premier has said the town halls are about finding "blind spots" in the government's regulatory framework.
Alberta Ministers face barrage of opposition to data centres

But, as with the previous events, nobody who spoke Thursday expressed any excitement about having the major computing complexes built in the province in the first place. One caller did say he was excited to be on the call with "the premier and her entourage," but he didn't ask a question or mention data centres.

The event started with Smith addressing many of the concerns the government has already heard, including about water use, location selection and setbacks, and potential electricity bill hikes — all issues that callers would bring up.

Water usage was a popular topic, with many callers questioning Smith and her ministers for saying that projects to date — namely the $13-billion campus north of Edmonton being proposed by tech giant Meta — will have limited water use.
The facility is to have a closed-loop cooling system, and both the company and the government have said its annual water use would be equivalent to a golf course.

One caller, identified as David from Calgary, asked why the province wasn't also accounting for the water that will be used by the adjacent $4.6-billion natural gas power plant, built solely to power Meta's facility.
"They'll be using loads of water. I mean, enormous amounts," he said.

items: Alberta minister faces more fury at second town hall on AI data centres

blocks.text: Smith said his point was well taken, but also said other heavy industries use massive amounts of water. She specifically mentioned a pulp mill in northern Alberta that she recently toured, saying it used seven billion litres of water per year.
"We don't say that you're not allowed to use water at all," she said.
Another caller, Peggy, asked why the government was willing to risk bringing in more heavy water users when parts of the province have seen water restrictions in recent years.
"It doesn't seem like a really smart, long-term idea," she said.
The issue of jobs also came up when one caller asked whether Albertans would be prioritized.

Smith said that was the goal, adding it was also why the referendum her government has scheduled for Oct. 19 will feature questions about whether Alberta should take more control over immigration and temporary foreign worker rules.
"That's certainly what I think should be done, and I want to just make sure that Albertans agree with us on that," the premier said.
Thursday's event also saw the government poll callers and those online about whether they supported setbacks to protect communities from having data centres built too close to homes.

items: Alberta Utilities Commission rejects power plant for Olds data centre plan

blocks.text: Proximity to homes is why a provincial regulator rejected a major data centre project last week in the town of Olds, north of Calgary. Smith had said on Wednesday that her government was already considering developing guidance for setbacks.
Wright shared that 57 per cent of respondents "strongly supported" the measure.

He also conducted another poll at the end of the event, asking those on the call to identify their greatest concern about data centres, with options including electricity affordability, grid reliability, water use, or other. The results weren't shared before the call ended.
Thursday's town hall began just hours after the Opposition called for a moratorium on AI data centres until stricter rules are put in place.
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters that Smith's government has rushed ahead and rubber-stamped projects without clear guidelines or by first hearing Albertans' concerns.
Projects should go through impact assessments to ensure significant community benefits, permanent jobs, and that life-cycle plans for when facilities run their course are in place, he said.

items: Man planning protests against data centres as Alberta government announces town hall events

blocks.text: They're the concerns he said his party heard most when it hosted its own data centre town halls over the summer.
"The UCP failed to create a process that Albertans can have confidence in," Nenshi said.
He said his party's proposal would provide certainty for residents and those behind the projects.
The rejection of the Olds proposal, which had been turned down once before for other reasons, represents a government failure for not having clear expectations for developers, Nenshi added.
"There is no framework in place, and they're making it up as they go along," he said.
"Would a company like that want to invest in Alberta again after they were treated this way by the government?"

items: Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered

blocks.text: The province didn't immediately respond to questions about the NDP's call for a moratorium on Thursday.
The issue of reclamation did come up during the town hall when a caller asked who would be stuck with the infrastructure should a data centre be abandoned.
Glubish said it would fall to the province. He said he was confident another company would come in and take the warehouse for "pennies on the dollar."
He also said an abandoned power plant would be considered a new asset for the province, and that the government would look to keep it running so that power is still fed to the electricity grid.
Smith added that reclamation for data centres was different than wind turbines, which her government requires operators to have clean-up plans for before being built.
"We have a high level of confidence that those [data centre] buildings will be able to be used for something else," she said.
The government's fourth and final data centre town hall is scheduled for Sept. 11 in Grande Prairie, though the premier isn't scheduled to attend.

articles.title: ‘Confluence of errors’ led to Belgian tourist Celine Cremer’s death in Tasmanian wilderness, coroner finds
articles.summary: Coroner finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solstice

blocks.text: Overlapping errors, including a lack of preparation in near-freezing winter weather, contributed to the death of a Belgian tourist on a wilderness track.
Celine Cremer set off on a walk at Philosopher Falls in Tasmania’s remote north-west on 17 June 2023 and was reported missing almost 10 days later.
Extensive initial police efforts found no trace of the 31-year-old before private searches organised by her friends and family discovered her remains near a river in January 2026.
In findings published on Friday, the coroner, Madeleine Wilson, ruled Cremer died between 17 and 21 June, 2023 as a result of an accident.
Her death followed a “confluence of errors” that began when she took a walking track towards Magnet Dam after visiting the Philosopher Falls lookout.
“The track to Magnet Dam was not well defined and she wandered off track and became lost,” Wilson said.
“The deviation from the track occurred late in the day, four days before the winter solstice, at which time the afternoon light was starting to fade.”

blocks.caption: Searchers scoured wilderness in 2023 near the Philosopher Falls track in Tasmania in the hunt for Cremer. Her remains were found earlier this year. Photograph: Tasmania police

blocks.text: Overnight temperatures in the area at the time were close to freezing and Cremer had insufficient clothing, including nothing waterproof, Wilson said.
Phone reception was intermittent and she lost her mobile, which was her only form of communication, late in the afternoon on the day she set out.
Her phone was found by a search party of volunteers in December 2025.
Recovered data showed she took several photos and videos between 2.21pm and 2.42pm and used Google maps several times afterwards with the last input recorded at 4.18pm.
It is likely Cremer got lost around 3.49pm and subsequently became disorientated without her phone and mistakenly changed direction, the coroner said.
“It is not possible to determine the route taken once Cremer lost her mobile phone, to her final resting place in the Arthur River,” Wilson said.
It was possible Cremer slipped and fell, or tried unsuccessfully to cross the river.
Cremer had travelled to Australia in 2022 on a working holiday and was planning to return to the mainland four days after the Philosopher Falls walk.
after newsletter promotion
Wilson praised the efforts of a private search company and volunteers which ultimately led to the first discovery of Cremer’s remains.
The police response to the missing person report was appropriate and their search efforts were guided by “accepted methodologies”.
Police efforts were somewhat limited by weather, Wilson said, noting water levels in the Arthur River were significantly higher in 2023 than when her remains were found.

blocks.caption: The car of then-missing Belgian tourist Celine Cremer in northwest Tasmania in 2023. Photograph: Tasmania police/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tasmania Police has committed to a review into the use of private search groups in missing persons investigations, including consideration of formal protocols.
Cremer failed to follow standard safety precautions, such as taking appropriate equipment and telling people where you are going, Wilson said.
“Walkers should familiarise themselves with these standard safety messages before embarking on short walks, day walks or multi-day hikes,” she said.
“Walkers should also be aware that mobile coverage is often intermittent or unavailable in remote areas of the Tasmanian wilderness and should plan accordingly.”

Wilson recommended the local council put up signs at the entrance to the Philosopher Falls track, explaining it is not managed for recreational use and the surface is degraded, uneven and may be hazardous.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, flooding is possible in flood-prone areas under the yellow warning level, including:

articles.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
articles.summary:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor…

blocks.text: In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.
Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

blocks.caption: Meta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.
Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”
It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Protests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya. Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”
The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.
That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

articles.title: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules
articles.summary: The AI startup has been at loggerheads with the Pentagon over the use of AI by the US military.

blocks.text: A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless".

The company argued in the lawsuit that Defense Secretary Pete Hegeth overstepped his authority with the new designation. It followed Anthropic's refusal to allow the military to use its AI models for things that included surveillance or autonomous weapons.
US district judge Rita Lin said in the ruling that citing national security "is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics".
Anthropic welcomed the ruling. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon and the White House for comment.
Anthropic is focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology," a spokesperson told the BBC.
Judge Lin said in the court filing that the Defense Department had acted unlawfully to order firms that do business with the US military to boycott Anthropic.
The Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk in February - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.
It marked the first time an American company had been publicly designated as such.
Anthropic's lawsuit said the government's actions were both "unprecedented and unlawful".
The Claude-maker said its models were not reliable enough to be safely used in weapons systems for the military. It added that it opposed its use for domestic surveillance as a violation of rights.
The Pentagon said at the time that private companies should not be able to constrain military action.

The White House had previously said Anthropic was "a radical left, woke company" attempting to control military activity" and argued the military was beholden to the US Constitution, "not any woke AI company's terms of service".
The Pentagon also argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over what the company could do with its technology.
Anthropic said in its lawsuit that its business had been impacted by the government's actions and its right to freedom of speech had been violated.
Judge Lin said during an earlier round in the lawsuit that the government was trying to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI.
"This appears to be classic First Amendment retaliation," the judge added.

articles.title: South Korea to re-examine 310,000 missing person cases after fake record scandal
articles.summary:
Renewed scrutiny comes after police officer accused of falsifying records in order to close the cases of people who were later found dead

South Korean police will re-examine about 310,000…

blocks.text: South Korean police will re-examine about 310,000 missing persons cases closed over the past three years, prompted by a scandal in which an officer was arrested on suspicion of falsifying records to close files on two people who were later found dead.
The case has drawn national attention, with President Lee Jae Myung ordering an investigation into the police handling of it and telling the force to draw up a reform plan.
The interior minister, Yun Hojung, apologised to the public on Wednesday, saying the case had exposed a structural flaw in the way police handle missing persons.

The scandal has renewed scrutiny of how South Korea handles missing adults. More than 70,000 were reported missing last year, with 99.7% of cases closed without a full-scale search. Of those, 931 people were found dead.
Under Korean law, only children, autistic people, and people with dementia or mental disabilities are formally treated as missing.

That status allows police to request phone location data, issue emergency alerts to every phone in the area and match family DNA. Everyone else is classified as a runaway, with none of those tools automatically available.
The arrested officer worked on the missing persons team at Jeju Western police station on the southern holiday island.

He is accused of closing the file on a 37-year-old woman, Jang Mi-ran, about two and a half hours after her partner reported her missing in mid-May. The officer allegedly told him he had contacted her and that she did not want her location disclosed, but police say they found no record of such a call.
Her body was found on Monday in a palm farm about 400 metres from where she had been staying, 104 days after she was last seen. Police have not established a cause of death.

The same officer is also accused of closing the case of a man in his 60s on the day his family reported him missing in early July. His body was found on Saturday. Separately, two other people reported missing in Jeju were found dead.

The officer has denied wrongdoing, saying he had contacted the two missing people before closing the cases, according to the Jeju Provincial Police Agency. He was arrested this week and faces charges including dereliction of duty and falsifying official electronic records.
The review is due to be completed by November, the Yonhap news agency reported, with any cases suspected of improper handling to be reopened.
In the past decade, politicians have introduced more than 10 bills to extend search powers to missing adults, but none has passed.
Critics say adults should be free to disappear if they choose and warn that police tracking powers would be exploited by creditors chasing debtors and by abusers looking for partners who have fled.

articles.title: Federal judge again halts Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting in midterms
articles.summary:
President’s directive stalls for a second time about a week before the first postal ballots are due to be sent out

A federal judge on Thursday halted – at least for the moment – attempts to…

blocks.text: A federal judge on Thursday halted – at least for the moment – attempts to implement Donald Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting.

The president’s directive stalled for a second time about a week before the first mail ballots are due to be sent out for the rapidly approaching midterm elections. In the US district court, Judge Indira Talwani placed a 14-day hold on the government implementing the order in a case that could be headed back to the supreme court, which on Monday overturned an earlier ruling of hers that had blocked Trump’s order from taking effect.

Talwani wrote in her ruling: “Plaintiff states have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms.”

The latest ruling came in advance of a 3 September hearing after Democrats and voting rights groups refiled their lawsuits to comply with the recent supreme court decision. The high court’s conservative majority did not rule on the legality of Trump’s executive order. Still, it said the legal challenges against it that led Talwani to initially freeze it were filed too soon.
Since then, the administration has issued a formal rule intended to govern whether the US Postal Service will deliver states’ mail ballots – effectively restarting the legal fight.

The whipsawing legal battle has major ramifications for the midterms. Nearly one-third of Americans vote by mail and election officials contend there is not enough time to revise their systems to comply with the new postal service directives.
The postal service says it will not deliver mail ballots unless states provide a list of voters who should receive them and format the envelopes in a certain way.

Democrats and voting rights groups contend the demand is unconstitutional. The constitution, they note, grants states and, in some cases, Congress the power to make election rules – not the president or postal service.
That reasoning led courts to block Trump’s first executive order, issued last year, that sought to change election procedures, such as requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register.
The president has long targeted mail voting – even though he uses it himself – and falsely blames the system for his 2020 election loss.
A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that mail voting fraud occurred in about four cases out of every 10m mail ballots cast.
Trump issued the executive order in March targeting mail voting, his second related to elections since he returned to office.

Opponents quickly sued, but the administration argued the claims were premature because it had not issued rules outlining how it would implement the order. The administration won an initial case in Washington DC, with that reasoning, but Talwani placed injunctions against implementing the order for the November midterms in two separate cases she heard in Boston.
The supreme court’s conservative majority on Monday struck down one of those holds, finding it was premature.

Talwani, nominated to the bench by Barack Obama, removed the second injunction on Wednesday. The plaintiffs then moved to refile their cases, citing the postal service’s publishing of its final rule, in hopes of winning a more durable victory. It is likely the case will again end up in front of the supreme court.

blocks.text: We’re closing this page now and moving our live coverage of the Nepal-Tibet disaster to a new blog here.
You can also see our fresh rundown of what we know on day three and our latest full report, as well as a visual guide to how the flooding unfolded. Thanks for following along.
Summary of the latest: rescuers search for hundreds of missing
Here’s a snapshot of the latest developments in the Nepal-Tibet disaster to bring you up to speed.

items: Rescue teams and military helicopters have been searching on Thursday for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous Nepal-Tibet border after a huge torrent of water and mud swept through communities following a glacier collapse.
More than 390 people were killed, authorities in Nepal and China said, and more than 1,400 were missing, including hundreds of foreigners and pilgrims.

Nepal and China both warned of fresh ⁠flooding risks in the Himalayas. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border faced a “high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake formed by debris blocking a ​river at the flood site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting.

More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 39 from Australia, 33 from the UK and 25 from Canada.
Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
The Red Cross said about 93,000 people might have been affected, while assessments continued in hard-to-reach areas. It launched an emergency appeal for $31m to respond to the disaster.

blocks.caption: A local resident cleans debris from a drinking water tap after the floods in Devighat in the Nuwakot district of Nepal on Thursday. Photograph: Sunil Pradhan/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

items: US president Donald Trump said the flooding was terrible to see, describing how “strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks”.
Nepalese officials said dozens of bridges were destroyed and nearly 40km of roads damaged, complicating search efforts.

The Nepalese army had rescued more than 100 people by helicopter, an army spokesperson said. Army teams also evacuated people trapped inside facilities linked to the Trishuli hydropower project, he said. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for medical care.
Rescuers found bodies in Nepal’s Chitwan district, hundreds of kilometres downstream from the hardest-hit areas.
The Nepal Red Cross Society said it had shifted focus from rescue to large-scale relief operations in the flood-hit districts.
China’s premier, Li Qiang, arrived in Gyirong on Thursday to direct rescue efforts, alongside 500 military and paramilitary personnel.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said he ordered the release of $2m from the UN’s central emergency response fund to help with medical care, shelter and water.With agencies

blocks.text: Continuing now from the post on the latest breakout by country of at least 1,468 people missing from the Nepal-Tibet disaster, care of the AFP news agency.

These numbers are from the Nepal tourism board’s updated figures, unless noted.

Spain: four (Spanish foreign ministry. The Nepal tourism board put the figure at three)

Portugal: three (Portuguese foreign ministry and Nepal tourism board). The foreign ministry also said one person had been located.
Netherlands: two
Italy: three missing (Italian foreign ministry), with two rescued (Nepal tourism board)

blocks.caption: A truck stuck in mud in Bidur, in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, after being swept away by flood waters on Thursday.  Photograph: China news service/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ireland: two

Rescued
Switzerland: one
