Nationalities unconfirmed
The figure on missing that China released on Thursday from its side of the border included 260 foreigners, but no breakdown on nationalities was provided.
Eight people whose nationalities had yet to be confirmed had been rescued, the Nepal tourism board said.
China warns of high flood risk from rising lake

Chinese authorities have warned that an artificial lake formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border faces a “high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream”, according to state media.

“According to forecasts, inflows into the lake could reach about 3 million cubic meters over the next three days amid continued rainfall, increasing the risk of a breach that could send floodwaters downstream and potentially cause further damage in areas including Gyirong Port and elsewhere downstream”, state news agency Xinhua said late on Thursday, cited by AFP.
Almost 1,500 missing – the numbers by country
More than 1,400 people are still missing and 392 have been confirmed dead after the flash floods and landslides on the Nepal-Tibet border.

Here’s the latest tally of the missing, care of Agence France-Presse. As it points out, double-counting of dual nationals, matching bodies with people listed as missing and the chaos of a calamity can all contribute to fluctuations both upwards and downwards in the figures.
At least 1,468 missing in total
Nepal’s disaster agency said 910 people were unaccounted for on Thursday, including at least 517 foreigners. It did not give a breakdown of the nationalities of the foreigners.
Across the border with Tibet, China said 558 people – including 260 foreigners – were missing. Together, the total missing on both sides of the border is 1,468.
Nepal’s tourism board on Thursday put the number of missing tourists and travellers – Nepali and foreign – at 667 in total. Its further breakdown of the nationalities is included below.
Nepal

The new Nepal tourism board figures on Thursday said that 127 Nepali visitors were among the 667 it listed as missing. It was not immediately clear how many Nepali residents of the area were unaccounted for.
China

China’s foreign ministry said nearly 100 Chinese nationals were among the missing in Nepal. The Nepal tourism board said 24 Chinese were unaccounted for. That was in addition to the 558, including 260 foreigners, missing on its the Chinese side of the border.
India
Nepal’s latest tourism board figures showed 178 people from India were missing. Eleven others had been rescued.
United States

Ninety US citizens were missing, the state department said, adding that three had been rescued and it was not aware of any US fatalities. The Nepal tourism board put the figure at 65 unaccounted for earlier Thursday.
Ukraine

Ukraine’s foreign ministry said on Thursday evening that the total number of Ukrainians listed as “out of contact” was 56. “According to the verified information available, there are currently no Ukrainians among the injured or deceased as a result of the disaster,” it added.

blocks.caption: A member of the Nepalese security forces with a sniffer dog search for survivors in Nuwakot district on Thursday.  Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Malaysia
Prime minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday that more than 50 Malaysians in Nepal were unreachable. The Nepal tourism board put the number at 51.
Australia
The number of Australian nationals missing following the floods has risen to 39, foreign minister Penny Wong said on Friday.
United Kingdom
Thirty-three people from the UK were missing, the Nepal tourism board figures showed.
Canada

The tourism board said 25 Canadians were among the missing on Thursday. But Canadian foreign minister Anita Anand said the government was “aware of 30 Canadians and permanent residents in Nepal and Tibet whose whereabouts and well-being have not yet been confirmed”.
South Korea

South Korea’s foreign ministry said on Wednesday that nine hydropower workers were out of contact in the Rasuwa district following the floods. The Nepal tourism board said Thursday that four South Koreans had been rescued.
To be continued in another post
Almost 40 Australians missing in floods

blocks.caption: Nick Visser

blocks.text: Nick Visser
The number of Australians missing in the Nepal floods has increased from 35 to 39, the Australian foreign minister has said, also pledging A$5m ($3.6m) in aid for affected communities.
Penny Wong said the Australian government was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response” to the flooding.

double quotation markWe understand at least 39 Australians are among those reported missing. Australian officials are working urgently to confirm their welfare and provide assistance to those affected.
Wong said on Friday the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.
double quotation markThe extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.
Further to the last post, the formation of a barrier lake was captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team on Thursday, state broadcaster CGTN reported.
The footage showed masses of brown water ​accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet. The water had already submerged bushes and trees and appeared to push against a barrier of debris and stones.
Rainfall forecast over the coming week will exacerbate the threat, Chinese state media said, citing the Chinese water resources ministry.
“The volume of water is continuing to increase, ⁠and so is the risk,” Zhu Jinfeng, a researcher at the water resources ministry’s hydrology ​department, told state broadcaster CCTV.
Heeding ​the warning, some rescue workers in ​Nepal began moving towards higher ground on Thursday, Reuters reports.
Among them was Pawan Koirala, who ​began moving away from ‌the river bed along ​with his team of ​13 after the warning was issued. He said:
double quotation markWe are here for rescue and don’t want to be near the danger zone.

blocks.caption: A rescuer helps a resident through heavy mud in Trishuli, Nepal. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Fears rising lakes could burst and cause new floods

Nepal and China have both warned of fresh ⁠risks of flooding in the Himalayas as two lakes that have developed on either side of their border threaten to burst in a region still ⁠grappling with the disastrous flash flooding.
Both countries have blamed the flood on a glacier collapse that pushed rock, ice, mud and debris into river systems ⁠in the mountains.
Nepal’s disaster authority issued a notice on Thursday warning that a lake formed by debris blocking a ​river at the flood site was rising and ‌at risk of bursting.

“Residents ‌of the lower banks ... passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special ‌caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas,” the authority said, cited by Reuters.

blocks.caption: Satellite imagery showing a lake that formed at the site of the glacier collapse, amid fears the lake could burst. Photograph: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/Reuters

blocks.text: China warned that 3m cubic metres of water – the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools – are expected to flow into an already dammed lake on its side of the border over the next three days, creating a high risk of a breach, with peak flow expected around Monday.
Red Cross launches $31m appeal for disaster response
The Red Cross has launched an emergency appeal for $31m to respond to the catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet.

The Switzerland-based International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) launched the drive for 25m Swiss francs a day after releasing 1m francs to support immediate lifesaving efforts.
The appeal is to cover the emergency disaster response as well as medium- and longer-term recovery over the next two years.

“While we are getting a clearer picture of the scale of devastation, we know that entire villages were washed away and needs will grow in the coming hours and days,” IFRC secretary general Jagan Chapagain said in a statement.
double quotation markCommunities that have lost homes and livelihoods will need sustained support as they recover and rebuild.
The IFRC said:

double quotation markCurrent estimates suggest around 93,000 people may have been affected, while assessments continue in hard-to-reach areas. The remoteness of the affected areas, combined with damaged infrastructure, is making it harder both to assess the full scale of the disaster and to deliver assistance to people who need it most.

When Suman Shrestha opened his phone at work and saw vision of a thick, muddy wall of flood water smashing into towns in his country of birth, he almost did not believe what he was seeing, write Henry Belot and Kat Wong.
“It was awful – I called my family to see if this was really happening and to see if the news reports were right,” says Shrestha, who moved to Australia from Kathmandu in 2017.

It wasn’t long until the truth hit home. Like many of the 210,000 people who were born in Nepal but now call Australia home, Shrestha has spent the last 24 hours scrambling to find out if his loved ones are safe.
“I can see that lots of my friends are missing,” says Shrestha, who now lives in Gosford. “We can’t get in contact with them because the communications have been cut off in that area.”

Nearly 1,300 people are missing and at least 389 have been killed in Nepal and Tibet by the flood, which was caused by an avalanche of ice and rock on Wednesday. At least 39 Australians have been reported missing in the area, including a child as young as 11.
Number of Australians missing in Nepal increases to 39
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong has confirmed the number of Australians missing in the Nepal floods has increased overnight from 35 to 39.

In a statement on Friday morning, Wong said the government was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response to the catastrophic floods along the Nepal-China border, including through a $5 million assistance package for affected communities.”
“We understand at least 39 Australians are among those reported missing. Australian officials are working urgently to confirm their welfare and provide assistance to those affected.
She said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.
“The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.”

blocks.caption: Security personnel rescue flood victims in Nuwakot, Nepal following the outburst from a glacial lake in Tibet. Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
Floodwaters inundate homes and damage local infrastructure, while rescue and relief operations continue in the affected area. Photograph: Sanjit Pariyar/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
A man walks past a house damaged by flash floods in Devighat, Nuwakot, Nepal. Photograph: Sunil Pradhan/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: A nurse said his relatives were “swept away” by the devastating flash floods in Nepal, as he launched a fundraiser to support those affected by the disaster.
Rajendra Pudasaini, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said Nepal was witnessing an “irreplaceable loss”, adding that the country was “paying the price for global warming”.

The nurse, who works at Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow, Essex, told the Press Association: “My wife’s auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well.
“They’re gone. The speed the water came, they couldn’t be saved, they were just swept away.
“The town and the villages were swept away, it’s a tragic thing.”
Officials said about 90 US citizens remained unaccounted for Thursday. Many of the missing were on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.
Among those on a guided tour was Venus Rajnikant Patel, a 45-year-old Indian-born US citizen who recently moved from St Louis to Cincinnati to help his family.
Patel’s friend Jolene Gosha said she and her friends knew Patel was in Nepal and were devastated when they realised he was staying at a hotel along the border where the floods swept through.
“We’re just hoping, hoping that by some chance he was able to climb his way out of it,” Gosha told the AP news agency.
“I don’t want to give myself false hope because I know the reality is that he’s probably not with us.”
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said the number of out-of-contact foreign nationals had increased to 517.

articles.byline: Robert Mackey (now); Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell and Tom Ambrose (earlier)

blocks.text: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'
Donald Trump summoned the press pool to the Oval Office to witness him signing an executive order that directs the Department of the Interior to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
This comes after trade talks between Canada collapsed over the weekend and led to a fray of tariffs between Washington and Ottawa.
Trump claimed the name change was something “I’ve been thinking about for a long time”.

“Canada treats us very badly,” the president said. “People oftentimes they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with on trade, and I said that’s easy. Canada, they are the worst, and they feel entitled, and just we can’t have that.”

A 50% tariff on several Canadian imports kicked in on Saturday, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

This, of course, is not the first time the president has made renaming a body of water a priority. At the beginning of his second term in office he issued an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America”.

Trump appeared to joke that there could be more to come: “We have a Gulf and we have a Lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’, Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney noted. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”

blocks.text: Trump posts presidential rankings with himself at the top and 11 previous presidents missing

Two minutes before Air Force One landed in Houston on Thursday, Donald Trump posted a visual ranking of US presidents on his social media platform that described him as the “greatest” president, in a list that omitted, without explanation, 11 of his predecessors.

As critics of the president quickly pointed out, the illustrated ranking of presidents was an altered version of one published in Life magazine on 1 November 1948. The original illustrated an article about the rankings compiled by the Harvard professor Arthur M. Schlesinger Sr. who polled 55 historians, journalists and political scientists and asked them to rate presidents in one of five categories: great, near great, average, below average and failure.

In the article published the day before the 1948 election, Schlesinger explained that he had left out three presidents, William Henry Harrison who died after a month in office; James Garfield, who was shot four months after his inauguration; and Harry Truman, who was still serving out the term his predecessor Franklin D Roosevelt had been elected to before his death.
The date of the illustration explains why another eight presidents are missing from the list that puts Trump at the top.
Dwight Eisenhower, John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson, Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, Ronald Reagan, George H W Bush and George W Bush all, of course, were elected after 1948.

But the graphic was updated to add not just Trump, who was two years old when the original was published, alone in a new category “greatest” but also to add to the list of “failures” at the bottom the names and images of Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Jimmy Carter.

The only other president to serve since 1948 to be added to the list was Bill Clinton, who, perhaps by dint of having socialized with Trump, made his way into the “average” category, along with Herbert Hoover, whose reputation has fallen since 1948.

The original Schlesinger list was topped by six presidents: Abraham Lincoln, George Washington, Franklin Roosevelt, Woodrow Wilson, Thomas Jefferson and Andrew Jackson. Only Lincoln was rated that way by all 55 of the experts.
US Geological Survey changes Lake Ontario to Lake America at Trump's order

Within hours of Donald Trump’s order, the US Geological Survey officially changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in its Geographic Names Information System on Thursday. “The base maps for GNIS are in the process of being updated to reflect this name change,” the agency says on its website.
Trump's Great Lakes declaration echoes first-term 'Sharpiegate'

The Oval Office event on Thursday in which Donald Trump summoned the White House press corps and had them record him signing an executive order rebranding Lake Ontario to “Lake America” came one day after he first announced his intention to do so on TikTok.
In that social media video, also recorded in the Oval Office, Trump scratched out the name of the lake and scrawled his preferred name in a black Sharpie marker.
Trump’s video was quickly mocked by a Canadian satirist and even the governor of Wisconsin.
By Thursday, that hand-drawn alteration to the map had been replaced by a more polished map with the new name displayed on an easel beside Trump’s desk as he signed his order, also using a Sharpie.

blocks.caption: A map labeling Lake Ontario as “Lake America” was displayed in the Oval Office on Thursday as Donald Trump signed an executive order amid the ongoing trade war he started with Canada.  Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

blocks.text: The image of Trump taking a Sharpie to a map, and then having a more polished version of his alterations presented to the media in the Oval Office, echoed an incident during his first term, when he insisted that a hurricane might hit Alabama, and then refused to admit that he had been wrong.

In that case, when Trump invited the press corps into the Oval Office, on 4 September 2019, he showed a forecast map that he had altered with a black marker, presenting it as proof that he had been right and the National Weather Service wrong, when he warned residents of Alabama earlier that week that they were in the likely path of Hurricane Dorian.

blocks.caption: In 2019, Donald Trump held up a chart that showed the original projected track of Hurricane Dorian from the National Weather Service that he had altered by drawing a black line on it to suggest that Alabama might be hit. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

blocks.text: In a section of her memoir on “Sharpiegate”, Trump’s then press secretary, Stephanie Grisham, confirmed that Trump had made the alteration himself.

Before calling in the media, Grisham wrote, Trump had expressed anger that the map, then a week-old projection of the storm’s likely path “sitting on an easel by his desk”, showed the hurricane threatening Florida and Georgia but not, as he’d tweeted, Alabama.
Trump then took a Sharpie from his desk, Grisham recalled, and drew a black line to include Alabama in the path, insisting to his staff that this was the original projection for the storm.

Grisham, whose book is littered with the remains of half-truths and outright lies she’d told on Trump’s behalf, claimed that Trump was right about the threat to Alabama, despite the fact that none of the forecast cones predicting the storm’s path ever included the state.
Michelle R Smith

A senior Democratic senator is calling for a criminal investigation into the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, following reporting by the Guardian that indicated he lied during Senate confirmation hearings last year.
Ron Wyden of Oregon said: “RFK’s platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake. There are consequences for lying to Congress.”
The Guardian’s reporting was based on letters that were obtained – by this news outlet and the Associated Press – following a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Wyden said in a statement to the Guardian that he would be pressing Republican colleagues, who currently control the Senate, to issue a criminal referral of Kennedy to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. “And when Democrats retake the majority in the Senate, RFK will be at the top of the list of Trump officials the finance committee will hold accountable for endangering American families,” he said. Wyden currently serves as the top Democrat on the finance committee.
Trump turned acronym for the Great Lakes from Homes to Shame, Democrats say

After Donald Trump brought a Sharpie to the knife fight with Canada he started, by ordering the federal government to start calling Lake Ontario “Lake America”, Democrats pointed out that the change would ruin the acronym for the five Great Lakes – Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior – taught to schoolchildren: Homes.
An acronym for the Great Lakes used to be HOMES,” New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, posted. “Thanks to Donald Trump, it’s now SHAME.”
Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, followed by sharing audio of children singing a song that uses the Homes acronym as a mnemonic.
The Michigan Democratic party chair, Curtis Hertel also invoked the ruined acronym in a statement.

“As Trump renames Lake Ontario and changes the Great Lakes’ acronym from HOMES to SHAME, what’s actually shameful is Trump’s reckless trade war with Canada that’s throwing our state’s economy into chaos and causing costs to skyrocket even higher,” Hertel said. “Michiganders need relief, not a rebrand – and we’re ready to hold every Michigan Republican accountable for standing with Trump, this stupid stunt, and their cost-raising agenda.”
Fired Stars and Stripes journalists sue the Pentagon, and Hegseth, for wrongful termination

Three journalists who were fired by the Pentagon from a US government-funded news outlet sued the US Department of Defense in federal court in Washington DC on Thursday arguing that their dismissals were illegal and violated their First Amendment rights to free speech.

The three journalists were all employees of Stars and Stripes, which their court filing calls “the U.S. military’s independent news source since the Civil War with a long history of editorial independence, free from news management or censorship by military command.”

The news outlet’s former publisher, Max Lederer, editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and Middle East correspondent, Lara Korte, allege, in the language of the complaint, that the defense department and the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, “are attempting to fire Plaintiffs for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations, its need to reach all servicepersons, and in retaliation for their publication of a news report on deteriorating conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln during its extended tour of duty in the Mid-East.”
Slavin says he was dismissed for supposed “insubordination” during an interview with CBS News in which he objected to potential censorship by the US military. Korte took part in the same interview.

“The spark that moved Defendants to act was a news report published by Stripes on August 11, 2026,” the suit alleges. “The article broke a major story about deteriorating conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln. It reported that the aircraft carrier’s 5,000 Sailors have endured food and water shortages, disrupted mail service, long workdays, and little time off for months on end, and that the long deployment and physical hardships were impacting Sailors’ physical and mental health”.

The day after that article was published by Stars and Stripes, the suit contends, “Defendants ordered Plaintiff Max Lederer, Stripes’ Publisher, to present Notices of Separation to Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte. The notices charged them with Insubordination for the statements they made five and one-half weeks earlier on CBS”.

“Stripes’ historical editorial independence is critical to its core mission of gathering and providing unbiased, credible journalism to the U.S. military community, particularly servicemembers and their families stationed overseas,” the suit also says.

“Lederer did not deliver the notices,” the suit explains. “Instead, he decided then and there to retire, and informed the Stripes’ staff via email. Mr. Lederer took this step because he did not want to be part of Defendants’ scheme to illegally punish Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte for exercising their First Amendment rights.”

Lederer was dismissed shortly after announcing his impending retirement, effective at the end of September. He said the Pentagon had installed a new deputy publisher, an active duty service member, under him at the newspaper without his prior knowledge.
Ontario is an indigenous name that predates both the US and Canada, Canadian prime minister explains
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, points out on social media that the name of the lake Donald Trump presumed to rename on Thursday comes from the language of the indigenous Wendat people.

“The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big’, Carney wrote. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America.”

“We know that America is changing,” Carney added. “Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
As a Canadian government website explains, the country’s name is also derived from an indigenous word.

double quotation markThe name “Canada” likely comes from the Huron-Iroquois word “kanata,” meaning “village” or “settlement.” In 1535, two Aboriginal youths told French explorer Jacques Cartier about the route to kanata; they were actually referring to the village of Stadacona, the site of the present-day City of Québec. For lack of another name, Cartier used the word “Canada” to describe not only the village, but the entire area controlled by its chief, Donnacona.
New York congressman denounces Trump's Lake Ontario rebranding stunt

Among those deeply unimpressed by Donald Trump’s stunt to direct federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario and Lake America is Tim Kennedy, a Democratic congressman who represents a western New York district that borders Ontario and co-chairs the bipartisan House Northern Border Caucus on US-Canada affairs.
Kennedy said in a statement on Thursday:

double quotation markIf Donald Trump spent half as much time trying to make life more affordable as he does trying to rename bodies of water, working families might actually be able to afford their rent, utility bills, and food costs. His pathetic proposal to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” proves what we already know him to be: a petty, vindictive, failed president. By declaring economic war on Canada, our strongest ally and New York’s largest trading partner, President Trump is waging that same war on border communities like Western New York, and we have been paying the price. Canadian tourism to New York is down 26 percent and Canadian spending is down 28 percent. After picking fights with our allies and losing illegal wars of choice with our adversaries, President Trump is cementing his place as the worst president in the history of our country.
Here's a recap of the day so far

items: Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”. This comes as the trade war between the US and Canada escalated in recent days, and has seen both countries levy tariffs on hundreds of each other’s imports. The renaming of bodies of geographic features to spite neighbors and exert national pride is a familiar play for Trump, who issued a similar order rebranding the Gulf of Mexico as “the Gulf of America” at the start of his second term.

Trump also told reporters that he’s had “good talks” with Russian president Vladimir Putin, and insisted that “he’s not going to be attacking a Nato territory”. This comes after speculation continues to circulate around CIA director John Ratcliffe’s covert visit to Moscow this week, and reports that have emerged that say the spy chief’s trip was expressly to convince Putin to not take action against Nato allies.

Documents obtained by the Guardian and interviews with military leadership show the war in Iran has depleted the US Navy’s budget. Consequently, the service branch has had to reallocate money intended for its payroll and from other reserves to fund combat operations. The financial strain comes after the protracted war has depleted US weapons stockpiles and led to counterattacks on bases throughout the region.

House Democrats have launched an investigation into Donald Trump Jr’s venture capital firm, 1798 Capital. The president’s son serves as a partner for the firm, and now Democrats on the judiciary committee are asking the company’s founders to turn over records to detail the firm’s “miraculous” recent success. But Democrats likely have little authority to enforce that request while they remain a minority in Congress. More here

Karoline Leavitt departs from her role as the White House press secretary. President Trump’s outgoing press secretary, who had been a key mouthpiece for the administration since the start of Trump’s second term, addressed reporters for perhaps the last time earlier today. Leavitt described the parting as “bittersweet” and told the press pool that she would “miss you guys.”

Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr appears to have lied during congressional hearings last year. Newly obtained documents show that Kennedy lied to lawmakers last year about the intent of his 2019 visit to Samoa. In the hearings, ahead of his confirmation as the nation’s top health official, Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine crusader, told lawmakers that his trip to the island had “nothing to do with vaccines”. But the newly uncovered documents undermine that testimony, including one in which Kennedy told the Samoan prime minister that he wanted to study vaccination on the island. Kennedy’s visit came months ahead of a measles outbreak on the island that killed more than 80 people.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has left Washington for Houston, Texas to attend a Republican National Committee (RNC) fundraiser and campaign on behalf of attorney general Ken Paxton, who is vying to win the US Senate seat in the state.
Canada drops US seafood from sweeping tariff list
While the US and Canada continue to escalate a tit-for-tat trade war, Canadian officials have opted to back down from tariffs on a particular American export: seafood.

In a social media post on Thursday, Canada’s Department of Finance said it would remove seafood and fish products from a slate of counter-tariffs prepared against the United States. Canadian officials said the move was intended to “protect against broader economic harms”, even as the nation retaliates against the new US duties.
After a tentative deal between the two nations fell apart last week, US tariffs against Canada took effect, and Canadian authorities responded in kind.

Susan Collins, a Republican Senator from Maine facing a competitive re-election race this year, said in a social media post that she was grateful to the Canadians for pulling back from seafood tariffs. If imposed, she said, such a measure would have been devastating to her state’s lobster industry.
“I urge the US to respond to this show of good faith from our Canadian friends by returning to the negotiating table and working to amicably resolve this trade dispute,” Collins wrote.

Chuck Edwards, the North Carolina Republican facing a censure vote in Congress over allegations that he sexually harassed a pair of staffers, has issued a letter urging his colleagues to reject the disciplinary measure.

A report early this month by the House ethics committee recommended Edwards’ censure on the grounds that he’d engaged in inappropriate conduct toward a pair of young female staffers. That conduct, according to the committee, included sending lavish gifts and affectionate notes to the women, as well as inviting them to “intimate dinners and vacations”.

Edwards, in a letter dated earlier this week, said the committee –which argued the congressman’s actions made the women feel uncomfortable and pressured – overstepped in equating his conduct to misconduct or sexual harassment. “An affectionate friendship is not a sexual proposition,” Edwards wrote. “A gift is not sexual misconduct. A compliment is not sexual misconduct. Poetry is not sexual misconduct. Socializing with a colleague is not sexual misconduct. Caring deeply about someone with whom you have worked and come to know for years is not sexual misconduct.”

In light of the committee’s findings, Edwards abandoned his campaign for reelection earlier this month. North Carolina Republicans selected Jennifer Balkcom, a member of the state’s House of Representatives, as the party’s replacement nominee for the general election.
Trump insists that Putin will 'not be attacking a Nato territory' as speculation circulates after CIA director's visit to Moscow
Donald Trump told reporters today that he’s had “good talks” with Russian president Vladimir Putin, and insisted that “he’s not going to be attacking a Nato territory”.

This comes after speculation continues to circulate around CIA director John Ratcliffe’s covert visit to Moscow this week, and reports that have emerged that say the spy chief’s trip was expressly to convince Putin to not take action against Nato allies.
Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'
Donald Trump summoned the press pool to the Oval Office to witness him signing an executive order that directs the Department of the Interior to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
This comes after trade talks between Canada collapsed over the weekend and led to a fray of tariffs between Washington and Ottawa.
Trump claimed the name change was something “I’ve been thinking about for a long time”.

“Canada treats us very badly,” the president said. “People oftentimes they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with on trade, and I said that’s easy. Canada, they are the worst, and they feel entitled, and just we can’t have that.”

A 50% tariff on several Canadian imports kicked in on Saturday, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

This, of course, is not the first time the president has made renaming a body of water a priority. At the beginning of his second term in office he issued an executive order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America”.

Trump appeared to joke that there could be more to come: “We have a Gulf and we have a Lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

Trump administration officials are seeking to radically accelerate the deportation of hundreds of thousands of Haitians who were previously living in the US under the aegis of a humanitarian program, according to documents obtained by The New York Times.

The Times reports that the administration is seeking to start deportation flights to Haiti weekly – as opposed to its previous pace of once a month. If put into effect, that could increase the number of Haitians flown out of the country by hundreds of people per month.

The Trump administration has deemed the island nation safe enough for those who fled it to return, even as the country remains mired in anarchy and gang conflict. The violence there has led the administration to reroute deportation flights away from the embattled Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince, to a smaller city 120 miles away.

The more than 300,000 Haitians slated for removal from the country were previously allowed to work and reside in the US under Temporary Protected Status. But President Trump has taken aim at their inclusion in that program since early in his second term, and was able to terminate it for Haitians after a June supreme court ruling cleared the administration’s path.

articles.title: Tate brothers blast US jail conditions as they seek bail in UK extradition fight
articles.summary: Andrew and Tristan Tate's legal team argued in a Miami court that the two were not a flight risk.

blocks.text: Andrew and Tristan Tate have told a Florida court they should be released from jail so they can fight extradition to the UK on charges of rape and trafficking.
Wearing tan jail uniforms, the brothers maintained they did not commit the alleged crimes as they slammed conditions in US custody.

Government lawyers argued that the two were a flight risk and had bragged about having multiple passports, while defence attorneys said the two social media influencers' high profile would make it almost impossible for them to flee.
US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis will issue a written ruling at a later date on whether to grant bail to the dual British-US citizens. The two were arrested in Miami on 19 July.
During Thursday's hearing, defence lawyers said the pair had complied with the terms of their release while they battled the UK charges and another case in Romania.
US authorities took the men into custody last month after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled dozens of new charges against them.
The British authorities have until 16 September to submit a full extradition request.
The brothers, who arrived in court in shackles, were questioned in turn by their defence attorneys and government lawyers as they took the stand.
Andrew Tate, 39, declared he has "never committed the crimes I'm accused of".
Tristan Tate, 38, described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little sunlight and exercise.
"It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he told the court, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
"It's death by scurvy," he said, adding that he had lost 14lb (6.3kg).
The British Embassy filed court documents asking the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK pursues extradition.
US government lawyers pushed back against the brothers' claims that they had exaggerated their wealth to massage their online personas.
The federal attorneys said the Tates had access to resources that could help fund an escape and they had bragged about having multiple passports.
But Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer, testified that to support himself financially, he "had to go back to the boxing ring against heavier, younger opponents", according to CBS News.
"I've said some stupid things, but sometimes you have to shake the internet to get noticed," he testified about his online statements, according to CBS.
"This is the reality of the internet.
"I'm being treated like El Chapo," he added, referring to the Mexican drug kingpin, "but I have a perfect record in the court system".
Under questioning from his attorney, Joseph McBride, Andrew Tate denied he was a human trafficker.
The defence also called Natasha Sesay, from England, to testify in support of releasing Andrew Tate.
She described a five-year romantic relationship, saying she had had one child with him and was expecting a second.
"It's nice having him at home," she told the court, reports CBS.
Sesay also said that despite his online persona, Andrew Tate "has never ever been violent toward women", according to CBS.
The UK has brought a total of 59 criminal charges against the Tates, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.
The British authorities filed 21 charges last year against the brothers, then 38 additional counts last month.
The combined charges involve seven accusers, UK prosecutors said.
The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.
"If I go to England they will lock me up," Tristan Tate said on the stand in Miami on Thursday, "and take everything I've ever worked for".
He also said the Romanian charges had "destroyed my entire life", reports CBS.
"They took everything, even the savings accounts for their [his children's] college funds. This case is make or break for me."
The Tates built an influencer empire in the so-called manosphere, showcasing a lifestyle of conspicuous wealth and excess.
Andrew Tate accumulated millions of followers among an audience of primarily young men.
The White House has said President Donald Trump will not intervene in the extradition case of the brothers, who have been vocal supporters of him.

blocks.text: British Columbia
A third grizzly in a family of four well-known bears in the West Kootenay has been killed.
Wildlife officials say bear had spent most of its life eating food from humans and was deemed high-risk
Listen to this article

blocks.caption: Three out of four grizzlies in a family that was frequenting Nelson, B.C., have been killed. (The Ursa Project)

blocks.text: A third grizzly in a family of four well-known bears in the West Kootenay has been killed.
A sow and three yearlings attracted attention in the community of Nelson as they travelled throughout the community.
Wildlife officials said they had become a danger as they were habituated to humans and rummaged through yards and garbage.

The mother bear, which had previously been relocated from Nelson and returned, was killed earlier this month as was one of its yearlings, which the B.C. Conservation Officer Service said was not a suitable candidate for relocation due to its age and health. The young bear walked with a limp, either from injury or deformity.

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior
Grizzly bear family returns to Nelson, B.C., after attempted relocation

blocks.text: The two other yearlings, a male and female, were relocated but soon turned up again in the community of Christina Lake.
While the female has since moved on, officials say the male continued to frequent residential neighbourhoods and was deemed unsuitable for a second relocation attempt.
The service said Thursday that "the male yearling was dispatched, in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines."
Poor food sources
Provincial wildlife biologist Garth Mowat said the "bears were really habituated to people."

"We had lots of good indication that the bears had been eating human food for most years of their lives. We did this translocation as kind of a last effort and a hope that these bears would revert to wild food and we could save part of the family group."
Andrew Milne with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service said killing bears is only used as a last resort.

items: Young grizzly bear with limp killed in Nelson, B.C., sparks rally

blocks.text: "Killing wildlife in the name of public safety takes a toll on all these officers," he said. "We don't take these decisions lightly and we try to do as much as we can with what we have."

Mowat said with drought conditions throughout the B.C. Interior, berry crops are poor and more bears will be looking to come into communities in search of food. Officials are once again warning people to remove any possible attractants including fruit trees, garbage and bird feeders in order to prevent human-wildlife conflict.

articles.title: Heavy rains to prevail over parts of Luzon as habagat persists
articles.summary: Several areas in Luzon, including Metro Manila, are expected to experience heavy rains on Friday, August 28, as the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to affect the country, state weather bureau…

blocks.text: A low pressure area (LPA 08i) is being monitored inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) as of 2 a.m. Friday, Aug. 28, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Several areas in Luzon, including Metro Manila, are expected to experience heavy rains on Friday, August 28, as the southwest monsoon or habagat continues to affect the country, state weather bureau PAGASA said.
As of 5 a.m. on Friday, PAGASA weather specialist Obet Badrina said that heavy rains are likely over Metro Manila, the Ilocos Region, parts of Central Luzon, Calabarzon and Occidental Mindoro.
The affected areas in Central Luzon include Bataan and Zambales.
The rest of Luzon will generally have cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms, particularly over the eastern portion of the island, Badrina said.
Palawan and the Visayas may likewise experience cloudy weather with chances of scattered rain showers.
Meanwhile, Mindanao will have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers.
Badrina said Mindanao is not expected to experience prolonged rainfall, with relatively warm weather prevailing over the island.
LPA monitored inside PAR
As of 2 a.m. Friday, August 28, PAGASA was monitoring a low pressure area (LPA) inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).
The LPA, designated LPA 08i, has a medium chance of developing into a tropical depression within the next 24 hours, PAGASA said.
Heavy rainfall
PAGASA's heavy rainfall outlook due to the southwest monsoon showed that several areas could receive 100 to 200 millimeters of rain, while others may record 50 to 100 mm from Friday through Sunday.

articles.title: Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic dead
articles.summary: BELGRADE, Serbia — Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief who was convicted of war crimes for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, died in a hospital on Thursday, according to a…

blocks.caption: Ex-Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic gestures from the defendant box during the hearing of the final verdict on appeal against his genocide conviction over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II, on June 8, 2021, at the International Residual Mecha…

blocks.text: BELGRADE, Serbia — Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief who was convicted of war crimes for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, died in a hospital on Thursday, according to a United Nations international tribunal.

Mladic, who had suffered several strokes in recent months, was serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity after overseeing the Srebrenica slaughter, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
His conviction for wartime killings as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage following the fall of communism led the media to dub him the “Butcher of Bosnia.”
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced.
Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
Serbian state officials and Mladic’s family had appealed for his release due to his failing health, but those calls were rejected by the Hague tribunal.
A representative of the Mothers of Srebrenica victims’ association, reacting to Mladic’s death, told AFP that his name would always “symbolize genocide.”
“That will never be erased from his name,” said Sehida Abdurahmanovic, who believes her missing brother was among those killed in Srebrenica.
Srebrenica
In the war’s most infamous atrocity, Serb forces under Mladic’s command executed 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had sought shelter in Srebrenica, which was meant to be a UN-protected enclave.
Their bodies were dumped in mass graves, many of which were dug up and reburied in an attempt to hide the evidence.
The few who escaped told harrowing stories of murder, torture and rape by Bosnian Serb forces.
In November 1995, the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) indicted Mladic, who was dismissed from his post but evaded capture for another 16 years.
At first, he led a life of luxury, pampered by the military in Serbia, where some to this day see him as a hero.
But the pressure mounted on him after Milosevic fell from power in 2000. Mladic was finally arrested in May 2011 and transferred to The Hague.
He was convicted in 2017, with the life sentence upheld on appeal in 2021.
On the streets of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, Hava Suljic told AFP she welcomed the news.
“I’m delighted to know there is one less war criminal walking around in this world,” Suljic, a Bosnian Muslim from Srebrenica, said.
But reactions in the Serb entity of divided Bosnia were in stark contrast.
Former Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik said Mladic’s death had “hit hard” and that the Republika Srpska “will not forget his role,” the Serb statelet’s public broadcaster reported.
Locals who spoke with AFP in the Republika Srpska’s capital, Banja Luka, called Mladic the “greatest.”
“The greatest man has died, the greatest general of the Serbian people,” pensioner Dragan Beric said.
‘Epitome of evil’
Mladic was also found guilty of orchestrating a wider campaign of ethnic cleansing to drive Muslims and Bosnians out of key areas to create a so-called Greater Serbia.
The tribunal said at the time that the crimes committed were “among the most heinous known to humankind.” Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al Hussein described him as “the epitome of evil.”
But many Serbs continued to revere a military commander who portrayed himself as a “simple man” whom fate had chosen to protect his people.

His age has always been a matter of dispute. He claimed to have been born in March 1943, but the tribunal listed his birth year as 1942. Local media widely reported that he had died at age 84.

articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's order comes after the trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.
Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.
He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.

Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, adding in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever."

When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application. , external
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.

There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters. While the US president has broad discretion over how his country officially recognises landmarks, other countries do not have to follow.
Canada does not have to recognise name changes made by other countries and officials there have dismissed the idea.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media, "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston agreed, saying "We're into some real foolishness now. It's Lake Ontario, buddy."
"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," said Industry Minister Melanie Joly on Tuesday.

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.
As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it wasn't a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade".
Trump said he'd been thinking about renaming the lake "for a long time".
"So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," Trump said.
"Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

The name change request comes amid a trade dispute that has seen US-Canada relations fall to new lows, with insults thrown back-and-forth between the Trump administration and Canadian officials over the past week.
There was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table sometime in the future.

Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said in a post on X that the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French "and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future US trade actions".
"We look forward to further constructive US clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty".
Trade talks collapsed at the last minute late on Friday night, with both sides accusing the other of demanding last-minute changes to a tentative deal.

Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic".
She wrote, "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect".

Other Democratic lawmakers in the US also criticised the order on social media, calling for the Trump administration to get back to negotiating on a trade deal. Some mocked Trump's idea and posted their own ideas to change the names of other landmarks.

Wisconsin's governor joked, "I just renamed Lake Michigan Lake Wisconsin," in a social media post with a video of himself signing a napkin on one of the Great Lakes. "See, I can sign napkins that say things, too," he added.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, "won't be calling it" Lake America.
Meanwhile, Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing, "We're on it, Mr. President!"

"The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA".

articles.title: PH may be caught in US rivals’ ‘crosshairs’ – Tinio
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the…

blocks.caption: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, speaks during a meeting with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, right, at the Pentagon, Monday, July 21, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the Philippines in the “crosshairs” of its rivals.

“In the event of a war between the US and China over the Taiwan issue, we can infer that China would target US facilities—both military and commercial—located in the Philippines. Our concern is that the US presence in the country is situated within our strategic and critical economic infrastructure,” Tinio said in a statement released on Thursday.

Tinio’s statement followed his heated exchange with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro during the House committee on appropriations’ hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of National Defense last Tuesday, Aug. 25.

During the hearing, Tinio raised reports that US soldiers had attempted to enter the Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation Industrial Authority in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, where the new Philippine Navy dry dock is set to be established.
Teodoro dismissed claims about US interest in the dry dock, saying the presence of foreign troops was for the Balikatan loading exercise.
For Tinio, however, the incident was part of a broader pattern of Washington’s agenda in the country.
He cited the US-led Pax Silica, the US Navy’s use of Subic Bay for repairs and plans for an oil depot in Davao Gulf.

Tinio said the growing US presence in strategic military and economic facilities was particularly concerning because the Philippines lacks the capacity to defend these assets should geopolitical tensions escalate.
“How is the Philippines? The Gulf states are rich countries. They can afford high-tech missile defenses. How are we? What is the capability of the Armed Forces to defend these facilities?” he asked.
Tinio called on the public to remain vigilant against “foreign manipulation and intervention.”
“We must oppose all efforts to sell us out,” he added. /mcm

articles.title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move

blocks.text: Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario, making it Lake America, amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

The order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases. But Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers, or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.
The move follows a similar action the president took on the first day of his second term in office, when he signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.

“We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he told reporters, sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “Maybe we’ll change them both.”
Propped behind the US president was a large map of the Great Lakes region, with “Lake America” printed in red lettering above Lake Ontario.

Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, rejected the US’s attempt to rename the body of water, explaining in a post on social media that its name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote on X. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia, responded: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
Several US governors in the Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change.
“New York won’t be calling it that,” the state’s governor, Democrat Kathy Hochul replied. New York shares a border with the lake.

Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, recalled that school children learn the acronym H-O-M-E-S for the names of the five great lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. And the Wisconsin governor, Democrat Tony Evers, mocked the move by sharing a video of himself changing the name of Lake Michigan to Lake Wisconsin, signed on a restaurant napkin.

The latest tweak of Canada’s nose by the US president comes as tensions fray between the US and its northern neighbor. Over the weekend, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed and the US imposed a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

“They want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said, a nod to his previous suggestions that Canada should become the “51st state” in the union, a prospect that has enraged Canadians. “But they want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that any more.”

Trump complained about a $60bn US trade deficit with Canada, which economists note is attributable almost entirely to US imports of oil; without that exchange, the US runs a sizable trade surplus. Trump claimed that American farmers were being charged a 400% tariff; about 97% of US agricultural exports to Canada enter duty-free under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, though over-quota eggs, milk and dairy have Canadian tariffs of up to 300%.

“As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade. Sad,” Trump said after signing the executive order updating the Department of Interior’s naming conventions. “Even the military: we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada. But we defend Canada.”
Both Canada and the United States are Nato members and have treaty obligations of mutual defense under the North Atlantic Treaty, the Ogdensburg Agreement and numerous other treaties.
Trump claimed the name change was something he had been considering for “a long time”.
“We’ve notified all the various people we have to notify,” he said after signing the order … This is official effective immediately.”
An administration official noted that the lake bordering Canada and the state of New York has most of its volume in the United States and that the deepest part of the lake is in US territory.

The state of emergency was extended on Aug. 21, but Forests Minister Ravi Parmar told journalists in Summerland Thursday that the tools are no longer necessary.

"We are not done with this wildfire season. We still have many days and weeks ahead. We know that our fire seasons are more intense and they are longer. But we don't need these tools at this time," Parmar said.

He encouraged tourists to return to the Okanagan to help businesses get back on their feet.

articles.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: Hundreds have died or are missing in Wednesday's flooding and landslides on the border of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.text: Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border
ByOlivia Ireland and Henry Moore
Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.
Search and rescue operations are continuing after Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials describe "huge scale loss".
There are risks of more floods: a lake of rising water has formed at a site along the China-Nepal border - prompting fears it could burst its banks.
Here is what we know so far.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on Wednesday

blocks.text: Image source, Nepal Army via EPA
Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on Wednesday
What caused the deadly landslide?
Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating flood.
However, the US Geological Survey has clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.
Debris flow from the collapse "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" the USGS said.

blocks.caption: Map showing the path of floodwaters along the Lende Khola, Bhote Koshi and  Trishuli rivers in northern Nepal after a glacier collapse near the Tibet border. The collapse sent ice and rock debris into the river, triggering flooding that destroyed a border checkpoint and continued downstream past…

blocks.text: Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.
Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".
Cook said his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.
He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.
He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".
Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet.
He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood."
One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.

Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.

A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu.
Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.
In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.
Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.
Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.

In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.
Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.
Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopter
How many people are dead and missing?
The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear.
Nepali police say at least 389 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East.

In its latest update on Thursday evening, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 910 people were still missing. This included 517 foreign citizens, 44 members of the Nepal Army and 28 Nepal police officers.
Meanwhile, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday that the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558.
Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.
The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists were still missing, 33 of which were UK nationals, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.
It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.
The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.

blocks.caption: Police officers carrying an elderly woman who survived the flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district of Nepal

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
How are governments responding?
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response.
China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.
In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance".

UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.
The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.
Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border
What countries are the missing tourists from?
Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including:

items: India - the Nepal Tourism board says 288 nationals from neighbouring India are missing
China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal
US - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missing
Ukraine - Ukraine's foreign ministry says 53 Ukrainian nationals are missing
Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say
Australia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will rise
UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing
Canada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal says 24 Canadians are reported missing

blocks.text: Smaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump's trade ambassador's recent comments about Canada's auto industry suggest the level at which it's integrated throughout North America could remain a major sticking point if talks do resume.
Trump and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have repeatedly said that the administration wants Canadian auto manufacturing jobs to move south of the border.
In a Canadian exclusive interview with CBC News, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer was asked about the future of the U.S. and Canada's integrated auto sector.
"We have a big gap in our manufacturing employment here, and autos is a big part of that," Greer told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton on Wednesday.
WATCH | USTR blames Canada for failed trade talks:
U.S. trade rep disputes why talks fell apart | Canadian exclusive

"I don't think this is any secret — we believe that the process of globalization for the United States, of integrating with other economies — even our close neighbours with whom, you know, we trade a lot — we think that has had some negative effects, especially in places like Michigan and Ohio and Pennsylvania and Wisconsin," he said.
When asked if the goal of the Trump administration is to remove auto manufacturing from Canada entirely, Greer said the aim is to "re-industrialize" in general.

"I understand why the Canadians, you know, want to have as much as they can get and try to expand concessions from the U.S.," he said. "But we are focused on doing what's good for America and accommodating Canada to the extent we can."

Greer was the American lead on trade talks that fell apart last week. Both American and Canadian officials have said that U.S. tariffs on finished vehicles and Canadian auto parts were outstanding issues in those negotiations.

items: LeBlanc welcomes U.S. decision 'withdrawing positions' on language, culture
Trump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands

blocks.text: Canadian negotiators sought to have those tariffs reduced from the 25 per cent rate, but argued that the U.S. at the last minute sought to exclude heavy- and medium-sized trucks from that relief. The Americans, including Greer, dispute that the exclusion was a last-minute ask on their part.
Heavy and medium trucks would include some models of Ford's F-Series pickups and General Motors' Silverado which are both made at Ontario plants that employ roughly 20,000 workers.
Greer said medium- and heavy-duty truck duties were "separate" from the auto tariffs the Trump administration had offered lower.
WATCH | Canada 'will continue to fight' for auto jobs, says industry minister:
Canada 'will continue to fight' for auto jobs, says industry minister
Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufactures' Association, said Greer's recent comments shouldn't come as a surprise.
"The president has said it, the secretary of commerce has said it … they want cars made in the U.S. and not in Canada and so you don't have to tell me that again," Volpe told CBC News.

Since the first few weeks of his second term, Trump has said "we don't need [Canada] to make our cars." The president repeated that claim in the Oval Office on Thursday after signing an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.
WATCH | Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario:
Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’

"We want to make the cars here. They can make their own cars if they want and they can continue to make their cars for Canada. But we don't want them to make cars for the United States of America," he said.

Last fall, Lutnick told an audience in Toronto that he wanted to use tariffs to drain auto assembly from Canada. Sources told CBC News just prior to last week's deal falling apart that Lutnick was dissatisfied with what was on the table, specifically around auto tariffs.
Auto rep 'encouraged' by Greer's remarks

Brian Kingston, president of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers' Association, said he's "encouraged" by Greer's comments on the goal of re-industrializing in the U.S. He said that industrializing the American automotive industry will by necessity include Canada.
"It's not unexpected that we're going to see heightened rhetoric following the breakdown of negotiations," Kingston told CBC News.

"[Greer] did not say 'Canada can't have an auto industry.' And in fact, Canada should be doing everything in its power to protect our industrial base and strengthen it. So how do we do that? We're going to do that by strengthening our auto industries together, which are tightly integrated."
Trump threatened to double tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles and non-CUSMA-compliant auto parts in the new year after the talks fell apart last week.
Kingston said continued retaliation will threaten the entirety of the North American auto industry.

"If we can't find an off ramp in lower tariff rates, it makes the industry across North America less competitive and therefore it will reduce their ability to compete with manufacturers in other parts of the world," he said.
WATCH | A closer look at Greer's comments:
How true are Jamieson Greer's claims on the Canada-U.S. trade fallout? | Hanomansing Tonight
Despite the breakdown in negotiations, Kingston said he thinks a deal is still within reach.
"Cooler heads will prevail. But we do need to stop the cycle of retaliation and start talking again," he said.
Volpe said he hopes the Trump administration realizes it doesn't make sense to separate the Canadian and American auto sectors.
"Countries don't make cars. Industries in those countries make cars," he said.
"When you have the ambassador come on and say Canada is the source of the decline of U.S. auto, that's like saying your right foot is the source of the pain in your left foot."

items: The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs
What we know about how the Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: Volpe says he's encouraged by Greer conducting an interview with Canadian media, saying it could be a sign that the topic of Canada-U.S. trade is breaking through in the Trump administration.
He said regardless of where trade discussions go from here, Canada will have to own up to whatever deal it signs.

"If we do a deal that signs off the auto sector, then we own that. It's not the fault of the Trump administration who says that they want something from us. If we hand it to them, then it's on us," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
