articles.title: Marcos confers Order of Sikatuna on outgoing Japanese envoy Endo Kazuya
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of Sikatuna, Rank of Datu (Grand Cross), Gold Distinction.
During their meeting, Marcos thanked the Japanese envoy for his contributions to strengthening the Philippines’ relationship with Japan, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said.
The President recognized Endo for promoting bilateral exchanges and deepening cooperation between the Philippines and Japan in areas of defense, security, and development cooperation.

Meanwhile, the award cited the envoy’s support for initiatives aligned with the Philippines’ priorities in infrastructure, education, transportation, maritime domain awareness, and human resource development.

“Endo was likewise recognized for advancing Japan’s longstanding commitment to peace and development in Mindanao, including its support for the peace process, grassroots development and the transition of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao,” the PCO said.

“The citation also highlighted the ambassador’s efforts to mobilize humanitarian and development assistance from the Japanese government during natural disasters and recent regional crises,” it added.
Additionally, Marcos acknowledged Endo’s initiatives that fostered friendship, mutual understanding, and goodwill between the Filipino and Japanese peoples.
The Order of Sikatuna is conferred upon individuals who have rendered exceptional and meritorious service to the Philippines.
The Philippines and Japan are celebrating 70 years of normalized relations this year and 11 years of strengthened strategic partnership since 2015. /gsg

The union representing American air traffic controllers has acknowledged allegations that two members left work early shortly before an Air Canada regional jet crashed at LaGuardia Airport in March, killing two pilots.

blocks.text: The union representing American air traffic controllers has acknowledged allegations that two members left work early shortly before an Air Canada regional jet crashed at LaGuardia Airport in March, killing two pilots.

U.S. media reports suggest the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is looking to fire the two flight controllers, who allegedly clocked out roughly an hour before their shift ended, leaving a pair of colleagues at the LaGuardia tower without backup.
The National Air Traffic Controllers Association confirmed the allegations, first reported by the Wall Street Journal on Thursday, in an emailed statement.
"NATCA is actively discussing these allegations with FAA leadership. We believe those discussions are the appropriate forum for addressing the matter," the union said.

items: FAA adding transponders to all its airport vehicles after Air Canada plane's deadly LaGuardia runway crash
Montreal airport installs memorial to Air Canada pilots who died in LaGuardia crash

blocks.text: The U.S. federal agency has not addressed the accusations directly but said it is "committed to holding employees accountable."
"We will not compromise the safety or efficiency of the National Airspace System," the FAA said in an email.

Shortly after 11:30 p.m. ET on March 22, an air traffic controller cleared an Air Canada Express plane to land less than two minutes before green-lighting a fire truck to cross the active runway. The resulting collision left two Canadian aviators dead and sent more than 40 people to hospital.

Footage shows the jet speeding along the rain-streaked strip as the truck crosses its path, veering away too late from an impact that unleashed a trail of smoke and debris as the plane skidded more than 100 metres farther, its cockpit obliterated.
The controller recognized the danger moments beforehand, instructing the truck to "stop" — 12 times in 10 seconds — but receiving no reply.
WATCH | Driver didn't realize 'stop' order was for them:
LaGuardia driver didn't know 'stop, stop, stop' warning was for them: NTSB
A preliminary report from the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board in April found that system failures and communication issues played a key role in the accident.
Experts have praised the pilots — Quebecer Antoine Forest and Ontarian MacKenzie Gunther, who flew for Air Canada Express carrier Jazz Aviation — for their quick braking that likely saved lives.

Conservationists have long been working to keep a rare species of bird from disappearing entirely from the United Kingdom. 'He's at the top of his game,' conservationist says of 10-year-old Montague's harrier

blocks.text: LISTEN | Interview with conservationist Mark Thomas:
As It Happens6:13 One 'absolutely prolific' male bird is keeping his species alive in the U.K.
Conservationists have long been working to keep a rare species of bird from disappearing entirely from the United Kingdom.

But any recent success they've had in protecting the Montagu's harrier's British population can largely be attributed to the mating prowess of one "absolutely prolific" male, says conservationist Mark Thomas.
The 10-year-old stud in question is called AU — the chemical symbol for gold — and he's sired 16 juveniles over the course of his life, including 10 in the last two years.
"He's at the top of his game," Thomas, the species lead for Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), told As It Happens guest host Paul Hunter.
"He is single-handedly propping up this species in the U.K. There's no two ways about it."
'It's been a great year'
Montagu's harriers are migratory birds of prey who spend their winters in Africa and parts of Asia, and return to Europe every spring to breed.
Globally, their population is on the decline, and listed as a species of least concern on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List.
In the U.K., the RSPB says, the already rare birds have been rapidly declining, and threatening to disappear from the country altogether.

At their peak in the 1950s, there were about 30 breeding pairs in the U.K., which dropped to zero in the '70s, before rising back to 13 in the mid-aughts. That was followed by another steep decline when there were zero breeding pairs reported between 2000 and 2003.
"We're desperate to try and save the birds we have currently," Thomas said. "And it's been a great year."

blocks.caption: One of the two Montagu harrier nests in the U.K. this summer. (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds)

blocks.text: That's thanks to AU.
After successfully raising four chicks in 2025, the so-called "golden boy" returned again this year to do his acrobatic mating displays in the hopes of catching the eye of some willing females.
"He'll fly to, like, a thousand feet in the air and then he'll do these amazing twist and turns flashing his wings," Thomas said. "The females will then appear. They will chase him around."
This year, Thomas said, three females were fighting for AU's attention.
"The three had a big fight, and they got down to two. And then the two stayed, and nested with him."
Protecting the nests
AU fathered six chicks between his two mates, four female and two male.

Conservationists are hopeful that his sons will one day return to the U.K. to breed. Two of his male offspring from 2025 have already been spotted in the country, though they're not yet old enough to breed.
"That's really good new in terms of the population continuing," Thomas said.
The six new hatchlings are spread evenly among two nests, roughly one kilometre apart in a top-secret location, somewhere on a British farm.
Only the scientists and the landowners know where the nests are located, and the researchers constructed barriers around them to protect the baby birds from predators and other threats.
"This is one of the most exciting birds we have in the U.K. and to work on it is a dream every single day," Thomas said.
"It's also quite a lot of responsibility as well, you know, to know that you are handling the chicks of a bird that has only got two nests in the whole United Kingdom."

blocks.caption: A female Montagu's harrier chick is one of six of its species to hatch in the U.K. this year. (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds)

blocks.text: Montagu's harriers are a lowland species that prefer to nest in marshes and river plains. When no suitable habitat is available, they tend to nest instead among the crops on farmland, putting them at risk of being destroyed by agricultural machinery.
"So the RSPB's role is to find these nests, liaise with the farmers, work very closely with them and then safeguard the chicks in their nest," Thomas said.
Tracking the youngsters
That should be easier in the future, if all goes according to plan.
For the first time, the RSPB has attached satellite trackers to two juvenile harriers, one from each nest.

blocks.caption: For the first time, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds has affixed two juvenile Montagu's harriers with satellite trackers. (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds)

blocks.text: The young birds will soon be ready to leave their nest and migrate, and the RSPB will be able to see exactly where they go, and where they end up should they return.
If they survive and return to the U.K. to breed, Thomas and his team should easily be able to find their nests and spring into action once again.
"We've never done this with juveniles before," he said. "So we're absolutely kind of, you know, on tenterhooks waiting to see what the data shows."
Interview with Mark Thomas produced by Sarah Jackson

articles.title: Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children
articles.summary: Prosecutors argued Clancy made a calculated decision to murder the children, while the defence argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children.

For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter.
The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them.
The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty.
The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday.
In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole.

The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time.
If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life.
Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's lawyer, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise".

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency.

One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury.
Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings.

"It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopaedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification.
Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

blocks.text: Ten Toronto residents on a trek in Nepal are unaccounted for after deadly flash flooding in the country this week, according to a representative of the group that organized the trip.

Leslie Crespi, a U.S.-based community liaison for the Isha Foundation in North America, a non-profit spirituality group, told CBC News Network on Thursday that the 10 are among 80 members of the foundation still missing.
The 10 were among 12 Canadians on the trek, Crespi said.
"At this particular time, we haven't had any communication with the 80 people that were involved," Crespi said in an interview from McMinnville, Tennessee.

The co-ordinator of the trek contacted the Isha Foundation at 9:07 a.m. on Wednesday, after the group arrived at an Chinese immigration centre in Gyirong County, Tibet. The flash flooding hit that particular area at 9:14 a.m., she said.

"Since that time, we haven't had any communication with those people who are involved. We've been in close contact with the embassies, with officials, with everybody that we can to be plugged into what's happening and to get continuous updates," she said.

The group, which includes people from 19 countries, was returning from the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a sacred pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. The journey has significance to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon followers.

items: Toronto's Nepali-Canadian community waits for word of loved ones after flash floods

blocks.text: Crespi said families of the group members are in shock.
"It's devastating news; it's very, very hard to believe. This was incredibly unexpected and the magnitude of this flood is just something you can't get your mind around," she said.
"These people are like family to us.… Some people have been with us for over 20 years, so it has taken a devastating effect on all of us here."
'Everybody is in panic mode'
Nepali community leaders gathered for an emergency meeting in Mississauga on Thursday to talk about tracking down missing loved ones.
The leaders said the community will ask the Canadian government will help rescue the people unaccounted for.
80 members missing from Isha Foundation
Punya Marahatta, senior vice-president of Non-Resident Nepalese Association in Toronto, said seeing videos on social media is adding to the stress.
"Everybody is in panic mode," he said.
The community leaders said the first step is for families with missing loved ones to register their names with the federal government.
Global Affairs Canada aware of missing Canadians
Global Affairs Canada said in a media update on Thursday it was aware of about 30 missing Canadian citizens and permanent residents in Nepal and Tibet.
"Given the extremely difficult circumstances on the ground, this number will fluctuate as new information comes in," Global Affairs Canada said.

"Our consular officials are working urgently to establish contact with them and confirm their safety. They are also reaching out to travel agencies, local authorities and likeminded countries to gather additional information."
Global Affairs Canada said it is deploying five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and co-ordinate with local officials and partners and will provide further resources as needed.
Anita Anand, minister of foreign affairs, said Canadian officials are working urgently to get in touch with missing Canadians and confirm they are safe.

items: Death toll at least 359, with more than 1,000 missing in Nepal, Tibet after catastrophic floods

blocks.text: GlobalMedic, a disaster relief charity based in Etobicoke, said it has offered to deploy its point of source water purification units, family emergency kits and drones to Nepal to help people affected by the disaster.

Point of source water purification units can be installed in feeding centres and hospitals to provide access to clean drinking water, while a family emergency kit contains a point of use water purification kit, hygiene items and a portable solar light.

GlobalMedic said it can help in mapping out the extent of the damage and provide search and rescue support. The teams collect data that provide information to emergency responders so better aid decisions can be made.
With files from Hanna Lee and Naama Weingarten

articles.title: Infinity Mirror Rooms artist, Yayoi Kusama, dead at 97. Her polka-dotted life in pictures
articles.summary: Artist Yayoi Kusama, who has died at 97, was one of Japan's most revered contemporary artists. Her work was exhibited around the world, often prompting long queues as people flocked to see her…

image.caption: Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese artist known for her colourful psychedelic canvas art and immersive Infinity Mirror Rooms exhibits, has died. She was 97. (Steve Eichner/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Artist Yayoi Kusama, who has died at 97, was one of Japan's most revered contemporary artists. Her work was exhibited around the world, often prompting long queues as people flocked to see her colourful, immersive installation art.
Japanese artist, whose work was exhibited around the world, was known for her signature polka dot paintings
Listen to this article
Estimated 3 minutes
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

blocks.caption: Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese artist known for her colourful psychedelic canvas art and immersive Infinity Mirror Rooms exhibits, has died. She was 97. (Steve Eichner/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Artist Yayoi Kusama transfixed the world with her unique perspective — often expressed by blanketing her canvases, sculptures and museum installations in a mesmerizing, endless swarm of her trademark polka dots.

Kusama, whose death at 97 in a hospital in Tokyo was announced on Thursday by her studio, became one of Japan's most revered contemporary artists. Her art travelled the globe to be exhibited in famous galleries, including the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, and the Museum Ludwig in Germany.

blocks.caption: People walk through the art installation Infinity Mirror Room during a preview of the new major exhibition of legendary Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany, in March. (Martin Meissner/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Perhaps among her most famous creations, her Infinity Mirror Rooms installations have spawned long queues at museums, including at Toronto's Art Gallery of Ontario where visitors flocked to see the Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors exhibition in 2018. The show's popularity led the gallery to purchase, with crowdfunded support, the permanent installation Infinity Mirrored Room — Let's Survive Forever.

blocks.caption: Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli's Field features Kusama's signature polka dots on stuffed phallic shapes surrounded by mirrors. Standing in the room alone, as the piece is meant to be experienced, creates a hallucinatory scene with the viewer's reflection making them an unavoidable part of the expe…

The pumpkin motif appears in many of Kusama's works dating to the 1940s and, in 1993, this piece, titled All the Eternal Love I Have for the Pumpkin, appeared in the Venice Biennale. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Like her signature orange bob wig, her works have become instantly recognizable, featuring her trademark repetitive psychedelic motifs that include bright, colourful swirls, worms, netting, and most often polka dots, sparkling balls or dots of lights.

blocks.caption: Kusama is seen wearing Louis Vuitton, a fashion brand she partnered with in 2012. (Steve Eichner/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images)
Kusama visited Paris for her multi-site exhibition on in 2001. (Alain Nogues/Sygma/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Kusama frequently said she painted the way she saw the world: covered in spots, much like the hallucinations she said she had from childhood.

blocks.caption: A woman views the artwork My Eternal Soul Series during a preview of an exhibition of Kusama's work at the Museum Ludwig in March. (Martin Meissner/The Associated Press)
The sculpture A Bouquet of Love I Saw In the Universe by Kusama is seen at an exhibition at Martin-Gropius-Bau in April 2021 in Berlin. (Adam Berry/Getty Images)

Visitors stand inside Kusama's metal, fibreglass, urethane, paint and stickers installation titled With All My Love for the Tulips, I Pray Forever, 2013 at National Gallery Singapore in June 2017 in Singapore. (Suhaimi Abdullah/Getty Images)

blocks.text: She dealt with years of mental health challenges and recurring visits to psychiatric institutions and was once ostracized by the cultural elite in Japan for her avant-garde style, according to the New York Times. And yet despite those challenges, the artist, whose canon includes installations with phallic fabric sculptures and naked performance pieces, provoked public discourse and became a fixture of the art world.

blocks.caption: An art installation of furniture, clothing and other items covered in phallic-like objects is seen in New York in 2012. (Steve Eichner/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Kusama was born in 1929 in Matsumoto, Japan, and moved to the United States to pursue her art in 1957.

In the late '60s, while Kusama lived in New York City, she held "happening" antiwar performances where she painted circles on people's bodies and, once, even a horse. While the performances gained media attention they also resulted in arrests for obscenity.

blocks.caption: At Kusama's 'happening' antiwar performances, like this one on July 14, 1967, she painted circles on people's bodies. (Seymour Wally/NY Daily News/Getty Images)
Kusama's I Spend Each Day Embracing Flowers is seen at David Zwirner's 19th street gallery in New York City in 2023. (Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

blocks.text: "I want to create a thousand paintings, maybe two thousand paintings, as many as I can draw," she told The Associated Press during an interview in 2012. "I will keep painting until I die."

blocks.caption: Paintings and flower sculptures with the title Flowers that Bloom Now appear at the David Zwirner gallery in New York City in 2017. (Stephanie Ott/picture alliance/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As her fame grew, fashion brands began to take notice. Kusama signed on with Louis Vuitton in 2012 under then-creative director Marc Jacobs. She also signed on with other licensed products, with her illustrations appearing on teacups, key chains and T-shirts.

blocks.caption: Yayoi Kusama x Louis Vuitton immersive fashion and art pop-up is seen at Harrods in 2023 in London. (Jim Dyson/Getty Images)

A sculpture of Yayoi Kusama sits atop the Louis Vuitton's Champs Elysees store in 2023 in Paris. Kusama licensed her art for many products, including teacups, key chains and T-shirts. (Edward Berthelot/Getty Images)
Kusama, centre, appears with Louis Vuitton leadership at the Louis Vuitton and Yayoi Kusama collaboration unveiling event in New York City in 2012. (Neilson Barnard/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Kusama was a visionary not only on canvas and sculpture but in other mediums; the artist was also a filmmaker and author, having published several novels. She told The Associated Press that her creative process was so mysterious that there were times when she even surprised herself.
"I think, 'Oh I drew that? I was thinking that,'" she said.

blocks.caption: Dots Obsession: Infinity Mirrored Room is seen in 2008 at the contemporary art centre Le Spot in Le Havre, France. (Robert Francois/AFP/Getty Images)
A tourist looks at Kusama's Yellow Pumpkin sculpture in Naoshima, Japan. (Education Images/Universal Images Group/Getty Images)
Kusama's Love Forever features hexagonal mirrors surrounding two peepholes through which viewers can see their faces repeated infinitely. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Three of Canada's big banks shared cautiously sunny outlooks for the economy on Thursday, sharply contrasting expressions of anxiety and frustration from scores of smaller businesses grappling with the fresh reality of a full-blown trade war with the United States.
More big banks posted Q3 financial results Thursday amid escalating trade war

blocks.text: Three of Canada's big banks shared cautiously sunny outlooks for the economy on Thursday, sharply contrasting expressions of anxiety and frustration from scores of smaller businesses grappling with the fresh reality of a full-blown trade war with the United States.
Royal Bank of Canada, Toronto-Dominion Bank and CIBC reported financial results before Thursday's opening bell on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

Together, this trio of Canadian banking giants has as much as $6 trillion worth of assets on their balance sheets. With vast portfolios of mortgages, auto loans and other debt products for consumers and businesses, and client networks spanning Canada and the U.S., these goliath institutions have a unique vantage point from which to monitor the impact of tariffs.

"The Canadian economy has proven to be resilient. The improvements in employment and GDP seen in Q2 maintain a cautiously optimistic outlook that the economy will continue to expand," RBC CEO Dave McKay said on the bank's quarterly conference call Thursday morning.

"While Canada and the U.S. have yet to come to a longer-term solution, we note the average effective tariff rate remains low, at approximately six percent, with over 80 per cent of exports remaining duty-free.”
Investment 'super cycle' to the rescue

On Thursday, TD Bank CEO Raymond Chun referred to an emerging "super cycle" for investment in Canada, spurred by government spending in areas like infrastructure and national defence. According to TD Economics, Ottawa and the provinces have over $1 trillion in announced projects already approved or on the table through 2035 and beyond.
"In Canada, trade tensions have not dampened investment opportunities, as governments seek to drive new activity," Chun said.
"More could be rolled out across Canada over the coming decade in a historic investment super cycle," he added. "We are very well positioned to benefit from this activity."
CIBC CEO Harry Culham said he has "measured confidence" about the back half of 2026.
"The trade environment will continue to evolve, and we are not going to speculate on where it lands," he said on Thursday, speaking on his bank's conference call with stock market analysts.
CIBC chief risk officer Frank Guse said that CIBC is closely monitoring Canada's labour market for signs of weakness.
A recent Oxford Economics study prepared for the Canadian American Business Council found more than 100,000 Canadian jobs could be lost if the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) was eliminated.
BMO Capital Markets predicts the latest round of U.S. tariffs will carve roughly half a percentage point from Canadian growth, mostly through weaker business confidence and investment.
WATCH | Trump's trade czar speaks to CBC News:
EXCLUSIVE Interview: USTR Jamieson Greer on why Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart

On Wednesday, National Bank's CEO Laurent Ferreira said Canada's economy has "demonstrated resilience" over the past 18 months. Like his peers, he also praised Ottawa's large-scale investment plans, as well as the newly announced government aid measures for workers and businesses impacted by U.S. tariffs.

"Energy, power infrastructure, and the recent icebreaker contract announcement are great examples of our country moving in the right direction," Ferreira said, referring to a commitment announced by the federal government to build six icebreaker ships in Quebec.
He also praised the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' June decision to lower its domestic stability buffer, allowing banks more flexability to lend to struggling businesses.
On Tuesday, the CEO of Bank of Montreal and Scotiabank separately called the Canada-U.S. trade war manageable.

On the Toronto Stock Exchange, shares of Canada's big banks continue to trade near all-time highs. The iShares S&P/TSX Capped Energy Index ETF, a basket of Canadian bank stocks, has soared over 46 per cent year-to-date.

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. He was also a Columbia University energy journalism fellow for 2025.

articles.title: Russia says UK ‘playing with fire’ amid reports CIA chief has warned Kremlin not to attack Nato
articles.summary:
Moscow threatens retaliation after Andy Burnham says UK will help Ukraine start producing long-range missiles

Russia has said it could retaliate against the UK for its support of Kyiv by…

blocks.text: Russia has said it could retaliate against the UK for its support of Kyiv by striking military targets inside and outside Ukraine, amid reports that the director of the CIA warned the Kremlin against attacking Nato during a secretive visit this week.

Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, said on Monday the UK would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start ⁠its own production of Storm Shadow ​long-range ​cruise missiles. France has also agreed to supply missile technology. Maria ⁠Zakharova, Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said on Thursday Britain and France were “playing ⁠with ​fire”.

Responding to the latest Russian threats, a Ministry of Defence official reiterated UK support for Ukraine. “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion. Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies,” they said.

The Wall Street Journal reported that a visit by John Ratcliffe, the CIA chief, to Moscow on Tuesday had followed a US intelligence assessment that Russia could be planning to test Nato with a limited assault on an allied country. This could range from a cyber-attack to a small-scale incursion, probably in a Baltic nation.
Russia has made frequent threats against Ukraine’s western allies during the war, including thinly veiled nuclear threats and others apparently aimed at diplomatic missions in Kyiv.

blocks.caption: K2 Black Panther main battle tanks will be deployed by Poland near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region as Nato countries neighbouring Russia move to increase their military readiness. Photograph: Roman Koziel/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Asked ‌to comment ‌on the reports of Ratcliffe’s visit – and despite Thursday morning’s threat against UK targets – Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said: “A lot of this kind of scare-story material is being published right now. Of course, it has ‌nothing to do with reality and nothing to do ​with the intentions of the Russian Federation.”
The intense scrutiny around the Ratcliffe trip and Russia’s intentions comes amid a new report over shortfalls of missile interceptors available in Europe.

A report by the Associated Press says the US military is experiencing a “beyond critical” shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe largely driven by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, according to a US defence official in Europe and a Nato official, raising concerns about vulnerabilities in Nato countries to a potential Russian attack.

The US defence official said the most concerning shortfall involved Patriot missile interceptors, which can shoot down Russia’s high-speed ballistic missiles. The Nato official confirmed the low inventories of Patriots among American and Nato forces in Europe. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.

Russia is believed to be contemplating a further escalation of its war with Ukraine after months of escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s oil refining infrastructure and other sites, which are imposing an increasing economic toll.

blocks.caption: A Japanese government sign in Tokyo says ‘the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan’s territory’, referring to the Russian-controlled Southern Kuril Islands. Russia has invoked its nuclear threat against Japan over the claim.  Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Kremlin has adopted ever more bellicose rhetoric, much of it aimed at a domestic audience, as the war in Ukraine has been brought to its doorstep.

In the space of a few days Russia has invoked the threat of its nuclear arsenal against Japan over its territorial claim to the disputed Kuril Islands. It has described relations with the US as a “crisis” and at a historic low point.
Ratcliffe’s reported warning mirrored one made by his predecessor, William Burns, in 2021 before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – which Moscow also denied it was contemplating.
after newsletter promotion

Concerns over Moscow’s intentions have been increasing amid a rise in incidents of Russian hybrid warfare attributed to Moscow across Europe, from cyber-attacks and drones to arson, at facilities associated with supporting Ukraine’s war efforts.

Russia and the US have tried to play down Ratcliffe’s meeting with his Russian counterparts: Trump on Wednesday described the visit as “semi routine”. However, the unusual nature of the encounter has caused intense speculation in the west and Russia.
The US president continued to play down the encounter on Thursday, telling Axios that Ratcliffe had arrived in Moscow with “no message” and claiming there was “nothing unusual” about the meeting.
Asked later by reporters about reports about the CIA director Ratcliffe had delivered a warning to Russia, Trump replied: “I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack.”

Nato countries neighbouring Russia have moved quickly to increase their military readiness. Poland this week announced it had taken delivery of its first shipment of South Korean Black Panther main battle tanks, which will be deployed near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
Cezary Tomczyk, Poland’s deputy defence minister, said this month Warsaw was preparing for the possibility of a full-scale conflict.
Tomczyk told Super Express media: “We are preparing for war, hoping it never happens.”

articles.title: Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn
articles.summary: Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe

blocks.text: The devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal and Tibet has heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.

Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.

A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2.
“Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,” the US Geological Survey said.

The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution.

Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but many observe that glaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal.

blocks.caption: Flooding in the Bhotekoshi River has affected low-lying areas along the riverbanks and nearby homes in Nuwakot, Nepal.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together.

Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site.
“These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre.

A series of intense heatwaves has hit the region since early this year and affected countries around the world. Another factor here was the monsoon season, which saturated the soil and swelled rivers.

Disasters like this were foretold. In 2023 the UN’s top scientific advisory body warned that previously ice-bound landmasses – from permafrost tundra to mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.

“Every increment of warming will multiply and intensify future hazards from cryosphere regions,” observed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in its sixth synthesis report. “Floods, landslides and freshwater shortages from glacier retreat and snow loss pose a serious threat to mountain regions across the world.”

Average global temperatures are nudging closer to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Even faster warming is occurring in alpine and polar regions because the loss of snow and ice is removing the thermal insulation of the land.

Dr Richard Waller, a senior lecturer in physical geography at Keele University, said: “The progressive loss of snow and glacier ice results in the surface being less reflective, so it absorbs more solar energy and heats up. In combination with atmospheric warming, this is leading to the melting of mountain permafrost.

“Think of the high mountains like this as shattered bedrock glued together by ice-filled joints. As the permafrost and the ice-filled joints melt, then there’s the potential for these types of catastrophic failure.”

blocks.caption: A destroyed building in Devighat, Nuwakot. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP

blocks.text: The thaw is altering the shape, colour and solidity of the landscape, creating or expanding glacial meltwater lakes and, in the long term, threatening the origin of many rivers and the drinking supplies of populations downstream. In many parts of Asia, hundreds of millions of people depend on the rivers such as the Ganges and the Brahmaputra that descend from the glaciers.

Scientists have high confidence that glacier retreat is caused by human-driven global heating. This has caused glacier collapses from the Alps to the Andes. In the Langtang catchment area in Nepal, glacier loss rates have increased more than fourfold since 1964, a study has shown.

This has contributed to a loss of life on multiple occasions. A smaller flood hit the Bhotekoshi River in July 2025 and in 2015, the Langtang Lirung mountain was hit by an earthquake-induced avalanche that destroyed Langtang village.

As emergency services look for bodies and humanitarian relief groups mobilise for survivors, others are asking where next. Waller said any high mountain areas with glaciers and permafrost could be vulnerable, including the European Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, Andes and beyond.

As glacier weakening accelerates, Pritchard called for greater disaster preparedness. “More avalanches and more floods are inevitable, particularly as lakes grow in front of the retreating glaciers,” he said. “Early warning systems are urgently needed to protect the people living in these valleys.”

articles.title: Search is on for at least 33 Britons missing after flash floods in Nepal and Tibet
articles.summary: Rescue teams try to locate nearly 1,400 missing people, mostly tourists, while police report recovery of 389 bodies

blocks.text: Rescue teams in Nepal are searching for at least 33 British nationals who are among those missing after flash floods ravaged its border with Tibet, killing more than 380 people.
Nearly 1,400 people are missing, most of them tourists, authorities have said, after a glacier collapse triggered floods that roared down valleys and razed entire villages.
Nepal police said 389 bodies had been recovered and the number of injured and rescued people had reached 466.
Nepal’s national disaster risk reduction and management authority said the number of out-of-contact foreign nationals had increased to 517.
The tour company Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – travelling with the operator.

Another tour company, the Trekkers’ Society, said among the British citizens who had been completing one of its tours to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash were four males aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five women aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.

The tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said a 13-year-old girl was among the missing British nationals and two Irish citizens were also missing. They were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash and crossing into Tibet from Nepal when they became trapped at the border as the flash floods struck.
Other missing British nationals with Alpine Eco Trek are three men aged 65, 64 and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63 and 65, according to travel logs.

The tour company Himalayan Glacier US told the BBC it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests, including two British citizens, who were en route to Mount Kailash. Fishtail Tours, a Nepali travel agency, said one British person was missing.

blocks.caption: A damaged bridge in Galchhi, Nepal. Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

blocks.text: Among those missing with links to the UK are Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent, who was making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash.
Her brother Shambhu wrote on social media: “My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home.”
Leena Bector, a director of a care agency from Slough, west London, is among 27 travellers associated with the Fishtail Tours and Travels group currently unaccounted for.
Hema Amin, from Croydon in south London, started a pilgrimage to Gosainkunda lake on Monday that was supposed to last until 4 September.
Her husband, Sunil Amin, told Sky News: “I keep trying to call her. I’ve been trying, trying, trying.”
Nabhi Nandan Das, 64, a Hindu priest from south London, was leading a group on a tour to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar.

Mala and Bipin Patel, from Coventry, went missing after travelling to Nepal and Tibet on a pilgrimage. Their son, Anant Patel, told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information about their whereabouts.

Pramod Poudel, from Uckfield, East Sussex, told the BBC that his wife, Sumitra Sapkota, as well as his parents, brother and uncle, had been caught in flash flooding. He said he would fly to Nepal on Thursday night to try to make contact with them.

blocks.caption: Pramod Poudel said his wife, Sumitra Sapkota, had been caught in the flash flooding along with his parents, brother and uncle. Photograph: Family Handout

blocks.text: Poudel said: “I guess there is no power so they can’t charge their phones – to be honest, it’s a very hard and difficult time at the moment.”
In an emotional interview, he said: “I have seen pictures of where my home town used to be … and there is nothing there now.”

Andy Burnham has pledged an initial £5m in UK government support and offered to send emergency responders and rescue support to assist Nepal’s disaster response efforts. Speaking to journalists during a visit to south Wales, he said: “It’s a devastating picture that is emerging from what has happened in Nepal. Scenes that we’ve never seen the like before, I don’t think, certainly the scale of the devastation.

“So there is immediate action being taken. We are deploying consular support staff to the region so that British nationals will be able to access support 24/7. Obviously there are a number of British nationals who currently are thought to be missing and we’ll be providing all the support we can to their families in what is a very distressing and devastating situation.”
He added in a statement: “In the past, Nepal has been there for Britain in our hour of need, and we will be there for Nepal in its hour of need right now.”

King Charles said he and Queen Camilla were heartbroken and sent their “most profound sympathy” to those affected. “Many in the United Kingdom have strong, deep and personal ties to this part of the world,” he said.
The Prince and Princess of Wales also expressed their shock. “We are thinking of everyone caught up in this terrible disaster,” they said.

The president of the Nepal Centre for Disaster Management, Bishal Nath Upreti, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the flash floods were like a “tsunami from the sky”. He said: “It’s a huge debris, and in fact, after the 2015 earthquake, this is one of the largest disasters that we have [had] in Nepal.”

He added: “It was such a huge amount of water. You can imagine it is 20m cubic metres excess water on the river … Villages and villages along the almost 40 to 50 kilometres were completely wiped out.”

The Nepal tourism board said on Wednesday that 33 UK citizens were among the foreign nationals unaccounted for. At least three people had died in Tibet, according to China’s state broadcaster CCTV, while the Xinhua news agency said 558 people were unaccounted for in the region.
Rescuers are racing to locate people missing in the mountainous Rasuwa region, which borders China’s autonomous region of Tibet and is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The UK minister Pat McFadden told Times Radio the picture was “not completely clear yet”, with “many, many more” people understood to be missing than those reported by the Nepalese authorities, and no clear figures from China yet.
He said: “In terms of missing Britons, my colleague the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has posted on social media phone numbers that people can call for further information.
“But it’s a fast-moving picture. We don’t have a full picture yet of the numbers missing.”

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said it was “deeply saddened by the loss of life and devastation caused by the floods in Nepal”. It added: “British nationals in Nepal should follow local authority advice and exercise caution while travelling. For consular assistance call (+44) (0)207 008 5000 or (+977) (0)14237100.”

articles.title: Marcos sends condolences, offers prayers to Nepal flash floods victims
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border. He also offered…

blocks.caption: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (Photo from Bongbong Marcos / Facebook)

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border.
He also offered prayers for strength of the calamity victims.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flashflood yesterday,” Marcos said in his social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
The Nepal Tourism Board reported that one Filipino traveler was missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, preliminary records showed that 644 travelers had been reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a briefing earlier that the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration were coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos. /apl

articles.title: Greek Orthodox priest and cult musician clarifies views on homosexuality
articles.summary:
Father Dionysios Tabakis says his views are those of Orthodox church, ‘nothing more, nothing less’

A Greek Orthodox priest whose home-recorded album of drone metal and religious dubstep has…

blocks.text: A Greek Orthodox priest whose home-recorded album of drone metal and religious dubstep has made him a cult figure in experimental music circles has issued a statement in which he has clarified his stance on homosexuality and the Greek radical right.

“As can be seen from my musical expression, I am in favour of unity, love, empathy and help for every needy, wronged and suffering person in life,” Father Dionysios Tabakis said in a public statement shared with the Guardian. “Whoever they are, whatever they believe, whether they are a saint or a sinner.”

The musician-priest’s political views have come under scrutiny over two blogposts he wrote in 2024, around the time that Greece became the first Christian Orthodox-majority country to legalise same-sex marriage.

The posts on the Orthodox Christian WordPress blog The Doors The Doors referred to gay people as “Sodomites”, gay marriage as a σοδομικὸ τερατούργημα (“sodomitic monstrosity”) and the same-sex marriage bill as “blasphemous”.
In a statement released on Tuesday, Tabakis said: “My view on homosexuality is the same as that of the Orthodox church for 2,000 years, nothing more, nothing less.

“We owe homosexual people love and acceptance because many have at times experienced great rejection from their environment, especially from their families. Over the years, homosexual people have also come to me for confession, and I have always received them with acceptance and love.”

In his statement, Tabakis still appears to refer to homosexuality as a sin: “I also always respect the freedom of my fellow man. After all, with freedom we sin, and with freedom we repent. It is better to sin with freedom than to be virtuous with oppression.”

The Orthodox priest’s debut album Paradise Metal earned a critics’ score of 7.6 from the experimental music bible Pitchfork, and Tabakis was profiled in international media including the Guardian and the New York Times.

In a separate controversy, a 2013 YouTube video that recently resurfaced on Greek social media showed Tabakis performing a sanctification at the opening of an office building for Golden Dawn, the neo-Nazi party that held seats in Greece’s parliament between 2015 and 2019.
The group was criminalised in 2020, and its leadership handed prison sentences for murder, assault and weapons possession.

In his statement, Tabakis said he performed the consecration in an official duty and at the request of his superior authority, and that he also attended other consecration ceremonies connected with other political and municipal groups.

Heat Crimes, the Greek record label that issued Tabakis’s debut album, told Pitchfork: “In Greek Orthodox practice, priests routinely perform agiasmos, blessing ceremonies for homes, shops, businesses, schools, public institutions, military facilities and other premises. A politician or political organisation inviting a local priest to bless new premises therefore does not, by itself, establish that either the priest or the church endorses that organisation. The important distinction is between performing a religious blessing and giving a political endorsement.”
In his statement, Tabakis said he was against nationalism “because it has only brought blood and wars to humanity”.

“The only ones who have interests in nationalism and borders are the weapons factories that spread death. Besides, my grandparents from Crete fought Hitler and nazism, so I follow their spirit. In fact, one reason I have removed the frets from my guitar is my mental need not to be confined to borders.”

articles.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
articles.summary: Police have arrested a 19-year-old male suspect after an incident in which two people were killed near the German capital.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said.
Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used.
It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school.
One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported.
The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported.
Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide".
"The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger.
"I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said.
State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence".
The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday.
Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come.
"We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said.
A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added.
Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany.

articles.title: Ratko Mladic, war criminal and former Bosnian Serb military leader, dead
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in Europe's worst atrocity since the Second World War, has died.

Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in Europe's worst atrocity since the Second World War, has died.
Was among trio convicted by UN court for massacring Muslims in former Yugoslavia

blocks.caption: Former Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic sits in the court room in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 8, 2021, when the United Nations court rejected an appeal of his convictions for genocide and other crimes. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in Europe's worst atrocity since the Second World War, has died.

Mladic died in UN custody on Thursday, his lawyer Dragan Ivetic said, without giving a cause. The former general had spent ​his last months in the hospital ward of the UN detention centre holding him in a suburb of The Hague, Ivetic added.

The slaughter in Srebrenica was the grisly culmination of a war that had lasted over three years, in which Mladic pounded the besieged capital Sarajevo daily with the artillery, tanks, mortars and heavy gunfire of his nationalist Serb army, killing 10,000 people.
The dead from Srebrenica were bulldozed into mass graves over four days in July 1995, some of them dug up and relocated to remote mountains so ‌as to hide evidence of the killings.

The goal, as determined by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), was "ethnic cleansing" — the forcible expulsion of Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian lands for a Greater Serbia.
The tribunal found that Mladic, together with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.

"I do not recognize this court," Mladic, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" by his opponents, said at an ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017 he shouted that it was "all lies."

blocks.caption: Bosnian Muslims carry coffins containing remains of 10 newly identified victims of the Srebrenica massacre, during a mass burial ceremony in Potocari, Bosnia on July 11. (Armin Durgut/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Karadzic, also convicted of genocide in 2016, and Mladic topped the ICTY wanted list for years ​after Western powers ended the war. But until Milosevic was toppled by a popular uprising in 2000, Mladic lived securely — if discreetly — in Belgrade.
Milosevic died in detention on March 11, 2006, ⁠a few months before a verdict in his four-year tribunal ⁠trial for genocide and other war crimes in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo.
Taunted peacekeepers

The army Mladic created to fight in Bosnia was a ‌model of ruthlessness. In some of the most horrific examples, prisoners suffocated in the heat after being forced to eat salt and denied water; were starved and raped in prison camps; were made to jump off a bridge and shot; and were gunned down at night by the hundreds after being driven out of detention with chemical gas.

"For me Mladic is a symbol of all horrible crimes that happened during the war — our girls were raped, and boys killed, only because they ⁠were Muslim," said Munira Subasic, whose son and husband were killed by Bosnian Serb forces after they overran Srebrenica.

Mladic had a cameraman film the blitz on the encircled enclave of Srebrenica, haranguing Dutch UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands. Srebrenica supposedly had "safe area" status, meant to protect civilians from ethnic cleansing.
"We give this town to the Serb ‌people as a gift," Mladic said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who once held the area as part of the Ottoman Empire.
When NATO tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops defiantly seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.

In November 1996 Mladic and top generals gave in to strong Western pressure that he step down as ordered by Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who succeeded ​Karadzic and was later jailed for her role in war crimes.
According to his son, Mladic was born in 1943, although official documents indicated a birthdate a year earlier.
He was an officer in the old communist Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia's disintegration began in 1991.

blocks.caption: A defaced mural depicting Mladic is shown in Belgrade on Thursday, with a Cyrillic inscription reading, 'Only God and no one else.' (Andrej Isakovic/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia's Muslim-led secession, Mladic was picked to command ⁠the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70 per cent of the landlocked country.

Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down as 22,000 troops of the UN Protection Force ⁠stood by more or less helplessly, with orders not to take sides.
A combination of Western pressure, covert American arms and training for Croats and Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladic's army. Determined NATO strikes did the rest.
Despite Western appeals, ⁠the reformists ruling Serbia after Milosevic's fall did not dare move against a man who ​was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.

items: Mladic's conviction in UN court upheld

blocks.text: When he was ​finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. His right arm ⁠was lame, the apparent result of an untreated stroke. He looked nothing like the burly general of the mid '90s.
He suffered a heart attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.
His appeal against conviction was rejected in 2021, as were repeated requests for his release on compassionate grounds, including in recent weeks.

articles.title: How a glacier collapse may have caused Nepal-Tibet disaster
articles.summary: BANGKOK — A huge piece of ice that fell thousands of meters from a glacier into a river below may have unleashed the disaster in Nepal and Tibet that killed at least 180 people. Here is what…

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality, along the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: BANGKOK — A huge piece of ice that fell thousands of meters from a glacier into a river below may have unleashed the disaster in Nepal and Tibet that killed at least 180 people.
Here is what experts believe happened so far:
Glacier collapse
A glacier collapse in Nepal’s mountains near Tibet appears to have triggered the disaster.
“A large chunk of glacier fell from about 5,200 meters (about 17,000 feet)… into a valley,” said Simon Cox, principal scientist at New Zealand’s GNS Science.
It “transformed into this raging mass of debris… where it picks up rocks and sediment and trees and anything in the way and fires it on down through the canyon,” he told AFP.
The wall of water first impacted a border post, as documented in terrifying CCTV footage showing mud and debris engulfing the area as people fled before it.
It then travelled downstream into Nepal, flooding villages and bringing down bridges and buildings.
Seismic activity
The glacier collapse was large enough to register as a seismic event, initially mistaken for an earthquake.
But after further analysis, the US Geological Survey determined “that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.
The collapse registered as a 5.2-magnitude “seismic event”, which took place at 8:37 am local time (0252 GMT).
Estimating just how much of the glacier collapsed will take time, Cox said, but it could range from “half a million cubic metres to tens of million cubic metres.”
Detective work
With the affected area largely inaccesible, experts are using satellite imagery and any available measurements on the ground to reconstruct the disaster.

“We can look at satellite imagery taken before and after the event, and try and see what has changed, essentially looking for what is missing from the mountains in the ‘after’ imagery,” said Lauren Vargo, a glaciologist at New Zealand’s Victoria University of Wellington.
Soon after the seismic activity was recorded, a nearby water monitoring station stopped transmitting, Nepali authorities said.
Stations downstream began going offline one by one, though water was registered reaching up to 12.3 metres high in Kalikhola, near the Tibet border at 2:14 pm, they added.
GLOFs
Early speculation suggested a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, a growing risk as glaciers melt due to climate change.
A GLOF occurs when a fragile debris wall holding back a lake of glacier melt suddenly collapses, unleashing the water behind it.
Some experts suggested a GLOF might have been involved.
“Water does flow within glaciers and flows beneath glaciers,” said Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast.
“But to my mind, the only reason why a large volume of water should all of a sudden flow down a valley is because it has been released,” he told AFP.

Other experts said they did not detect existing glacial lakes near the site of the glacier collapse, and theorised that water collected under the glacier might have cascaded down with the falling chunk.
The falling glacier ice could also have briefly dammed the river, collecting water behind it that was released when it dislodged.

Summer glacier melt upstream and monsoon rains would mean the rivers were already high, and the volume of water was also swelled by debris and mud picked up as it travelled kilometres from the initial collapse, added Cox.
Warnings
Nepali authorities first received word of a flood around 9:00 am local time, and began alerting areas along the Bhote Khoshi river to “stay on high alert and stay in safe areas”.
But is is unclear how many people received the warning, or how much time they would have had to respond.
“The reality is, if you are in a community underneath a large glacier and potentially a glacier lake where a GLOF could occur, then to some extent, it’s a ticking time bomb,” said McCallum.
And even for those receiving a warning, options would be limited, said Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio.
“Running will not help,” nor will trying to flee by vehicle, he told AFP, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination “like liquid concrete.”
The only solution is to climb up a hill, at least 20 feet (six meters), he estimated.
Climate change
While it is hard to immediately attribute any individual glacial event to climate change, the warming planet is a constant background stress on these ancient ice rivers, expert say.

Glaciers are retreating globally, creating disaster risks but also depriving downstream communities of vital water sources.
“The biggest way to mitigate the risk would be to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions to limit warming,” said Vargo. /dl

articles.title: Filipino traveler among hundreds missing in Nepal flash floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – A Filipino traveler remains missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on Wednesday evening, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday.…

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on August 27, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A Filipino traveler remains missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on Wednesday evening, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, its preliminary records showed that 644 travelers were reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.
Earlier, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro reported that there were no Filipino casualties in the flash flood as of Thursday morning, citing the Department of Foreign Affairs.
The board has yet to disclose any details about the Filipino tourist but noted that the information is still being verified and crosschecked with travel agencies and other local authorities.

“Following the devastating flash flood… Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Government of Nepal, Nepal Tourism Board, Tourist Police and tourism stakeholders are working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of tourists or travelers who were at or travelling through the affected areas,” the Nepal Tourism Board said in a statement.
At least 165 deaths were reported after the flash flooding, and the riversides of the four affected districts were left severely damaged. /dl

articles.title: Nepali PM Balendra Shah heads to flood-hit Nuwakot to assess damage
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah left early Thursday for a field inspection of flood-hit areas in Bidur, Nuwakot. Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal is…

blocks.caption: Courtesy of Prime Minister’s Office

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah left early Thursday for a field inspection of flood-hit areas in Bidur, Nuwakot.
Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal is accompanying Shah on the visit.
According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the team left Kathmandu by road at 9:30am for Bidur, one of the areas worst affected by the flooding.

During the visit, Shah and Lamsal will assess the physical damage firsthand and meet local officials, security agencies and elected representatives to discuss relief, rehabilitation and the restoration of disrupted infrastructure.
They are also expected to issue instructions to speed up the delivery of relief to affected communities and accelerate infrastructure reconstruction, the secretariat said.
Shah has been closely involved in the rescue and relief efforts since the flood entered the Bhotekoshi river from Tibet and caused damage downstream on Wednesday. /dl

articles.title: Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, dies in The Hague
articles.summary:
Bosnian Serb commander responsible for Srebrenica massacre dies in prison while serving life sentence for genocide

From the archive:

blocks.text: Ratko Mladić, the infamous Serbian general who was serving a life sentence for genocide committed during the Bosnian war, has died in prison in The Hague.

Mladić had been one of the main architects of the policy of ethnic cleansing during the Bosnian war. He was convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 killing of at least 8,000 Muslims in the UN-designated “safe area” Srebrenica, the worst massacre in Europe since the second world war.
Mladić, who was nicknamed the “Butcher of Bosnia”, had been in ill health after having a series of strokes.
A UN international tribunal confirmed Mladić’s death, saying he had died in hospital in The Hague earlier in the day.

“Mladić passed away today while hospitalised in The Hague,” the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals said in a statement, adding that judge Graciela Gatti Santana had ordered “a full inquiry into the circumstances” of his death.

Described by the former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al-Hussein as “the epitome of evil” after his conviction, Mladić was one of the most notorious figures of the war that killed more than 100,000 people and left more than 1 million homeless.

blocks.caption: The Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadžić (right) with Mladić in 1995. Karadžić was also sentenced to life imprisonment for genocide and war crimes.  Photograph: Ranko Cukovic/Reuters

blocks.text: He commanded his troops to “scorch the brains” of Bosnian Muslim people and had boasted of being a “Serbian god”.
The news of Mladić’s death was first broken on Serbian state television after his son, Darko, had spoken earlier about his father’s declining health.
Mladić was sentenced by a UN tribunal to life imprisonment in 2017 over genocide and war crimes committed during Bosnia’s 1990s war. He was arrested in Serbia in 2011 after 16 years on the run.

The slaughter in Srebrenica was the culmination of a brutal war that had lasted more than three ⁠years, during which Mladić oversaw the siege of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, which was pounded daily by artillery, tank and sniper fire, killing 10,000 people.

The goal of the Serbian leadership, which Mladić was tasked with implementing – as determined ⁠by the UN’s international criminal tribunal for ⁠the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) – was the forcible expulsion of ​Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian land for the creation of a greater Serbia.

The tribunal found that Mladić, together with the late Serbian president Slobodan Milošević and the Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadžić, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan.

blocks.caption: Slobodan Milošević. Photograph: Srdjan Ilic/AP

blocks.text: “I do not recognise this court,” Mladić said at an ⁠ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced, he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!”

The Serbian campaign culminated in the horror of Srebrenica when, after the withdrawal of Dutch UN peacekeeping forces, thousands of Bosnian men and boys were rounded up, killed and their bodies bulldozed into mass graves.

blocks.caption: Mladić (front left) entering Srebrenica in 1995. Photograph: Sipa Press/Rex Shutterstock

blocks.text: Mladić had the siege filmed to show him praising his “lads” and haranguing the UN peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands.
“We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who had once held the area as part ‌of the Ottoman empire.
The next day, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for slaughter.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A screengrab from 12 July 1995 shows Mladić speaking to a young Muslim boy after he had assured residents of Srebrenica they would be safe. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: When Nato tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited airstrikes, his troops seized UN peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets.

The son of a second world war partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladić was, according to his family, born in March 1943 in the tiny Bosnian village of Bozinovici, putting his age at death at 83 (though official documents recorded his date of birth a year earlier, in 1942).
Mladić was an officer in the communist Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia’s disintegration began in 1991.
When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia’s Muslim-led secession, Mladić was chosen to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70% of the country.

Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down, as 22,000 troops with the UN Protection Force stood by, more or less helplessly, under orders not to take sides.

blocks.caption: Ediba Salihović raises her hands as she reacts with other Bosnian women upon hearing the sentence at the end of Mladić’s trial in Potočari, near Srebrenica, in November 2017. Photograph: Amel Emrić/AP

blocks.text: A combination of western pressure, Nato strikes and covert US arms and training for Croats and ⁠Muslims gradually turned the tide against Mladić’s army. After the war, Mladić went into hiding, with the reformists ruling post-conflict Serbia not daring ​to move against a man who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs.

Mladić continued to insist he was “a simple man” chosen to protect his people. When he was finally arrested in 2011, he put up no resistance. He had a heart ​attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man.
This month, a UN doctor said Mladić’s death “may occur at any time”, possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected.

blocks.caption: Munira Subašić (pictured in 2019), from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs. Photograph: Anadolu Agency/Getty

blocks.text: Munira Subašić, from the Mothers of Srebrenica group, said she deplored that Mladić’s crimes were still being denied by many Bosnian Serbs. “Today, a major war criminal died, the criminal of the Balkans,” Subašić said. But while 31 years later mothers of victims were “still carrying the pain in our souls … we are still listening to denials, we are still listening to how Ratko Mladić was a hero for the Serbs”.

Elizabeth Evenson, the international justice director at Human Rights Watch, said: “The death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb army commander found guilty of genocide, including the massacre of up to 8,000 Bosnian men and boys after the fall of Srebrenica, Bosnia, in July 1995, is a reminder of the ongoing need for justice, truth, and reparations in the western Balkans.
“Full accountability for such terrible crimes, in Bosnia and elsewhere, demands commitment by governments to justice, even decades after the events themselves.”

blocks.text: UN Secretary-General António Guterres has expressed condolences over the loss of life and widespread destruction caused by severe flooding in Nepal and China on Wednesday.
Guterres was saddened by reports of deaths and people still missing, as well as extensive damage caused by the floods, his spokesperson said in a statement.
He offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery. He also expressed solidarity with all those affected.
In Nepal, the United Nations is supporting the government-led response, including efforts to assess the extent of the disaster and deliver immediate assistance, the statement said.
UN agencies and humanitarian partners are mobilising supplies and personnel to support affected communities.
Guterres praised emergency responders working to save lives and reaffirmed the UN’s readiness to provide further assistance. /dl
